records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.text: This part uses several constructions that share the word quantum but have different definitions. We begin with a linear-algebra question: how does one compare two ways of combining three vector spaces that carry symmetries? The answer supplies the local weights used later to build topological invariants. The opening example needs only tensor products and changes of basis; the representation-theoretic terms are introduced as they arise. Later subsections also use elementary complex analysis and the geometry already discussed. No physical interpretation is needed for the finite sums or special-function identities.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.text: The organizing operation is cutting and gluing. A decomposition gives intermediate labels; changing the decomposition gives a change-of-basis matrix or integral kernel. The quantum constructions make these operations exact. We first follow this idea from angular momentum to Euclidean tetrahedra and Regge’s description of curvature, and then to a finite sum that is independent of the triangulation. Later we turn to hyperbolic geometry: the figure-eight knot supplies an explicit finite sum whose growth gives the volume of two regular ideal tetrahedra.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.1 Six labels: recoupling and tetrahedral weights
records.text: 10.1 Six labels: recoupling and tetrahedral weights

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why start with representations?
records.text: Why start with representations?

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why start with representations?
records.text: A triangulated three-manifold has many descriptions: its tetrahedra can be assembled in different orders, and the triangulation itself can be changed. To build an invariant from local data, we need weights with exact rules for comparing these descriptions. Representation theory provides such rules. Combining representations uses tensor products; decomposing them into simpler pieces introduces intermediate labels; changing the order of decomposition produces a matrix. The identities satisfied by these matrices will become the identities needed for changing a triangulation. This is the reason for the algebra in this subsection.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why start with representations?
records.text: The Lie algebra 𝔰 𝔩 2 = 𝔰 𝔩 2 ( ℂ ) is the vector space of traceless 2 × 2 complex matrices, with bracket [ X , Y ] = X Y − Y X . A representation on a vector space V assigns to each X a linear operator ρ ( X ) on V , linearly in X , so that ρ ( [ X , Y ] ) = [ ρ ( X ) , ρ ( Y ) ] . It is irreducible if no nonzero proper subspace is preserved by all these operators. Thus an irreducible representation is a building block for a symmetry action.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why start with representations?
records.text: The finite-dimensional irreducibles are V j = Sym ⁡ 2 j ( ℂ 2 ) , j = 0 , 1 2 , 1 , 3 2 , … , dim ⁡ V j = 2 j + 1 . Here Sym ⁡ m ( ℂ 2 ) is the space of symmetric m -fold tensors on ℂ 2 ; its basis has one element for each possible number 0 , … , m of copies of the second standard basis vector. In particular, V 0 = ℂ is the trivial representation and V 1 / 2 = ℂ 2 is the usual matrix action. The name spin for j comes from rotations: the compact group S U ( 2 ) double-covers S O ( 3 ) , and the complexification of its Lie algebra is 𝔰 𝔩 2 . Integer spins descend to S O ( 3 ) ; nonintegral half-integer spins need the double cover. We use this familiar family because its tensor-product rule is especially explicit. At this stage j is a representation label, not an edge length.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Combining two building blocks.
records.text: Combining two building blocks.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Combining two building blocks.
records.text: On a tensor product the infinitesimal symmetry acts on both factors: X ( v ⊗ w ) = ( X v ) ⊗ w + v ⊗ ( X w ) . The Clebsch–Gordan rule says V a ⊗ V b ≅ ⨁ s = | a − b | a + b V s , s increases in steps of 1 . Each allowed V s occurs once. Equivalently, the triple ( a , b , s ) is admissible when it satisfies the triangle inequalities and a + b + s is an integer. The direct-sum sign means that every vector has a unique sum of components in these invariant subspaces.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Combining two building blocks.
records.text: For example, V 1 / 2 ⊗ V 1 / 2 = V 0 ⊕ V 1 , 2 ⋅ 2 = 1 + 3 . Choose an orthonormal basis e + , e − of ℂ 2 . The one-dimensional summand is spanned by e + ⊗ e − − e − ⊗ e + 2 , and the three-dimensional summand is the symmetric subspace, with basis e + ⊗ e + , e + ⊗ e − + e − ⊗ e + 2 , e − ⊗ e − . The antisymmetric vector is fixed by S L 2 because its transformation factor is the determinant, which is one. This gives a concrete meaning to a decomposition into irreducibles.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What the symbols B and F mean.
records.text: What the symbols B and F mean.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What the symbols B and F mean.
records.text: Now combine three factors and specify a desired output type V d . The vector space H d = Hom ⁡ 𝔰 𝔩 2 ( V d , V a ⊗ V b ⊗ V c ) consists of linear maps that commute with the symmetry action. Such a map is called an intertwiner . The dimension of H d counts how many copies of V d occur in the triple tensor product.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What the symbols B and F mean.
records.text: Choose, once and for all, a normalized inclusion C s a b : V s → V a ⊗ V b for each admissible triple. For example, C 0 1 / 2 , 1 / 2 ( 1 ) can be the antisymmetric unit vector just displayed. There are two ways to compose these inclusions: B s ( a b ) c = ( C s a b ⊗ i d V c ) C d s c , B t a ( b c ) = ( i d V a ⊗ C t b c ) C d a t . Both are maps from V d to the same triple tensor product. The parentheses record which two factors were combined first. The index s ranges over labels for which ( a , b , s ) and ( s , c , d ) are admissible; t ranges over labels for which ( b , c , t ) and ( a , t , d ) are admissible. Each collection is a basis of H d .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What the symbols B and F mean.
records.text: The letter B therefore denotes a basis intertwiner . The numbers F s t a b c ; d are defined to be the coefficients that express the first basis in the second: B s ( a b ) c = ∑ t F s t a b c ; d B t a ( b c ) . (10.1) For fixed a , b , c , d , this is an ordinary finite change-of-basis matrix, with row index s and column index t . The sum runs over the allowed intermediate types, not over vectors of V t . Normalization and phase choices for the inclusions matter: changing them changes the entries of F . One may use the S U ( 2 ) -invariant Hermitian inner products to make the bases orthonormal; F is then unitary.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A complete 2 × 2 example.
records.text: A complete 2 × 2 example.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A complete 2 × 2 example.
records.text: Take a = b = c = d = 1 2 . Applying the two-factor rule twice gives V 1 / 2 ⊗ 3 ≅ V 3 / 2 ⊕ V 1 / 2 ⊕ V 1 / 2 . Thus H 1 / 2 has dimension two. In the first basis we distinguish the copies by whether the first pair has type s = 0 or s = 1 ; in the second we use the type t = 0 or t = 1 of the last pair.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A complete 2 × 2 example.
records.text: The whole calculation can be seen in three tensor coordinates. Write u = e + ⊗ e + ⊗ e − , v = e + ⊗ e − ⊗ e + , w = e − ⊗ e + ⊗ e + . An intertwiner from V 1 / 2 is determined by its value on e + . For the following phase choices those values are B 0 ( a b ) c ( e + ) = v − w 2 , B 1 ( a b ) c ( e + ) = 2 u − v − w 6 , B 0 a ( b c ) ( e + ) = u − v 2 , B 1 a ( b c ) ( e + ) = u + v − 2 w 6 . To see why these vectors describe the two copies, the raising matrix ( 0 1 0 0 ) sends each of u , v , w to e + ⊗ e + ⊗ e + under the tensor-product action. It kills precisely the combinations whose three coefficients sum to zero. These form a two-dimensional space; applying its transpose, the lowering matrix, supplies the corresponding images of e − . The vectors above give two orthonormal bases of this same space. Their subscripts 0 , 1 record the antisymmetric or symmetric behavior of the chosen pair.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A complete 2 × 2 example.
records.text: Taking their inner products gives ( B 0 ( a b ) c B 1 ( a b ) c ) = ( − 1 2 3 2 3 2 1 2 ) ( B 0 a ( b c ) B 1 a ( b c ) ) . For instance, the upper-left entry is ⟨ ( v − w ) / 2 , ( u − v ) / 2 ⟩ = − 1 / 2 . The rows have norm one and are perpendicular, as a change between orthonormal bases requires. Although tensor products are associative, the bases selected by the two decompositions are different. Recoupling is the operation of converting between them. There is no asymptotic approximation in this example.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: From a basis change to a tetrahedron.
records.text: From a basis change to a tetrahedron.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: From a basis change to a tetrahedron.
records.text: The coefficients in (10.1) depend on six labels a , b , c , d , s , t . With conventional dimension and sign factors they are the 6 j -symbols . The name records these six representation labels; it does not refer to the size of the matrix. The four admissible triples ( a , b , s ) , ( s , c , d ) , ( b , c , t ) , ( a , t , d ) can be assigned to the four faces of a tetrahedron. Explicitly, on a tetrahedron with vertices 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , put a , b , s , d , c , t on edges 12 , 23 , 13 , 14 , 34 , 24 , respectively. Every face then carries one of the four triples. This explains the tetrahedral arrangement of a recoupling coefficient. Its interpretation as a metric tetrahedron requires an additional asymptotic statement.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: From a basis change to a tetrahedron.
records.text: Physics: from angular momentum to quantum geometry. In quantum mechanics a state is a vector, and a measurable quantity is represented by a self-adjoint operator. Rotations are generated by the three angular-momentum operators J x , J y , J z . For spin 1 2 these are Pauli’s familiar matrices: J x = ℏ 2 ( 0 1 1 0 ) , J y = ℏ 2 ( 0 − i i 0 ) , J z = ℏ 2 ( 1 0 0 − 1 ) . Here ℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2 π . They satisfy [ J x , J y ] = i ℏ J z and its cyclic analogues; after complexification this is the 𝔰 𝔩 2 algebra above. On V j , the squared total angular momentum 𝑱 2 = J x 2 + J y 2 + J z 2 has value ℏ 2 j ( j + 1 ) , and J z has the 2 j + 1 values ℏ m , m = − j , − j + 1 , … , j . Thus the representation label has a direct physical meaning [ 134 , Section 4.2] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: From a basis change to a tetrahedron.
records.text: For two independent spins, total angular momentum is 𝑱 ( 1 ) ⊗ I + I ⊗ 𝑱 ( 2 ) . The decomposition V 1 / 2 ⊗ V 1 / 2 = V 0 ⊕ V 1 says that their combined spin can be 0 (the singlet ) or 1 (the triplet ). For three spins one can first measure the total spin of the first pair, or of the last pair. These are different measurement bases. Wigner’s 6 j -symbols, also expressed as Racah recoupling coefficients, convert between them [ 135 , Section 1] . In our 2 × 2 example, prepare the normalized state B 0 ( a b ) c ( e + ) . Measuring the last pair gives t = 0 with probability | − 1 / 2 | 2 = 1 / 4 , and t = 1 with probability | 3 / 2 | 2 = 3 / 4 . The entries of F are probability amplitudes ; their squared moduli are probabilities.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: From a basis change to a tetrahedron.
records.text: The link to gravity is a further step. General relativity describes gravity through geometry; Regge replaces smooth geometry by glued flat simplices. In the large-spin limit a 6 j -symbol contains the geometric action of one Euclidean tetrahedron. Multiplying these amplitudes and summing internal labels therefore suggests a discrete quantum sum over geometries. Ponzano–Regge develops this idea in three-dimensional Euclidean gravity, and Turaev–Viro provides a finite deformation [ 132 ] . This is a model in three dimensions, not a derivation of four-dimensional physical gravity. The next paragraphs explain each step of the geometric connection.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Regge’s starting point: flat pieces can make a curved space.
records.text: Regge’s starting point: flat pieces can make a curved space.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Regge’s starting point: flat pieces can make a curved space.
records.text: Before interpreting a quantum symbol geometrically, consider a purely classical construction. Give each edge e of a triangulated three-manifold a positive length ℓ e , such that the six lengths of every tetrahedron determine a nondegenerate Euclidean tetrahedron. Glue the tetrahedra along matching faces. A shared face has the same three edge lengths on either side, so the identification is an isometry. There is no curvature inside a tetrahedron, and an interior point of a face also has a Euclidean neighborhood. Curvature can occur around an edge.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Regge’s starting point: flat pieces can make a curved space.
records.text: To see it, cut transversely through an interior edge. Each incident tetrahedron contributes a planar sector whose angle is its interior dihedral angle θ e Δ . The sectors fit into an ordinary flat disk precisely when their angles add to 2 π . The deficit angle ε e = 2 π − ∑ Δ ∋ e θ e Δ measures the failure of this condition. A positive deficit gives a cone with a missing wedge; a negative deficit gives an excess of angle. For example, a regular Euclidean tetrahedron has interior dihedral angle arccos ⁡ ( 1 / 3 ) . Five such tetrahedra around an edge give ε = 2 π − 5 arccos ⁡ ( 1 / 3 ) ≃ 0.12838822 radians . The individual pieces are flat, but their gluing is curved. There is no claim that five regular tetrahedra fit flatly around an edge.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Regge’s starting point: flat pieces can make a curved space.
records.text: This is the principle of Regge calculus [ 130 ] . In dimension three its curvature contribution is an edge length times a deficit angle. For a region with boundary, write E i n t and E ∂ for the interior and boundary edges. The zero-cosmological-constant action, with an overall physical constant suppressed, is S R ( ℓ ) = ∑ e ∈ E i n t ℓ e ε e + ∑ e ∈ E ∂ ℓ e ψ e , ψ e = π − ∑ Δ ∋ e θ e Δ . The boundary angle ψ e measures bending away from a flat half-space. The word action means a function whose stationary points give the equations of the model. Here the variables are the interior edge lengths; the boundary lengths are held fixed. The Euclidean Schläfli identity on each tetrahedron is ∑ e ⊂ Δ ℓ e ⁡ d θ e Δ = 0 . It cancels all the angle-variation terms in ⁡ d S R , leaving ⁡ d S R = ∑ e ∈ E i n t ε e ⁡ d ℓ e . Thus the stationary equations are ε e = 0 : locally flat geometry, although global topology and holonomy can still be nontrivial. This particularly simple conclusion is for three-dimensional gravity with zero cosmological constant. Regge’s original scheme also applies in dimension four, where curvature is concentrated on triangular faces and the corresponding weights are their areas.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Regge’s starting point: flat pieces can make a curved space.
records.text: For a single tetrahedron all six edges lie on the boundary. Its action is consequently S Δ = ∑ e ⊂ Δ ℓ e Θ e , Θ e = π − θ e Δ . Here Θ e is the exterior dihedral angle, the angle between outward normals to the adjacent faces. Keeping interior and exterior angles distinct will determine the phase in the next formula.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The Ponzano–Regge bridge: a Euclidean action inside a 6 j -symbol.
records.text: The Ponzano–Regge bridge: a Euclidean action inside a 6 j -symbol.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The Ponzano–Regge bridge: a Euclidean action inside a 6 j -symbol.
records.text: Return to the ordinary, undeformed Wigner 6 j -symbol, with the usual symmetric normalization rather than the raw entries of F . Choose six admissible positive spins j e 0 which are the edge lengths of a nondegenerate Euclidean tetrahedron, and let j e ( k ) = k j e 0 for positive integers k . The lengths appearing in the semiclassical formula have the half-unit shift ℓ e ( k ) = j e ( k ) + 1 2 . For large k these also determine a Euclidean tetrahedron Δ k . Write V k > 0 for its volume and Θ e ( k ) for its exterior dihedral angles. The Ponzano–Regge asymptotic formula is { 6 j } 𝒋 ( k ) = 1 12 π V k cos ⁡ ( ∑ e ℓ e ( k ) Θ e ( k ) + π 4 ) + o ( k − 3 / 2 ) . Ponzano and Regge proposed this relation [ 131 ] ; Roberts proved the nondegenerate Euclidean asymptotic and explains the equivalence of the shifted-length formulation used here with his fixed-shape formulation [ 91 , Theorem 1 and Section 6.1] . Lengths in this formula are measured in the dimensionless units set by the spins; inserting physical units restores the action scale in the phase.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The Ponzano–Regge bridge: a Euclidean action inside a 6 j -symbol.
records.text: Why is this surprising? The left side is a coefficient obtained by combining representations. The phase on the right is precisely the single-tetrahedron Regge action S Δ , while its amplitude contains the Euclidean volume. The cosine combines two opposite oscillatory phases, associated with the two orientations of the geometric configuration. This parallels semiclassical quantum mechanics: an action contributes a phase e i S / ℏ , and rapidly varying phases cancel except near stationary configurations [ 135 ] . This is an oscillatory large-spin limit; it does not assert exponential growth with hyperbolic volume. The Euclidean realization hypothesis matters: face triangle inequalities alone do not guarantee a Euclidean tetrahedron, and the displayed approximation does not cover a flat tetrahedron.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The Ponzano–Regge bridge: a Euclidean action inside a 6 j -symbol.
records.text: A regular tetrahedron makes the formula easy to evaluate. Put the same integer spin N on every edge. Then L = N + 1 2 , V = L 3 6 2 , Θ = arccos ⁡ ( − 1 / 3 ) , and the leading term is cos ⁡ ( 6 L Θ + π / 4 ) / 12 π V . For comparison, the exact symbol in this case is the rational number { N N N N N N } = ( N ! ) 6 ( ( 3 N + 1 ) ! ) 2 ∑ z = 3 N 4 N ( − 1 ) z ( z + 1 ) ! ( ( z − 3 N ) ! ) 4 ( ( 4 N − z ) ! ) 3 . This is the equilateral specialization of the finite Racah formula [ 136 , Eq. 34.4.2] . Rounded values are

The differences illustrate the approximation, not a certified error bound or a proof of its asymptotic order. Absolute differences are appropriate because the cosine can be close to zero. The regular-tetrahedron driver is described in the computational companion guide linked at the end of this section.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why sum over labels at all?
records.text: Why sum over labels at all?

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why sum over labels at all?
records.text: In the classical picture, choosing lengths specifies a geometry; varying them gives the Regge equations. A quantum construction asks instead for an amplitude with specified boundary data, allowing the unobserved interior data to vary. The elementary rule is already familiar from multiplying matrices: to compose amplitudes A and B , one sums ∑ s A a s B s b over the intermediate state s . Gluing many pieces applies this same rule repeatedly.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: Why sum over labels at all?
records.text: This suggests putting a 6 j -amplitude on each tetrahedron, multiplying the amplitudes for the pieces, and summing the labels of internal edges. Closing an internal representation index supplies a dimension factor: tr ⁡ ( I V j ) = 2 j + 1 . Precise gluing conventions also fix signs and normalization. In a large-spin geometric regime, the phases of the local weights are Regge actions, so this becomes a candidate for a discrete quantum sum over geometries. This is the motivation for the Ponzano–Regge state sum. Its ordinary spin labels are unbounded, however, and the resulting sum can diverge. A simple cutoff does not automatically preserve invariance under changes of triangulation [ 132 , Sections 2.1–2.4] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What Turaev–Viro repairs.
records.text: What Turaev–Viro repairs.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What Turaev–Viro repairs.
records.text: We would like a finite construction that retains the exact gluing rules, so the answer belongs to the manifold rather than to its chosen triangulation. Turaev–Viro achieves this by changing the recoupling theory and its allowed labels together. It uses a quantum group at a root of unity; it is not simply the ordinary 6 j -sum with all sufficiently large spins discarded.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What Turaev–Viro repairs.
records.text: For U q a l g ( 𝔰 𝔩 2 ) , the deformation parameter q a l g changes the tensor-product rules and the recoupling coefficients. The explicit formulas use quantum integers and factorials, beginning with [ n ] q a l g = q a l g n − q a l g − n q a l g − q a l g − 1 , [ n ] q a l g → n ( q a l g → 1 ) . (10.2) Thus [ 2 ] q a l g = q a l g + q a l g − 1 tends to 2 . The analogue of closing an ordinary representation index now gives the quantum dimension d j = [ 2 j + 1 ] q a l g . The full theory specifies the tensor products and their compatible recoupling maps; replacing factorials alone is not its definition. At the compact root q a l g = e π i / r , with integer r ≥ 3 , the resulting finite fusion theory has labels j = 0 , 1 2 , … , r − 2 2 , d j = sin ⁡ ( ( 2 j + 1 ) π / r ) sin ⁡ ( π / r ) . A triple is admissible when it satisfies the triangle inequalities, has integral total spin, and obeys a + b + c ≤ r − 2 . Both the recoupling coefficients and these rules depend on the same parameter; their compatibility preserves the identities needed for gluing [ 26 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A concrete gluing test: two tetrahedra or three.
records.text: A concrete gluing test: two tetrahedra or three.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A concrete gluing test: two tetrahedra or three.
records.text: Take a triangular bipyramid with base vertices 1 , 2 , 3 and tips 4 , 5 . One triangulation consists of tetrahedra 1234 and 1235 , which share the face 123 . Another consists of 1245 , 2345 and 3145 , meeting around the new interior edge 45 . The boundary of the solid is the same in both descriptions.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A concrete gluing test: two tetrahedra or three.
records.text: Fix the labels on that boundary. On the two-tetrahedron side there is no interior edge label to choose. On the three-tetrahedron side the label on 45 is internal, so it must be summed over its allowed values, with its dimension weight. The recoupling identity says that these two evaluations agree, with the prescribed normalizations. It does not say that one arbitrary term on one side equals one arbitrary term on the other.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: A concrete gluing test: two tetrahedra or three.
records.text: Algebraically this is the pentagon identity : four tensor factors have five parenthesizations, and the two routes around this pentagon give the same change of basis. Thus an associativity identity becomes a 2 ↔ 3 move on tetrahedra. An additional identity handles subdivision of one tetrahedron into four by inserting an interior vertex; it accounts for the vertex normalization. These local moves, with orthogonality of the recoupling maps, establish independence of the triangulation in the Turaev–Viro construction [ 133 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The state sum, with its ingredients now identified.
records.text: The state sum, with its ingredients now identified.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The state sum, with its ingredients now identified.
records.text: For a closed triangulated three-manifold the construction has the form Z r ( M ) = C r ( T ) ∑ admissible edge labels 𝒋 ∏ e ∈ E ( T ) d j e ∏ Δ ∈ T { 6 j } Δ , 𝒋 . (10.3) Here M is the manifold, T its triangulation, and E ( T ) the set of edges. A state 𝒋 assigns an allowed label j e to every edge, with an admissible triple on every face. For one state, multiply a quantum dimension d j e for each edge and a quantum 6 j -weight for each tetrahedron Δ . Then sum over states and multiply by the normalization C r ( T ) required by the subdivision move. The displayed notation suppresses convention-dependent sign and normalization factors in the local weights; these must be chosen consistently with the gluing identities [ 133 ] [ 38 , Sections 2.2–2.3] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: The state sum, with its ingredients now identified.
records.text: There are finitely many edges and finitely many allowed labels, so this sum is finite. It is often called a partition function : the total amplitude obtained by summing the weights of the allowed states. For a manifold with boundary one instead fixes the boundary labels and sums only the interior labels, using the associated boundary normalization. The result is an amplitude depending on those boundary data; gluing boundaries contracts their shared data. This is why the algebraic sum is useful both as a topological invariant and as a model of a quantum geometric amplitude.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What changes when we turn to hyperbolic geometry?
records.text: What changes when we turn to hyperbolic geometry?

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What changes when we turn to hyperbolic geometry?
records.text: We have followed three distinct steps: classical lengths give Regge’s geometry; large ordinary spins reveal a Euclidean action inside a local recoupling coefficient; a compatible finite quantum deformation makes a triangulation-independent state sum. At finite labels a state remains algebraic data, and need not specify a Euclidean metric.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: What changes when we turn to hyperbolic geometry?
records.text: The geometry of an asymptotic limit also depends on how the quantum parameter and labels vary. The compact-root scaling studied by Taylor–Woodward leads to spherical tetrahedra [ 26 ] ; the hyperbolic volume limits and noncompact constructions below use their own specified regimes. One should therefore carry the method forward—identify local weights, gluing identities and their geometric asymptotics—without replacing Euclidean by hyperbolic lengths in the Ponzano–Regge formula. The following subsection names the invariants and fixes the volume-limit conventions needed for that next step.

records.text: The first four objects are topological invariants with their prescribed normalizations. The last two supply analytic kernels and functions that enter the comparisons in this monograph. In particular, a local 6 j -weight is not already a three-manifold invariant.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.2 The invariants and their volume limits
records.text: The knot construction begins with a braid whose closure is the knot. A crossing acts by a braiding matrix on the tensor product of the strand representations; the Yang–Baxter equation gives the braid relation. A quantum trace, adjusted to the representation theory, closes the strands, and the prescribed normalization handles the moves that change the braid presentation [ 29 , Section 2] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.2 The invariants and their volume limits
records.text: For the colored Jones polynomial, the color N denotes the N -dimensional representation at generic parameter. We use the reduced normalization J N ( unknot ; q J ) = 1 , and specialize only after forming that polynomial. Murakami–Murakami identify this specialization with Kashaev’s invariant [ 82 ] . For a hyperbolic knot, the volume conjecture is lim N → ∞ 2 π N log ⁡ | J N ( K ; e 2 π i / N ) | = Vol ⁡ ( S 3 \ K ) . (10.4) The right side is the ordinary three-dimensional hyperbolic volume, not a volume of moduli space. The assertion concerns a sequence in which both the color and the root change.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.2 The invariants and their volume limits
records.text: The closed-manifold version used in Section 16 is the Chen–Yang asymptotic at their root ζ r = e 2 π i / r , with r odd: 4 π r log ⁡ | R T r ( M ; ζ r ) | → Vol ⁡ ( M ) , 2 π r log ⁡ T V r ( M ; ζ r ) → Vol ⁡ ( M ) . (10.5) These statements are conjectural in general, with theorems for specified families; the hyperbolic fillings of the figure-eight used later are covered by Wong–Yang [ 40 ] . The doubling relation between matching RT and TV theories explains the factor two between their leading logarithms. Exact identities require consistent choices: generally T V 𝒞 is the RT invariant of the categorical center, and the familiar modulus-square formula holds in the matching unitary modular setting [ 27 ] . One should not equate differently normalized S U ( 2 ) and S O ( 3 ) versions without conversion.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.2 The invariants and their volume limits
records.text: There are two root-of-unity subtleties. First, authors use parameters differing by a square: in a common convention q J = q a l g 2 . Within Chen–Yang’s conventions, the volume root e 2 π i / r differs from the standard compact root e π i / r ; the latter belongs to a different asymptotic problem [ 38 ] . Second, even where the numerical roots agree after changing notation, the colors may not belong to the same theory. At q a l g = e π i / N , the N -dimensional color has [ N ] q a l g = 0 and lies outside the retained simple labels of the level- N − 2 compact fusion theory. Reducing J N first and then specializing is essential. Thus the Kashaev limit should not be read as an allowed fixed-color observable in that finite unitary theory.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.3 A complete example: the figure-eight knot
records.text: For the figure-eight knot 4 1 , the root specialization is an especially simple positive sum: J N ( 4 1 ; e 2 π i / N ) = ∑ k = 0 N − 1 P N , k , P N , k = ∏ j = 1 k 4 sin ⁡ 2 π j N , P N , 0 = 1 . (10.6) Kashaev gives the product formula [ 28 , eqs. (2.2), (2.5)] . The following elementary asymptotic proof is presented by Murakami and credited there to Ekholm [ 29 , Section 3.2] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.3 A complete example: the figure-eight knot
records.text: The ratio of consecutive products is P N , k P N , k − 1 = 4 sin ⁡ 2 π k N . It is less than one before N / 6 , greater than one between N / 6 and 5 N / 6 , and less than one afterward. The global maximum is therefore attained at m N = ⌊ 5 N / 6 ⌋ , allowing an adjacent tie. To compare with the initial value 1 , use the elementary identity P N , N − 1 = N 2 : evaluating ( z N − 1 ) / ( z − 1 ) = ∏ j = 1 N − 1 ( z − e 2 π i j / N ) at z = 1 and taking absolute squares proves it. Positivity now gives P N , m N ≤ J N ( 4 1 ; e 2 π i / N ) ≤ N P N , m N . The two logarithmic bounds differ by log ⁡ N , which disappears after division by N . The remaining Riemann sum has an integrable logarithmic singularity at zero, and yields lim N → ∞ 1 N log ⁡ J N ( 4 1 ; e 2 π i / N ) = ∫ 0 5 / 6 log ⁡ ( 4 sin ⁡ 2 π x ) ⁡ d x . (10.7) The endpoint causes no difficulty: subtract 2 log ⁡ x near zero; the remaining function is continuous and the logarithmic part is controlled by Stirling’s formula.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.3 A complete example: the figure-eight knot
records.text: Define the Lobachevsky function by Λ ( θ ) = − ∫ 0 θ log ⁡ | 2 sin ⁡ t | ⁡ d t . Its elementary symmetry and duplication identities give lim N → ∞ 2 π N log ⁡ J N ( 4 1 ; e 2 π i / N ) = − 4 Λ ( 5 π / 6 ) = 4 Λ ( π / 6 ) = 6 Λ ( π / 3 ) = 2 v 3 = Vol ⁡ ( S 3 \ 4 1 ) , (10.8) where v 3 = 3 Λ ( π / 3 ) is the volume of a regular ideal tetrahedron. The complete figure-eight complement consists of two such tetrahedra. Its volume is approximately 2.02988321 .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.3 A complete example: the figure-eight knot
records.text: This calculation already displays the mechanism: an exact quantum sum, a logarithmic classical phase, a dominant critical point, and a geometric critical value. It also shows why selecting the critical point matters. For f ( t ) = ∫ 0 t log ⁡ ( 4 sin ⁡ 2 π x ) ⁡ d x , the stationary point t = 1 / 6 is a minimum, while t = 5 / 6 is the relevant maximum. Here positivity controls the entire sum. Complex-valued sums and integrals require a separate analysis of their contributing critical points and possible cancellation.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.4 Why dilogarithms occur
records.text: An elementary convergent product explains the terminology. For ε > 0 and | z | < 1 , set ( z ; e − ε ) ∞ = ∏ n = 0 ∞ ( 1 − z e − n ε ) . Expanding the logarithm and summing the geometric progression gives log ⁡ ( z ; e − ε ) ∞ = − ∑ m = 1 ∞ z m m ( 1 − e − m ε ) = − Li ⁡ 2 ( z ) ε + 1 2 log ⁡ ( 1 − z ) + O ( ε ) , (10.9) uniformly on compact subsets of | z | < 1 , with the logarithm continued from z = 0 . Indeed, ( 1 − e − t ) − 1 − t − 1 − 1 2 = O ( t ) for all t > 0 ; for | z | ≤ ρ < 1 the remainder is bounded by a constant times ε ∑ m ≥ 1 ρ m . This justifies summing the expansion despite unbounded m . The logarithm of this “quantum dilogarithm” has the ordinary dilogarithm as its leading term. Faddeev–Kashaev’s quantum pentagon identity deforms the classical five-term dilogarithm identity [ 30 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.4 Why dilogarithms occur
records.text: The geometry enters in two ways. For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with shape z in the upper half-plane, Vol ⁡ ( T z ) = D ( z ) = ℑ Li ⁡ 2 ( z ) + arg ⁡ ( 1 − z ) log ⁡ | z | . (10.10) The logarithmic correction matters: an arbitrary dilogarithm phase does not have volume as its imaginary part without the appropriate boundary terms. Also, ⁡ d Li ⁡ 2 ( z ) = − log ⁡ ( 1 − z ) ⁡ d log ⁡ z . Consequently differentiation of a sum of dilogarithms produces logarithms of tetrahedral shapes, which can impose gluing equations.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.4 Why dilogarithms occur
records.text: Here is a particularly direct version in the convention of Dimofte–Garoufalidis [ 31 , Section 5.1] . On a fixed logarithmic branch away from the limiting pole cuts, their tetrahedral quantum function obeys ψ ℏ ( Z + ℏ ) = ( 1 − e − Z ) ψ ℏ ( Z ) , log ⁡ ψ ℏ ( Z ) ∼ 1 ℏ Li ⁡ 2 ( e − Z ) + O ( 1 ) . (10.11) Putting ψ ℏ ∼ e S / ℏ in the difference equation gives e S ′ ( Z ) = 1 − e − Z . With z = e Z , the right side is the companion tetrahedral shape 1 − z − 1 . Thus a difference equation for a special function becomes an algebraic shape relation in the limit.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.4 Why dilogarithms occur
records.text: A state integral combines these tetrahedral functions with quadratic exponential factors determined by the gluing data and integrates over internal logarithmic variables. Differentiating its leading phase gives the logarithmic gluing equations; exponentiating them gives the familiar products of shapes around edges. The boundary variables are retained as arguments of the integral. The precise quadratic term, logarithm branches, and contour are part of the construction. The convergent product in (10.9) explains the mechanism in a simple domain; one cannot substitute a unit-modulus root into that product and assume it converges. The continued or noncompact functions used later have their own definitions and contour prescriptions.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: The word semiclassical means an asymptotic regime in which the quantum parameter tends to zero while the intended geometric data remain controlled. Much of the calculation is ordinary asymptotic analysis. Consider I ( ℏ ) = ∫ Γ e S ( x ) / ℏ a ( x ; ℏ ) ⁡ d m x , a ( x ; ℏ ) = a 0 ( x ) + ℏ a 1 ( x ) + ⋯ . (10.12) Suppose S is holomorphic near a nondegenerate critical point x * , a 0 ( x * ) ≠ 0 , and the amplitude has a classical-symbol expansion there, including the derivatives needed at each order. Let ℏ tend to zero along a fixed ray, and localize to an oriented steepest-descent contour through x * on which the real part of ( S − S ( x * ) ) / ℏ has a strict quadratic maximum. Taylor expansion, rescaling, and Gaussian integration give this localized contribution I x * ( ℏ ) ∼ e S ( x * ) / ℏ ( 2 π ℏ ) m / 2 a 0 ( x * ) det ⁡ ( − S ″ ( x * ) ) ( 1 + c 1 ℏ + ⋯ ) . (10.13) The contour orientation, the ray of ℏ , and the continued square root fix the phase. Extending the formula from this local integral to the whole contour requires a bound on its complement. For a real Laplace integral with a strict maximum this is the usual Gaussian formula; for a complex phase it is applied along suitable real m -dimensional contours in the complexified variables.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: This formula gives a useful translation of the physics terminology. The classical or tree-level contribution is the critical value S ( x * ) / ℏ . The one-loop contribution includes the Gaussian determinant and leading amplitude or measure factors. Higher-loop terms come from the higher Taylor derivatives and amplitude corrections. Feynman diagrams organize the Gaussian contractions needed to compute these coefficients; the terminology does not require an additional physical assumption. In logarithmic form one writes log ⁡ I x * = S 0 ℏ + ν log ⁡ ℏ + S 1 + S 2 ℏ + ⋯ , where ν depends on the integral’s normalization and any zero modes (kernel directions of the linearized operator). A geometric expansion of S 0 in a shrinking area or an inverse Dehn-filling slope is a separate expansion. The cubic and quintic Neumann–Zagier coefficients are not, on that account, quantum higher-loop coefficients.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: Torsion is the topological form taken by a determinant of linearized equations after gauge directions have been accounted for. For a flat holonomy representation ρ , the relevant cellular complex is C • ( M ; Ad ⁡ ρ ) , with the holonomy acting on the Lie algebra by conjugation. Its H 0 records infinitesimal stabilizers and its H 1 records infinitesimal deformations. Reidemeister torsion compares the specified cellular bases with bases adapted to the differentials, using an alternating product of determinants. Nonzero cohomology requires cohomology bases as well; for a cusped three-manifold, peripheral curves enter this normalization. This explains why adjoint torsion is a candidate for a semiclassical amplitude [ 32 ; 31 ] . In particular, the identification of the gluing-equation one-loop invariant with adjoint Reidemeister torsion is a conjecture in [ 31 , Conjecture 1.8] ; its formal Gaussian construction is not a general proof of that identification.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: An individual Hessian determinant is not the torsion by definition: measure factors, gauge directions, and basis conventions must be matched. In the surgery convention used below the relevant amplitude is proportional to Tor ⁡ − 1 / 2 . Section 16 supplies the actual peripheral and solid-torus factors and an established figure-eight comparison.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: There is also a global question. A Lefschetz thimble is a steepest-descent cycle attached to a critical point. Under the usual analytic hypotheses, the exact contour can be represented in an appropriate relative homology group as Γ = ∑ α n α 𝒥 α . The coefficients determine which saddles contribute. Their description can change across a Stokes locus as parameters vary; the exact integral can remain analytic while its decomposition into saddle contributions changes [ 33 , Sections 2–3] . To recover the asymptotic of a whole invariant, one must control these coefficients, all competing contributions, and cancellation. The figure-eight positive sum supplied this global control by an elementary inequality. A local geometric saddle in a general state integral supplies only its local contribution until these additional questions are settled.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: Finally, a degenerate Hessian changes the local model. At a simple fold, two saddles merge. After separating the nondegenerate transverse directions, the remaining phase has the form S ( x ; t ) = S 0 + x 3 3 − t x + higher terms . The substitution x = ℏ 1 / 3 y , t = ℏ 2 / 3 s gives S − S 0 ℏ = y 3 3 − s y + ⋯ . The resulting contour integral is an Airy integral, rather than a sum of two separately uniform Gaussian approximations. This explains the exponent 2 / 3 in the transition scale. For the regular family in Section 15 , the real small parameter is h = 2 π b 2 , so the geometric deformation has scale b 4 / 3 . When that deformation is proportional to boundary area A , the same scale follows from W ≍ A 3 / 2 and W / h = O ( 1 ) . The later theorem proves the contour and additive error estimates for its pole-cleared regular family and fixed bounded real transition parameter. Its volume-action parameter is ℏ v o l = h / 2 as in (14.24) ; this constant does not change the exponent 2 / 3 . The scaling argument alone does not prove a transition theorem. Figure 5 illustrates the cubic normal form and its stationary points; its parameter t is the local fold parameter above.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.5 Stationary phase, loops, torsion, and degenerate saddles
records.text: Figure 5. The cubic normal form for an Airy transition. The stationary equation is x 2 = t ; two stationary points merge at t = 0 . The scaling shown balances the cubic and linear terms in exp ⁡ ( i 𝒮 t / ℏ ) . This is a normal-form illustration, not the full phase or integration contour of a quantum invariant; normalization, amplitudes, and contour tails require the separate estimates in the text.

records.title: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states
records.text: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states
records.text: The connection with hyperbolic geometry can be phrased using flat connections. If 𝒜 is a connection one-form, its curvature is F 𝒜 = ⁡ d 𝒜 + 𝒜 ∧ 𝒜 . In a chosen trivialization the Chern–Simons functional has the form CS ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) = 1 4 π ∫ M tr ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∧ d 𝒜 + 2 3 𝒜 ∧ 𝒜 ∧ 𝒜 ) . (10.14) The trace convention fixes the periods and overall normalization. On a closed manifold its first variation is δ CS ⁡ = ( 2 π ) − 1 ∫ M tr ⁡ ( δ 𝒜 ∧ F 𝒜 ) . Thus the critical points are flat connections modulo gauge. The formal expression ∫ e i k CS ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) D 𝒜 motivates the theory; exact algebraic constructions of quantum invariants do not depend on treating this symbol as an ordinary convergent integral [ 32 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states
records.text: For the compact group S U ( 2 ) , the flat connections form the compact character-variety problem. Hyperbolic three-dimensional holonomy instead takes values in P S L 2 ( ℂ ) , with a lift to S L 2 ( ℂ ) when chosen. It supplies a distinguished complex flat connection. The correctly normalized complex Chern–Simons action contains both the volume and the Chern–Simons invariant. Analytic continuation and the choice of integration cycle connect these settings; merely changing the name of the gauge group does not specify the cycle [ 34 ; 33 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states
records.text: For a manifold with boundary, variation of the functional has a boundary term. This is the source of the symplectic form on boundary flat connections and the need to specify boundary data. Abstractly, a topological quantum field theory assigns a vector space ℋ ( Σ ) to an oriented surface, and a vector Ψ M ∈ ℋ ( ∂ M ) to a three-manifold with boundary. Gluing is a pairing: Z ( M 1 ∪ Σ M 2 ) = ⟨ Ψ M 1 , Ψ M 2 ⟩ , with orientation reversal supplying the dual space and the theory’s framing conventions understood. In finite root-of-unity theories this is finite-dimensional linear algebra. In the analytic models used for complex holonomy, a state is represented locally by a function or distribution of continuous boundary variables, and the pairing becomes an integral. Those analytic models require their own existence and convergence statements.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states
records.text: A polarization chooses which half of the conjugate boundary coordinates are arguments of the state. For a torus boundary, use the multiplier logarithms u , v of Section 16 . The Neumann–Zagier normalization is Ω ∂ = 1 2 ⁡ d v ∧ ⁡ d u , α ∂ = 1 2 v ⁡ d u . (10.15) The geometric deformations of the interior give a Lagrangian curve v = v ( u ) . A semiclassical boundary state associated with this branch has the form Ψ M ( u ; ℏ ) ∼ e Φ ( u ) / ℏ ( a 0 ( u ) + ℏ a 1 ( u ) + ⋯ ) , Φ ′ ( u ) = 1 2 v ( u ) . (10.16) The leading exponent is a primitive of the symplectic potential on the Lagrangian curve. This is the geometric content of the WKB (Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin) ansatz [ 35 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.6 Flat connections, Chern–Simons theory, and boundary states
records.text: This choice of half-boundary variables also explains the boundary correction to volume. With F ′ = v and F ( 0 ) = 0 , the note uses Φ = Φ 0 + F / 2 , with ℑ Φ 0 = V 0 the complete volume, while V ( u ) − V 0 = 1 2 ℑ F ( u ) − 1 2 ℜ u ℑ v ( u ) . (10.17) The last term is essential. The imaginary part of an action in an arbitrary boundary polarization need not itself be the incomplete hyperbolic volume. Section 16.10 derives this identity and the corresponding filling transformation explicitly.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions

records.text: Set P = v / 2 , so that Ω ∂ = ⁡ d P ∧ ⁡ d u . In the formal convention compatible with e Φ / ℏ , use operators u ̂ Ψ = u Ψ , P ̂ Ψ = ℏ ∂ u Ψ , [ P ̂ , u ̂ ] = ℏ . (10.18) The usual physical factor i has been absorbed into the parameter ℏ ; the formula defines the convention here. Acting on the leading exponential gives P ̂ Ψ ∼ Φ ′ Ψ = P Ψ . Thus differentiation becomes the classical longitude coordinate in the small- ℏ limit.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.7 Quantizing peripheral holonomy and performing surgery
records.text: In local eigenvalue coordinates m = e u / 2 and l = e v / 2 , the corresponding operators are multiplication and translation: m ̂ Ψ ( u ) = e u / 2 Ψ ( u ) , l ̂ Ψ ( u ) = Ψ ( u + ℏ ) , l ̂ m ̂ = e ℏ / 2 m ̂ l ̂ . Fixed signs from an S L 2 lift can multiply m and l ; they do not change this commutation relation. The factor e ℏ / 2 is the Weyl parameter in these coordinates. It should not be identified with every author’s variable called q .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.7 Quantizing peripheral holonomy and performing surgery
records.text: The classical boundary holonomies satisfy a polynomial relation A ( l , m ) = 0 on the appropriate character-variety component. To quantize such a relation is to seek a difference operator A ̂ ( l ̂ , m ̂ ; ℏ ) annihilating the boundary state. Substituting (10.16) gives, to leading order, A ( e Φ ′ ( u ) , e u / 2 ) = 0 . This recovers the classical curve because Φ ′ = v / 2 . It does not uniquely determine the exact operator: ordering and lower-order terms remain. Identifying a particular operator with a recursion for a particular quantum invariant is a further mathematical statement [ 34 ; 35 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.7 Quantizing peripheral holonomy and performing surgery
records.text: Dehn filling has a similarly concrete meaning. For a slope ( p , q ) , choose ρ , σ ∈ ℤ with p σ − q ρ = 1 and put a = p u + q v , b c o r e = ρ u + σ v . Then ⁡ d b c o r e ∧ ⁡ d a = ⁡ d v ∧ ⁡ d u . For q ≠ 0 the generating function G ( u , a ) = p u 2 4 q − u a 2 q + σ a 2 4 q (10.19) satisfies ⁡ d G = 1 2 b c o r e ⁡ d a − 1 2 v ⁡ d u on this relation. An integral transform with exponential kernel e G / ℏ therefore changes the boundary coordinate from u to a . Its stationary equation for Φ ( u ) + G ( u , a ) is exactly a = p u + q v . At the classical level, pairing with a solid-torus state imposes the geometric filling branch a = 2 π i ; the cone-angle family uses a = i θ . The full surgery kernel includes amplitude and topological normalization factors in addition to this exponential.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.7 Quantizing peripheral holonomy and performing surgery
records.text: In the closed-filling convention of this monograph, ℏ r = 4 π i / r . If the filled critical phase has imaginary part V , then | e Φ f i l l e d / ℏ r | = exp ⁡ ( r V 4 π ) . (10.20) This is the RT exponential in (10.5) . After the Fourier-kernel square-root normalization, the Gaussian change of boundary coordinate has dependence ( p + q v ′ ( u ) ) − 1 / 2 , up to its phase; the solid torus contributes further factors. This requires q ≠ 0 in the displayed chart and p + q v ′ ( u ) ≠ 0 at the saddle. The calculation in Section 16 makes each of these statements precise and states the hypotheses needed to pass from the geometric contribution to an exact invariant. Notice that the inverse level r − 1 and the inverse slope length | p + q τ | − 1 are independent small parameters; here τ = v ′ ( 0 ) is the complete cusp shape.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.8 Liouville theory, conformal blocks, and continuous fusion
records.text: Take 0 < b < 1 . The other quantum construction in this monograph starts in two dimensions. In Liouville theory the variable is a conformal factor ϕ on a fixed Riemann surface with reference metric g ; formally the new area element is e 2 b ϕ ⁡ d A g . The field is distributional, so this exponential and its point insertions require renormalization. The Gaussian free field is a generalized Gaussian function with inverse-Laplacian covariance. Gaussian multiplicative chaos constructs its exponential measure by smoothing the field, subtracting half the variance of the scaled field from the exponent, and taking a limit. In the subcritical range above this gives the rigorous random measures used here [ 68 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.8 Liouville theory, conformal blocks, and continuous fusion
records.text: The basic observables are the renormalized exponential insertions V α ( p ) ∼ e 2 α ϕ ( p ) . A correlation function is the averaged product C b ( 𝜶 ; 𝒑 ) = ⟨ ∏ i V α i ( p i ) ⟩ . It depends on the marked conformal surface. It is neither a three-manifold invariant nor, without a further operation, a measure on moduli space. The parameters governing conformal symmetry are Q = b + b − 1 , c L = 1 + 6 Q 2 , Δ ( α ) = α ( Q − α ) . (10.21) Here c L is the central charge and Δ the conformal weight . Concretely the infinitesimal symmetry algebra is the Virasoro algebra [ L m , L n ] = ( m − n ) L m + n + c L 12 ( m 3 − m ) δ m + n , 0 . A highest-weight vector has L 0 -eigenvalue Δ and is killed by L n for n > 0 ; its descendants are obtained with the negative generators. This representation theory determines the power series called conformal blocks [ 95 ] .

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.8 Liouville theory, conformal blocks, and continuous fusion
records.text: On a four-marked sphere with marks 0 , 1 , z , ∞ , a pants decomposition first combines two of the insertions. Fixing the intermediate representation with label α s gives a chiral conformal block : a holomorphic, generally multivalued function with a specified leading behavior, for example ℱ α s ( s ) ( z ) = z Δ ( α s ) − Δ ( α 1 ) − Δ ( α 3 ) ( 1 + O ( z ) ) . “Chiral” refers here to the holomorphic half. The full correlation pairs holomorphic and antiholomorphic blocks and integrates over the intermediate spectrum. Label the insertions at 0 , 1 , z , ∞ by α 1 , α 2 , α 3 , α 4 , respectively. For real external charges in the initial domain α i < Q / 2 , α 1 + α 3 > Q / 2 , and α 2 + α 4 > Q / 2 , the proved four-point decomposition has the form C b ( z , z ‾ ) = ∫ 0 ∞ ρ ( α 1 , … , α 4 ; P ) | ℱ Q / 2 + i P ( s ) ( z ) | 2 ⁡ d P , with normalization and products of three-point structure constants included in ρ . The explicit three-point constants are the DOZZ constants, named for Dorn–Otto and Zamolodchikov–Zamolodchikov. The relevant three-point formula and four-point decomposition have rigorous constructions and proofs in their stated domains [ 68 ; 60 ] . Here the charges in [ 60 , Theorem 1.1] are twice our α i . Continuing outside that domain can require additional residues when poles cross the spectral contour. For complex charges the two chiral factors must be continued analytically in the charges; the real-domain absolute-square notation does not prescribe that continuation.

records.text: Its explicit formulas use Barnes’ double Gamma function Γ b , a meromorphic analogue of the Gamma function with the two step sizes b and b − 1 , and the double sine S b ( x ) = Γ b ( x ) Γ b ( Q − x ) , S b ( x + b ) = 2 sin ⁡ ( π b x ) S b ( x ) , S b ( x + b − 1 ) = 2 sin ⁡ ( π x / b ) S b ( x ) , S b ( x ) S b ( Q − x ) = 1 . (10.23) These identities explain why sine factors and pole movements occur in the later calculations. The double sine is related to Faddeev’s noncompact quantum dilogarithm by shifted arguments and explicit Gaussian factors; conventions matter [ 96 , Appendix A] .

records.text: The first shift relation also explains its classical limit. Put L b ( x ) = b 2 log ⁡ S b ( x / b ) for real x in the fundamental strip. Then L b ( x + b 2 ) − L b ( x ) = b 2 log ⁡ ( 2 sin ⁡ π x ) . A smooth leading limit must therefore have derivative log ⁡ ( 2 sin ⁡ π x ) . Reflection fixes the constant, giving L ( x ) = − Λ ( π x ) / π for 0 < x < 1 . This is a formal derivation of the leading term; Lemma 15.2 supplies the uniform estimate used in the proof. records.text: The particular Liouville specialization in this monograph can be understood through a one-variable integral. Separate the constant part c 0 of the field from its nonconstant part. After the insertions have shifted the Gaussian field, let Z > 0 be the remaining random area factor and put s = ∑ i α i − Q b . With the overall normalization adopted in (12.2) , the integral over the constant mode is 2 ∫ ℝ e 2 b s c 0 − Λ L Z e 2 b c 0 ⁡ d c 0 = 1 b Λ L − s Γ ( s ) Z − s , ℜ s > 0 . (10.24) This is just the substitution t = Λ L Z e 2 b c 0 . The positive number Λ L is the cosmological constant, or coefficient penalizing total area. The formula explains both the Gamma factor in the correlation and the usefulness of removing that factor in the unit-volume normalization.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions

records.text: Now take the deficit weights of the flat cone metric: 0 < μ i < 1 , ∑ i μ i = 2 , α i = μ i 2 b . Then ∑ i α i = 1 / b = Q − b , and therefore s = − 1 . The raw integral (10.24) does not converge there. Its meromorphic continuation has a Gamma pole, whereas the continued unit-volume expression contains Z − s = Z : its first moment . The normalized random measure has the prescribed reference measure as its expectation. The reference factors cancel at these weights, leaving, in a coordinate with all marks finite, 𝔼 [ Z ] = 𝒜 μ ( 𝒑 ) = ∫ ℂ ∏ i | w − p i | − 2 μ i ⁡ d 2 w . (10.25) This is precisely the area of the flat cone metric that underlies the Thurston–Deligne–Mostow construction. The charge convention in the detailed probabilistic formulas is β i = 2 α i . Section 12 checks the continuation and integrability conditions and proves the exact finite- b identity.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions

records.text: The remaining factors in the correlation are pairwise powers of | p i − p j | , whose logarithms are pluriharmonic away from collisions. Consequently the operation that produces the geometric form is − 2 i ∂ ∂ ‾ log ⁡ C b u v = ω C H , μ , ⁡ d V C H , μ = ω C H , μ n − 3 ( n − 3 ) ! . (10.26) The correlation supplies a logarithmic potential; its logarithmic curvature supplies the form; the top exterior power supplies the moduli measure. These are three different operations. This is why the exact comparison does not identify an unmodified quantum amplitude with a WP or complex hyperbolic volume density.

records.source: 10 A geometric introduction to the quantum constructions
records.title: 10.9 Why a screening residue meets flat cone geometry
records.text: The name one screening has an equally concrete explanation. The insertion V b has conformal weight Δ ( b ) = b ( Q − b ) = 1 , so integrating it gives a conformally covariant insertion. At ∑ i α i = Q − b , one such insertion balances the background charge. Its chiral contour integrals are ∫ γ ∏ i ( w − p i ) − μ i ⁡ d w , the Deligne–Mostow periods. For four points the relevant twisted period space is two-dimensional, and changing contour bases gives the finite hypergeometric fusion matrix calculated in Section 13 . Generic Liouville fusion is still the integral operator (10.22) ; the 2 × 2 matrix is the exact change of basis for these finite periods. Identifying it with a residue of the continued infinite fusion operator also requires the spectral-continuation and tail input stated in Section 13 . The first-moment area identity does not require that additional spectral input. At balanced weights a logarithmic basis is needed. The auxiliary tetrahedron also need not be the convex realization of the original cone sphere. Section 14 checks that geometric comparison separately.

records.text: The last charge prescription is the pure heavy-charge scaling: the labels grow like b − 1 while the deficit weights stay fixed. Fixed labels with q → 1 , labels growing with the order of a root of unity, and the continuous b → 0 limit are different problems. records.text: The quantum part of this monograph can now be read along three routes. For the boundary-moduli comparison, begin with Section 12 , then follow the four-point residue and its normalization in Sections 13 and 14 . For the degeneration of an individual tetrahedron, use Section 11 , the regular family in Section 14 , and the uniform theorem for the cleared regular-family integral at bounded real Airy parameter in Section 15 . For three-manifold volume and surgery, Section 16 is largely independent of the Liouville calculations; its symplectic explanation is in Section 16.10 .

records.title: 11.1 Three different geometric quantities
records.text: The connection to the volume conjecture becomes precise only after separating three quantities: A = Area ⁡ ( ∂ P ) , W ( P ) = Vol ⁡ ℍ 3 ( P ) , V W P = ∫ ℳ ω W P d d ! . The first is a surface area, the second an enclosed three-dimensional volume, and the third a measure of a space of shapes. The ordinary knot volume conjecture concerns three-dimensional volume. For a hyperbolic knot, in the reduced colored-Jones normalization J N ( unknot ; q ) = 1 , its familiar form is lim N → ∞ 2 π N log ⁡ | J N ( K ; e 2 π i / N ) | = Vol ⁡ ( S 3 \ K ) . (11.1) This remains a conjecture in general; see the colored-Jones formulation in [ 82 ] and the tetrahedral results in [ 52 ] .

records.source: 11 Polyhedral degeneration and quantum volume asymptotics
records.title: 11.1 Three different geometric quantities
records.text: Suppose a family of compact convex polyhedra P A has hyperbolic boundary area A ↓ 0 . Make the geometric convergence precise by choosing isometries into a Klein chart for which the rescaled convex bodies A − 1 / 2 P A converge in Euclidean Hausdorff distance to a nondegenerate polyhedron P E of surface area one. The rescaled bodies then lie in a common bounded set, the hyperbolic volume density tends uniformly to the Euclidean density, and Euclidean volume is continuous under this convex-body convergence. Hence W ( P A ) = A 3 / 2 W E ( P E ) + o ( A 3 / 2 ) . (11.2) For the separate intrinsic path (8.1) , with fixed 0 < μ i < 1 , ∑ i μ i = 2 , and d = n − 3 , the moduli volume satisfies V W P ( A ) = 2 − d A d V C H ( μ ) + O ( A d + 1 ) by (8.11) in its final chamber. The normalizations are those of Section 8 . The different powers reflect different dimensions. Flattened Euclidean limits and changes of polyhedral combinatorics require additional care; they are not covered by the nondegeneracy hypothesis in (11.2) .

records.source: 11 Polyhedral degeneration and quantum volume asymptotics
records.title: 11.2 An explicit small-polyhedron expansion
records.text: A controlled model gives more than the leading power. Let Q be a bounded nondegenerate convex Euclidean polyhedron, and place P r = r Q in the curvature- − 1 Klein ball. Its Euclidean planar faces are hyperbolic geodesic faces. The Klein metric is g x = I 1 − | x | 2 + x x 𝖳 ( 1 − | x | 2 ) 2 . Its two tangential eigenvalues are ( 1 − | x | 2 ) − 1 and its radial eigenvalue is ( 1 − | x | 2 ) − 2 , so ⁡ d Vol ⁡ ℍ 3 = ( 1 − | x | 2 ) − 2 ⁡ d 3 x . Consequently, whenever r sup ⁡ Q | y | < 1 , W ( r Q ) = r 3 ∫ Q ( 1 − r 2 | y | 2 ) − 2 ⁡ d 3 y = ∑ k = 0 ∞ ( k + 1 ) r 3 + 2 k ∫ Q | y | 2 k ⁡ d 3 y = r 3 W E ( Q ) + 2 r 5 ∫ Q | y | 2 ⁡ d 3 y + 3 r 7 ∫ Q | y | 4 ⁡ d 3 y + ⋯ . (11.3) The series converges uniformly on Q for each r R < 1 , where R = sup ⁡ Q | y | . Its nonnegative remainder after k = m is bounded by 0 ≤ W ( r Q ) − ∑ k = 0 m ( k + 1 ) r 3 + 2 k ∫ Q | y | 2 k ⁡ d 3 y ≤ r 3 W E ( Q ) t m + 1 { m + 2 − ( m + 1 ) t } ( 1 − t ) 2 , t = r 2 R 2 . This follows by summing the scalar tail of ( 1 − t ) − 2 . It bounds truncation of this geometric series, not a quantum asymptotic error. The expansion is exact for the specified homothetic Klein path. It is not generally the fixed-conformal angle path (8.1) . Nor does it imply a Taylor expansion of this form at ideal, flattening, or otherwise uncontrolled degenerations. Unlike (8.10) , it is an infinite series: the finite polynomial for the moduli volume comes from a quadratic cohomology class and a top intersection.

records.text: For a compact hyperbolic polyhedron with interior dihedral angles α e and edge lengths ℓ e , Schläfli’s formula is ⁡ d W = − 1 2 ∑ e ℓ e ⁡ d α e . (11.4) For the Klein family above, write ℓ e ( r ) = r L e + O ( r 3 ) , α e ( r ) = α e E + r 2 b e + O ( r 4 ) . These parity expansions follow directly from the Klein model. For example, write two adjacent face planes of Q as n f ⋅ y = h f and n g ⋅ y = h g , with unit outward normals. Their unit Lorentzian normals at scale r are ( r h f , n f ) / 1 − r 2 h f 2 and ( r h g , n g ) / 1 − r 2 h g 2 , for signature ( − , + , + , + ) . Thus, with c e = cos ⁡ α e E = − n f ⋅ n g , cos ⁡ α e ( r ) = c e + r 2 h f h g ( 1 − r 2 h f 2 ) ( 1 − r 2 h g 2 ) , b e = − h f h g + 1 2 c e ( h f 2 + h g 2 ) sin ⁡ α e E . We take actual faces, so adjacent ones are not coplanar and 0 < α e E < π . The length expansion follows by integrating the Klein metric along the fixed Euclidean edge, which is a hyperbolic geodesic. The leading term of (11.3) and (11.4) imply ∑ e L e b e = − 3 W E ( Q ) . (11.5) Indeed, ⁡ d W / ⁡ d r = 3 r 2 W E + O ( r 4 ) , while the right side of (11.4) , divided by ⁡ d r , is − r 2 ∑ e L e b e + O ( r 4 ) . Thus the first curvature correction to the Euclidean dihedral angles already determines the Euclidean enclosed volume. The sign reverses if exterior dihedral angles are used. As a check, for Q = [ − 1 , 1 ] 3 every L e = 2 and b e = − 1 , so the sum is − 24 = − 3 ⋅ 8 . The same identity holds with ℓ e = A 1 / 2 L e + O ( A 3 / 2 ) and α e = α e E + A b e + O ( A 2 ) for a fixed-combinatorics unit-area limiting family whose expansions are differentiable in A . It uses W = A 3 / 2 W E + O ( A 5 / 2 ) with the corresponding differentiated remainder; a bare o ( A 3 / 2 ) estimate cannot be differentiated without control.

records.source: 11 Polyhedral degeneration and quantum volume asymptotics
records.title: 11.3 Schläfli, doubling, and degeneration/regeneration
records.text: Doubling a convex polyhedron across its faces produces a cone three-manifold with singular graph given by its edges. The cone angle along an edge is 2 α e , and its volume is 2 W ( P ) . A shrinking polyhedron therefore supplies a direct example of degeneration to a Euclidean cone three-manifold after rescaling. This is the geometric setting suggested by Hodgson’s thesis, Degeneration and regeneration of geometric structures on 3-manifolds [ 62 ] . Later precise regeneration results include Porti–Weiss [ 86 , Theorem 1.3] , whose input is a closed orientable Euclidean cone three-manifold with cone angles at most π which is not almost product. Those hypotheses are not automatic for a doubled convex polyhedron; in particular, 2 α e E can exceed π . No unrestricted regeneration theorem is being asserted here. The edge cone angles 2 α e are also distinct from the intrinsic vertex openings θ i of the boundary surface.

records.source: 11 Polyhedral degeneration and quantum volume asymptotics
records.title: 11.3 Schläfli, doubling, and degeneration/regeneration
records.text: Rivin’s Volumes of degenerating polyhedra—on a conjecture of J. W. Milnor is directly relevant [ 89 ] . It studies continuous extension of volume toward degenerate angle data, the Euclidean vanishing boundary, and quantitative control through Schläfli’s formula and polar geometry. Its estimates allow logarithmically growing volume derivatives at degenerations; continuity does not imply a smooth power series at every boundary point. The controlled small-polyhedron expansion above gives a particularly explicit local calculation on the Euclidean side of this broader degeneration picture.

records.text: Quantum 6 j -symbols provide a concrete bridge to three-dimensional geometry. Costantino’s hyperbolic-type theorem uses the evaluation ev ⁡ n ( [ n ] { 6 j } ) after removing a root-of-unity pole; its geometric value is the volume of the doubled truncated-tetrahedral block D ( 𝒖 ) [ 52 , Definitions 3.1–3.2 and Theorem 3.9] . It is not a formula for an unregularized value at that pole.

records.title: 11.4 The established tetrahedral quantum connection
records.text: For clarity, distinguish two results of Chen–Murakami. Fix a hyperbolic tetrahedron T with an ideal or ultraideal vertex and interior dihedral angles α e in the convention of (11.4) , and put ξ r = e 2 π i / r , r odd. Their Theorem 1 gives 2 π r log ⁡ | { 6 j } q = ξ r 2 R W | → W ( T ) for admissible half-integer labels with j e , r / r → ( π − α e ) / ( 4 π ) and with the sum of the three labels at a chosen ideal or ultraideal vertex at least ( r − 3 ) / 2 . The prefactor requires more: Theorem 2 assumes that η e = ( π − α e ) / ( 2 π ) have odd numerators and odd denominators, takes r through odd common multiples of those denominators, and uses exactly j e , r = r η e / 2 − 1 / 2 . Then | { 6 j } q = ξ r 2 R W | ∼ 2 π r − 3 / 2 ( − det ⁡ G ) − 1 / 4 exp ⁡ ( r 2 π W ( T ) ) , (11.6) where G f f = 1 and G f g = − cos ⁡ α f g for the incident face dihedrals [ 51 , Theorems 1–2, pp. 1–2] . The labels are in the source’s Racah–Wigner normalization, whose quantum integer uses q 1 / 2 = ξ r ; hence q = ξ r 2 here corresponds to q a l g = ξ r in (10.2) . Arbitrary convergent label sequences give the stated leading rate under Theorem 1, not automatically this refined equivalent.

records.text: At the Euclidean end, Roberts proves the Ponzano–Regge asymptotic for classical 6 j -symbols: Euclidean tetrahedral edge lengths and dihedral angles enter an oscillatory Regge phase, and Euclidean volume enters its amplitude [ 91 ] . This is an established appearance of Euclidean tetrahedral geometry in quantum asymptotics. It does not automatically identify the classical large-label limit with a chosen root-of-unity hyperbolic limit.

records.source: 11 Polyhedral degeneration and quantum volume asymptotics
records.title: 11.4 The established tetrahedral quantum connection
records.text: In particular, the stated Chen–Murakami theorem does not cover an arbitrary family of compact tetrahedra shrinking to Euclidean ones. At a Euclidean tetrahedron the angle Gram determinant vanishes, so the displayed fixed-shape prefactor itself warns of nonuniformity. A continuous classical volume limit, even with good quantitative estimates, does not by itself control the quantum Hessian, the prefactor, or the error term in a joint limit.

records.text: Suppose a suitable quantum object, in a specified geometric branch and choice of variables, has an exponential contribution exp ⁡ ( W ( P A ) / ℏ ) . Equation (11.2) then singles out the dimensionless ratio λ = A 3 / 2 ℏ , A ≍ ℏ 2 / 3 . (11.7) This is the regime in which geometric degeneration competes with the semiclassical limit. At this stage it is a scaling prediction; Section 15 proves an additive uniform Airy statement for the pole-cleared regular b - 6 j integral and fixed bounded real transition parameters. In that convention the volume-action parameter is ℏ v o l = π b 2 , whereas its fold parameter is h = 2 π b 2 ; see (14.24) . No claim for fixed nonzero volume or unbounded transition parameter follows. A different polarization may involve a Regge or Legendre-transformed action, so the quantum object and phase must be specified first.

records.text: There is a useful classical model making the potential role of the WP–Thurston limit explicit. Fix the weights and intrinsic path (8.1) . Let K ⊂ ℳ 0 , n be a compact measurable subset and assume the corresponding realizations obey A − 3 / 2 W ( P A ( X ) ) → W E ( P E ( X ) ) uniformly on K , with a continuous nondegenerate Euclidean limiting family. Define 𝒵 K ( A , ℏ ) = ∫ K exp ⁡ ( W ( P A ( X ) ) ℏ ) ω W P , A d d ! . (11.8) This is a constructed geometric integral, not an identification with a colored-Jones or other known quantum invariant. Take positive A , ℏ → 0 with A 3 / 2 / ℏ → λ 0 ∈ ( 0 , ∞ ) . The exponential then converges uniformly on K . By (8.5) , 2 A − 1 ω W P , A → ω C H , μ locally uniformly in form coefficients; taking its d th exterior power preserves this convergence. A finite coordinate cover of K therefore gives a common integrable bound and proves 2 d A − d 𝒵 K ( A , ℏ ) → ∫ K e λ 0 W E ( P E ( X ) ) ω C H , μ d d ! . (11.9) Extending this formula to the full noncompact space requires domination and control of collision and flattened strata. Identifying its measure and phase with those of an actual quantum state integral is a further mathematical problem.

records.text: This separates the two potentially compatible roles: enclosed three-dimensional volume supplies an action, while the WP form supplies a measure on boundary shapes. Their Euclidean limits are respectively Euclidean polyhedral volume and the Thurston–Deligne–Mostow measure. Establishing that both occur together in a particular quantum construction would provide the substantive connection to the volume conjecture.

records.text: There is a concrete reason not to identify the auxiliary tetrahedron in a fusion kernel with the convex realization of our cone sphere without further work. In the conventions of [ 96 , Sections 3–5] , the parameters satisfy α k = Q 2 + i ℓ k 4 π b , A k = e − 2 π i b α k + π i = e ℓ k / 2 − π i b 2 . (12.22) Here A k is the paper’s exponentiated tetrahedral parameter, not our geometric area A . Continuing a boundary length by ℓ i = i θ i gives an auxiliary dihedral parameter η i = θ i / 2 − π b 2 , modulo the chosen branch. Thus at the equal-angle Euclidean endpoint, and as b → 0 , the four external auxiliary dihedrals tend to π / 2 . The internal s , t edges are opposite. After reordering faces, the limiting angle Gram matrix would be G = ( 1 − cos ⁡ η s 0 0 − cos ⁡ η s 1 0 0 0 0 1 − cos ⁡ η t 0 0 − cos ⁡ η t 1 ) , det ⁡ G = sin ⁡ 2 η s sin ⁡ 2 η t . (12.23) For interior angles η s , η t ∈ ( 0 , π ) this is nonsingular. A nondegenerate Euclidean tetrahedron has a rank-three angle Gram matrix. Hence this real slice cannot converge to the generic Euclidean tetrahedron realizing our flat cone metric. An additional degeneration, a different real slice, or a different geometric identification is needed. This is an obstruction to the proposed identification, not to the existence of Liouville theory with cone charges.

records.text: There is also a finite- b shift in the charge convention. At a fixed classical opening θ i = 2 π ( 1 − μ i ) , the exact dictionary (12.22) gives α i = μ i 2 b + b 2 , whereas (12.1) uses α i = μ i / ( 2 b ) . The latter corresponds in that dictionary to the shifted opening θ i + 2 π b 2 . For unshifted flat openings the zero-mode parameter would be s = n / 2 − 1 , not − 1 . Thus the exact correlation identity is a specified charge specialization; it is not an identification with the finite- b kernel at unshifted classical cone angles. Indeed, treating the shifted openings as hyperbolic cone data would give the negative Gauss–Bonnet area − 2 π n b 2 .

records.text: There is a second, independent distinction. Along a heavy-charge path with deficit weights a i ( A ) , set α i ( A ) = a i ( A ) / ( 2 b ) and A = 2 π ( ∑ i a i ( A ) − 2 ) . Then exactly s = A 4 π b 2 − 1 . (12.24) The finite- b flat endpoint of this pure-heavy charge path is s = − 1 , the resonance used above. The original zero-mode convergence region s > 0 requires A > 4 π b 2 . In contrast, under the proposed joint scaling A ≍ ℏ 2 / 3 with ℏ ≍ b 2 , one has A / b 2 → ∞ and hence s → + ∞ . The exact residue identity therefore establishes a quantum origin for the Deligne–Mostow curvature without proving the uniform quantum degeneration proposed in Section 11 .

Two intermediate Virasoro channels contribute, their change of basis is an explicit hypergeometric connection matrix, and the invariant Hermitian pairing is exactly the flat area. At balanced weights, the two ordinary blocks coalesce and must be replaced by a regularized logarithmic basis.

The one-screening locus ∑ i α i = Q − b lies outside that domain. Meromorphic dependence of each integrand factor alone does not justify continuing the integral.
