records.title: Analytic input for the spectral derivation.
records.text: Continue from the initial domain along a specified path of complex charges, retaining every residue of a pole crossed by the contour. Locally, the deformed contours are required to coincide with Q / 2 + i ℝ outside a fixed compact set. Near a generic target point, separate the finitely many pinch contributions, including their reflected partners, and write the remaining term using a locally fixed contour Γ r e g avoiding all poles. Its integrand ℐ r e g ( α ; ε , η , z ) must be holomorphic in the charge coordinates through ε = 0 ; here η denotes the remaining charge coordinates. Any additional discrete terms left in this remainder must also be holomorphic there. Require normal absolute convergence: on every compact set K of these complex charge parameters and of noncolliding z in the chosen branch chart, there is G K ∈ L 1 ( ℝ ) such that on the common contour ends sup ( ε , η , z ) ∈ K | ℐ r e g ( Q / 2 + i P ; ε , η , z ) | ≤ G K ( P ) . (13.3) The same normal-convergence requirement is imposed on compact continuation neighborhoods along the path, after their crossed-pole terms are separated. If another contour prescription moves the ends, the connecting pieces at infinity must additionally have integrals tending to zero uniformly on those parameter sets.

records.title: 13.2 Why the screening integrals are the Virasoro blocks
records.text: To verify the block identification, the screening field has weight Δ ( b ) = b ( Q − b ) = 1 . Integration over a closed twisted cycle therefore commutes with the Virasoro action: its Ward commutator is a total derivative. A screening outside a circle separating 0 , z from 1 , ∞ gives intermediate charge a s , while a screening inside gives a s + b . The corresponding Euler arc integrals are S 0 = ∫ 1 ∞ w − μ 1 ( w − 1 ) − μ 2 ( w − z ) − μ 3 ⁡ d w = B ( 1 − μ 2 , 1 − μ 4 ) f 0 ( z ) , S 1 = ∫ 0 z w − μ 1 ( 1 − w ) − μ 2 ( z − w ) − μ 3 ⁡ d w = B ( 1 − μ 1 , 1 − μ 3 ) f 1 ( z ) . (13.13) The positive arc branches are phase-normalized versions of the twisted periods; closed Pochhammer contours justify the Ward-identity argument, with the same normalized functions. Dividing out the beta constants sets the leading coefficient to one. The leading exponents agree because Δ ( a s ) − Δ ( α 1 ) − Δ ( α 3 ) = − 2 α 1 α 3 , Δ ( a s + b ) − Δ ( a s ) = δ 0 . The screened intertwiner construction and uniqueness of the normalized Ward solution identify the functions at every level; see [ 95 , Section 18.1, eq. (224)] . Here 0 < a s , a s + b < Q , so these internal weights are positive and avoid the degenerate Verma weights at c L > 25 . No external degenerate field is assumed.

records.text: We now prove the area pairing directly from periods: 𝒜 μ ( z ) = h 0 | f 0 ( z ) | 2 + h 1 | f 1 ( z ) | 2 . (13.19) Together with the first-moment residue, this supplies an independent derivation of (13.10) . The complex beta integral is ∫ ℂ | w | − 2 p | 1 − w | − 2 q ⁡ d 2 w = π Γ ( 1 − p ) Γ ( 1 − q ) Γ ( p + q − 1 ) Γ ( p ) Γ ( q ) Γ ( 2 − p − q ) , (13.20) for 0 < p , q < 1 and p + q > 1 . Introduce positive Laplace parameters for the two powers, perform the Gaussian integral in w , and then use their sum and ratio as variables. The remaining integrals are an ordinary Gamma integral and B ( 1 − q , 1 − p ) , proving the formula.

records.title: 13.4 The Hermitian pairing and its direct verification
records.text: The area is a constant Hermitian form in the period basis. For δ 0 ≠ 0 , local monodromy has distinct eigenvalues 1 , e 2 π i δ 0 , so the form is diagonal in ( f 0 , f 1 ) . If δ 0 > 0 , sending z → 0 in the area integral and using (13.20) gives h 0 . If δ 0 < 0 , rescaling w = z u gives the leading coefficient h 1 . To determine the other coefficient, first assume also δ 1 ≠ 0 . Monodromy at 1 makes the Hermitian form diagonal in ( g 0 , g 1 ) , so the off-diagonal entry after the real connection matrix vanishes: h 0 𝖬 00 𝖬 01 + h 1 𝖬 10 𝖬 11 = 0 . Every matrix entry here is nonzero at these real nonresonant weights. Hence either already determined coefficient fixes the other; Gamma reflection gives precisely (13.9) . Continuity at δ 1 = 0 , with δ 0 ≠ 0 fixed, completes this argument without crossing the singular s -channel basis. For this continuity the area integrals are locally dominated: on compact sets of admissible weights their singular exponents stay below 2 , and their decay at infinity stays faster than | w | − 2 .

(13.21) Define H s = diag ⁡ ( h 0 , h 1 ) and H t = diag ⁡ ( π 𝔤 ( δ 1 ) 𝔤 ( μ 1 ) 𝔤 ( μ 4 ) , π 𝔤 ( − δ 1 ) 𝔤 ( μ 2 ) 𝔤 ( μ 3 ) ) . The connection preserves the area exactly: 𝖬 * H s 𝖬 = H t . records.text: Its integral can also be evaluated. At z = 0 , if δ 0 > 0 then 𝒜 μ → h 0 , while if δ 0 < 0 then 𝒜 μ ∼ h 1 | z | 2 δ 0 . In both cases the metric density has the form const. | z | − 2 ( 1 − | δ 0 | ) , giving cone angle 2 π | δ 0 | . At δ 0 = 0 the area has logarithmic growth and the end is a cusp. The same argument at 1 , ∞ gives the other two angles 2 π | δ 1 | and 2 π | δ ∞ | . This agrees with the three-ended cone-sphere completion described in [ 66 , Section 5] .

(13.26) For the last equality, order the weights as x 1 ≤ x 2 ≤ x 3 ≤ x 4 and put r = 1 − x 4 . The sum constraint forces x 2 , x 3 ≥ r . The three absolute bipartition differences have sum ∑ j = 1 3 | r − x j | = 1 − r − x 1 + | r − x 1 | = 1 − 2 min ⁡ ( r , x 1 ) . This proves the stated minimum formula. Under (13.3) and the stated contour-continuation conditions, the infinite spectral representation gives the same answer through its two pinches. The finite fusion transformation on the two-dimensional one-screening residue sector is the period connection matrix (13.16) , with (13.29) at the fully balanced point. records.text: The further comparison has two distinct outcomes. The finite screening operator can be matched explicitly to a specified b - 6 j normalization: its double-Gamma factors reduce to ordinary Gamma factors and its analytic quantum-group matrix is a sine matrix. Here the operator is fixed by the independent period calculation in Section 13 ; its interpretation through a continued infinite spectral representation retains the analytic input specified there. Its auxiliary angle Gram matrix approaches rank two, whereas a nondegenerate shrinking compact tetrahedron approaches rank three. A direct calculation for the regular compact family gives a cubic classical saddle and fixes the proposed joint scale. The exact integration coordinate requires care: a previously stated pole accumulation at the saddle came from an incorrect shift. The corrected dictionary below and the local pole-free strip identify the candidate quantum fold. Section 15 proves the uniform quantum Airy formula for this pole-cleared regular family and bounded real transition parameters, using the exact-integral contour and tail analysis. The finite screening calculation and the classical fold here do not supply those additional estimates.

With square-root branches fixed by continuation, the DOZZ-normalized vector 𝒢 s = C s ℱ s obeys lim ε → 0 ε ξ ( ξ + 1 ) Λ * 𝒢 s ( s j + ε ξ ; ε ) = h s , j ℱ s , j . (14.10) The two S b shift equations prove the second equality. At the screened labels this becomes m ( s j ) = 4 sin ⁡ ( π [ δ 0 − ( 2 j − 1 ) b 2 ] ) sin ⁡ ( π δ 0 / b 2 ) , (14.11) with the analogous formula for t k , δ 1 . records.text: The correction to the earlier pole argument is substantive. The exact quantum integrand is smooth at the correct fold; the remaining real- b resonances are an explicit scalar factor outside the integral. For example, at η = η E the scalar factor has candidate resonances along b 2 = 3 η E − π 2 π m , m = 1 , 2 , … . The numerator in (15.3) is nonzero for sufficiently small b , uniformly in each fixed physical window 0 ≤ ζ ≤ Z : the continuous positive function Ai ⁡ ( ζ ) has a positive minimum on [ 0 , Z ] , and the additive correction and error tend uniformly to zero. Thus zeros of the squared sine give genuine double poles of the original normalization in this window, including all sufficiently large m in the displayed sequence. For negative ζ , the additive asymptotic remains uniform even at zeros of Ai ; no uniform noncancellation or relative-error assertion is made there. The cleared quantity has the uniform asymptotic in the proposition even through these resonances.

records.title: 15.7 Interpretation and scope
records.text: In geometric terms, ζ = A 2 3 h 2 / 3 + O ( A 2 h 2 / 3 ) , A ≍ b 4 / 3 . The decaying Airy branch selected by the contour agrees with the decaying volume exponential: its classical saddle exponent is − 2 W / h = − W / ( π b 2 ) . The proposition is uniform for bounded ζ ; it does not, by itself, justify taking ζ → ∞ simultaneously with b → 0 or keeping a nonzero tetrahedral volume fixed. Those matching limits require additional estimates.

records.source: 15 A uniform quantum Airy transition for the regular family
records.title: 15.7 Interpretation and scope
records.text: This proves a quantum transition for one specified regular family, beyond the classical cubic calculation. Extension to arbitrary nondegenerate Euclidean tetrahedral shapes, comparison of normalizations used in a global state integral, and gluing into a topological invariant remain separate problems. In particular no new case of the colored-Jones volume conjecture, and no identification of the integrated quantum measure with the cone-metric measure, follows from this proposition alone.

records.title: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.text: There is a second route from volume optimization to a quantum-volume comparison: perturb a complete cusped structure by prescribing peripheral holonomy. This route has a particularly explicit answer. The critical-value response of the real concave optimization recovers the Euclidean cusp quadratic form. After passage to a holomorphic boundary potential, the local volume response is exactly the imaginary part of a Legendre critical value, and gives the filled volume when the geometric completion exists. Its Taylor coefficients reproduce the Neumann–Zagier expansion, and its Hessian is the derivative entering the torsion surgery formula. These are deductions from the established variational, deformation, and torsion identities cited below; no novelty claim is made.

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.1 Peripheral conventions and the two small parameters
records.text: Let M be an oriented, finite-volume, one-cusped hyperbolic three-manifold. Fix an oriented meridian–longitude basis ( μ , λ ) and the geometric deformation branch through the complete structure. We use logarithms of the P S L 2 ( ℂ ) multipliers, equivalently of the eigenvalue ratios, so that u = H ( μ ) , v = H ( λ ) , v ( u ) = τ u + c 3 u 3 + c 5 u 5 + O ( u 7 ) , B = ℑ τ > 0 . (16.1) Thus u is twice a local logarithm of an S L 2 eigenvalue, after removing its constant sign at the complete representation. In particular, the smooth filling equation is p u + q v = 2 π i , with the branch chosen continuously from the cusp. Using eigenvalue logarithms u ̂ = u / 2 , v ̂ = v / 2 instead gives p u ̂ + q v ̂ = π i and v ̂ = τ u ̂ + 4 c 3 u ̂ 3 + 16 c 5 u ̂ 5 + ⋯ . The oddness and the holomorphic potential are those of Neumann–Zagier [ 36 , Sections 4–6] .

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.1 Peripheral conventions and the two small parameters
records.text: For a primitive slope ( p , q ) put A = p + q τ , Q ( p , q ) = | A | 2 B , p u + q v ( u ) = i θ . (16.2) Here θ is an angular holonomy parameter. It is the cone angle when the local structure has the corresponding geometric cone completion; θ = 0 is the complete cusp and θ = 2 π gives a smooth hyperbolic filling when that completion exists. The quantity Q is the squared length of the slope on a Euclidean cusp cross section divided by its area. For sufficiently long slopes the small solution stays in one fixed holonomy neighborhood throughout 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2 π . Indeed, put h ( u ) = v ( u ) − τ u = O ( u 3 ) and t = q / A . Since | t | ≤ B − 1 , a sufficiently small disk has | t h ′ ( u ) | < 1 / 2 uniformly in the slope. The equation u + t h ( u ) = i θ / A then has a unique small analytic solution, uniformly for bounded θ and sufficiently large | A | , with u = O ( | A | − 1 ) . This is an assertion about a holonomy germ; the hyperbolic Dehn surgery theorem supplies the smooth geometric completion for sufficiently long primitive slopes [ 36 , Section 4] . Geometric completion is a separate statement from the analytic existence of this small solution.

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.2 What the linear term does to real volume optimization
records.text: Suppose a chosen ideal triangulation of the compact core of M has a positive complete geometric angle structure, with every ideal vertex link a torus. Use independent linear coordinates x on its full angle space, with tetrahedral and edge-angle constraints already imposed, and center them at the complete maximum x = 0 . Write 𝒱 ( x ) = ∑ tetrahedra Vol ⁡ ( Δ x ) , V 0 = 𝒱 ( 0 ) , K = − D 2 𝒱 ( 0 ) > 0 . Peripheral angular holonomies are affine in the angles and vanish at 0 in the selected branches. Thus there is a real linear map P such that P x = ( ℑ u ℑ v ) , L = ( p q ) P , L x = θ . The boundary intersection pairing gives rank ⁡ P = 2 , so L ≠ 0 . Together with K > 0 , this makes the constrained stationarity system invertible at 0 and gives a unique nearby interior maximizer for sufficiently small θ . These assertions use the full constrained angle space, not an arbitrarily restricted family of tetrahedral shapes.

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery

records.text: At that maximizer, the leading–trailing edge variations impose the missing real edge equations; the peripheral variation imposes the missing real filling equation. This follows from the angle-holonomy pairing and volume derivative in [ 37 , Lemma 4.4, Proposition 4.6 and Proposition 5.4] . It first identifies a local edge-glued holonomy solution. At θ = 2 π , an interior critical point on the corresponding slice gives a complete hyperbolic filling by their Theorem 6.1. For other angular slices we retain the local holonomy interpretation unless a cone completion is specified. For long slopes the small holonomy solution stays in this positive geometric neighborhood throughout a bounded angular interval, so the same constrained-stationarity identification applies there.

records.text: A precise closed-manifold analogue is the Chen–Yang volume conjecture. At the specified root ζ r = e 2 π i / r , with r odd, its absolute-growth statements are 4 π r log ⁡ | R T r ( N ; ζ r ) | → Vol ⁡ ( N ) , 2 π r log ⁡ T V r ( N ; ζ r ) → Vol ⁡ ( N ) . (16.20) The root and normalization matter; these are the Chen–Yang versions for hyperbolic manifolds [ 38 ] . We use absolute growth to avoid mixing the different Chern–Simons sign conventions in the literature.

records.text: For a boundary state whose geometric semiclassical phase satisfies Φ ( u ) = Φ 0 + 1 2 F ( u ) , ℑ Φ 0 = V 0 , the filling phase is 𝒯 θ ( u ) = Φ 0 + 1 2 𝒮 p , q ( u ; θ ) . (16.21) Possible real framing constants do not alter its imaginary part. With ℏ r = 4 π i / r , Proposition 16.1 immediately gives | e 𝒯 θ ( u θ ) / ℏ r | = exp ⁡ ( r 4 π V p , q ( θ ) ) . (16.22) In particular, the deformation of the geometric exponential is log ⁡ | e 𝒯 θ ( u θ ) / ℏ r e Φ 0 / ℏ r | = − r 4 π ( V 0 − V p , q ( θ ) ) . (16.23) Every classical coefficient in (16.16) therefore appears with precisely the required quantum exponential coefficient. At θ = 2 π , Yoshida’s complex-volume formula has this normalization; see the unnumbered filling formula and the potential normalization (5.9) on [ 40 , p. 456] . Quadratic and linear filling kernels also appear explicitly in [ 39 , equations (12)–(14)] ; their boundary coordinates and level conventions must be converted before numerical coefficients are compared.

records.title: 16.7 The closed quantum-volume statement and its local consequence
records.text: Proposition 16.2 (Conditional local quantum transfer). Suppose an exact surgery representation for a specified quantum invariant has, near the geometric branch, phase 𝒯 θ and a uniform classical-symbol expansion of its amplitude. Suppose the geometric critical point is nondegenerate, its steepest-descent cycle occurs with nonzero coefficient in the specified integration cycle, the net leading stationary-phase coefficient of that geometric sector is uniformly bounded away from zero, and the remaining integral or sum is exponentially smaller, uniformly on a chosen compact deformation interval. Then stationary phase gives the volume exponent (16.22) for the full invariant, with a uniform expansion on that interval. Without the last global condition, the same statement holds for the specified local geometric contribution.

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.7 The closed quantum-volume statement and its local consequence
records.text: Proof. At the geometric critical point, 𝒯 θ ″ ( u θ ) = p + q v ′ ( u θ ) 2 q ≠ 0 . Uniform stationary phase on the stipulated cycle gives a nonzero amplitude times e 𝒯 θ ( u θ ) / ℏ r , with powers of r − 1 and a Gaussian power of r according to the normalization of the kernel. Such powers contribute only O ( log ⁡ r / r ) to normalized logarithmic growth. The exponential gap permits the addition of the remaining terms without changing the leading growth. The critical-value proposition identifies the exponent with the geometric volume. ◻

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.7 The closed quantum-volume statement and its local consequence
records.text: For a general knot this proposition identifies the needed analytic input; it does not establish that input from a complete-point Kashaev asymptotic alone. A value at u = 0 does not provide a uniform boundary-state expansion near 0 , and a local critical point does not by itself specify its coefficient in the global surgery sum. The regular tetrahedral Airy formula in Section 15 concerns a different integral and does not supply that missing manifold-level information.

(16.24) Thus the same quantity controls the classical susceptibility and the Gaussian surgery integral. records.title: 16.8 The Gaussian factor and the torsion surgery formula
records.text: More precisely, suppose θ = 2 π gives a smooth hyperbolic filled manifold and the representation is its holonomy. Assume its adjoint representation is acyclic and its restriction to the compact core is regular for both μ and p μ + q λ : the peripheral invariant vector paired with either curve supplies a basis of the one-dimensional twisted H 1 , with the compatible boundary basis in H 2 . In the local holonomy chart this requires D * ≠ 0 ; the core is loxodromic, so sinh ⁡ ( w / 2 ) ≠ 0 . The change-of-peripheral-curve and surgery formulas for adjoint Reidemeister torsion then give Tor ⁡ p μ + q λ ( M u ) = ( p + q v ′ ( u ) ) Tor ⁡ μ ( M u ) , Tor ⁡ ( M p / q ) = Tor ⁡ p μ + q λ ( M u ) 4 sinh ⁡ 2 ( w / 2 ) , w = ρ u + σ v . (16.25) These are understood up to the standard torsion signs and consistent choices of square root. They are the identities used in [ 40 , equations (5.16) and (5.23)] . For the general regularity and change-of-curve statements, see [ 129 , Propositions 5.13–5.14] ; its Proposition 4.23(b), specialized to the adjoint representation ( k 1 , k 2 ) = ( 2 , 0 ) , gives the surgery factor up to the torsion sign. Consequently the expected full geometric amplitude is proportional to 2 sinh ⁡ ( w / 2 ) ( p + q v ′ ( u ) ) Tor ⁡ μ ( M u ) = 1 Tor ⁡ ( M p / q ) . (16.26) The identity shows what must accompany the boundary Hessian. Matching the Gaussian factor alone would leave out both the cusp torsion and the solid-torus amplitude. This one-loop comparison uses more information than the classical volume exponent. The closed-manifold torsion in this formula is evaluated at smooth filling; it is not being assigned to a generic cone holonomy. At the cusp endpoint θ = 0 the solid-torus factor vanishes, so a uniform quantum statement including that endpoint requires a separate normalization and analysis. The compact parameter interval in Proposition 16.2 is subject to its nonvanishing-amplitude hypothesis.

records.text: An independent calculation starts with the two regular ideal tetrahedra and their Lobachevsky volume. In the Neumann–Zagier presentation their shapes z 1 , z 2 satisfy z 1 z 2 ( z 1 − 1 ) ( z 2 − 1 ) = 1 , u = log ⁡ ( z 2 ( 1 − z 1 ) ) , v = 2 log ⁡ ( z 1 ( 1 − z 1 ) ) . Eliminating the shapes from these equations gives the local peripheral relation cosh ⁡ ( v / 2 ) = 1 + cosh ⁡ u − cosh ⁡ ( 2 u ) . Equivalently, with the eigenvalue variables m = e u / 2 and l = − e v / 2 , it is l + l − 1 = m 4 − m 2 − 2 − m − 2 + m − 4 , the nonabelian figure-eight A -polynomial relation in this choice of signs. The sign in l is essential: its complete value is − 1 whereas v ( 0 ) = 0 . The equation and the chosen tangent v ′ ( 0 ) = 2 3 i recover the cubic and quintic coefficients above. This is a local branch calculation, not a classification of the global curve or of fillings.

(16.29) This recovers the cusp shape directly from the optimizer. Put D 0 = p 2 + 12 q 2 . The unit angular-response vector is e = ( 6 q − p , − 6 q − p , p − 6 q ) T 2 D 0 . Using Λ ‴ ( π / 3 ) = 4 3 , Λ ⁗ ( π / 3 ) = − 8 3 3 , the six entries of E e occur in opposite pairs, so T 3 [ e , e , e ] = 0 . records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.9 A figure-eight benchmark and the scope of the conclusion
records.text: For this example there is also a theorem about the actual quantum invariants: Wong–Yang prove the leading RT asymptotic with relative error O ( r − 1 ) , and the RT/TV volume conjectures for every hyperbolic rational Dehn filling of the figure-eight knot [ 40 , Theorems 1.1 and 1.2] . Their leading amplitude is the inverse square root of adjoint torsion, with their specified overall constant. Thus the local consistency calculation above is contained in a stronger result in that example. The present discussion reorganizes the comparison around volume optimization and its derivatives; it does not produce a new case of the quantum-volume conjecture.

records.source: 16 Dehn filling, variational response, and quantum surgery
records.title: 16.9 A figure-eight benchmark and the scope of the conclusion
records.text: For a general knot, the unconditional results here are the classical critical-value identity and its coefficient dictionary. The quantum conclusion for a specified local geometric contribution follows under the stated stationary-phase hypotheses. Passing to the full invariant requires control of its exact surgery representation and all competing contributions. One should first keep the filling slope fixed while taking r → ∞ , and then study the long-slope coefficients. A simultaneous limit in which the slope grows with r requires uniform estimates not supplied by separate fixed-slope expansions.

records.text: The computational companion in experiments/quantum_surgery/README.md , with output at artifacts/quantum_surgery/result.json , checks finite formal series, canonical-coordinate identities, and the figure-eight angle-Hessian contractions in exact arithmetic. These fixtures check the displayed coefficient algebra. They do not compute a filled hyperbolic manifold or an exact quantum invariant, and do not establish convergence, a global integration cycle, or its noncancellation.

records.title: 16.10 The symplectic pairing behind the calculation
records.text: The pairing in Neumann–Zagier is the structure behind the preceding formulas. It identifies the peripheral variables as conjugate coordinates, makes the geometric deformation locus Lagrangian, and fixes the canonical transformation for Dehn filling. We record the normalization explicitly, since interchanging meridian and longitude or using eigenvalue rather than multiplier logarithms changes the displayed signs or factors.

records.text: For n ideal tetrahedra introduce independent ambient coordinates Z j = log ⁡ z j , W j = log ⁡ ( 1 − z j ) , Ω t e t = ∑ j = 1 n ⁡ d Z j ∧ ⁡ d W j . The actual shapes satisfy e Z j + e W j = 1 . Their product is a complex Lagrangian of dimension n in this 2 n -dimensional phase space. The logarithmic edge equations and peripheral holonomies are affine linear functions of X = ( Z 1 , … , Z n , W 1 , … , W n ) T .

records.text: Let C λ , C μ be the longitude and meridian coefficient rows, let R E be the edge-equation matrix, and set J 2 n = ( 0 I n − I n 0 ) , U = ( C λ C μ R E ) . For a triangulated manifold with h torus cusps, the original matrix identity is U J 2 n U T = 2 ( 0 I h 0 − I h 0 0 0 0 0 ) . (16.31) This is [ 36 , Theorem 2.2, equation (21)] , in their longitude–meridian row order. They normalize the coefficient-row pairing as ⟨ a , b ⟩ = 1 2 a J 2 n b T . Equivalently, the unnormalized coefficient pairing of peripheral curves is twice their oriented intersection number; edge rows pair to zero with one another and with all peripheral rows. The topological interpretation is proved in their Section 3. A geometric construction of symplectic bases is given in [ 42 ] .

Corollary 2.4 of [ 36 ] identifies the reduced form as Ω ∂ = 1 2 ∑ i = 1 h ⁡ d v i ∧ ⁡ d u i , α ∂ = 1 2 ∑ i = 1 h v i ⁡ d u i , ⁡ d α ∂ = Ω ∂ . For a modern formulation of the reduction, see [ 41 ] . The symplectic form lives on the ambient boundary phase space; its pullback to ℒ M is zero.

The real volume one-form is an exact modification of the imaginary part of the symplectic primitive: β = 1 2 ( r ⁡ d y − x ⁡ d s ) = ℑ α ∂ − 1 2 ⁡ d ( x s ) , ⁡ d β = ℑ Ω ∂ . All statements are local in the positive geometric neighborhood, where the maximum is interior and nondegenerate. Let K ( ξ ) = − D 2 𝒱 ( ξ ) > 0 at the maximizing point. The boundary intersection pairing gives rank ⁡ P = 2 , so the constrained implicit-function theorem supplies a unique nearby interior maximizer for every sufficiently small ( y , s ) . Stationarity in the internal directions enforces real edge gluing, so this maximizer lies on the same deformation branch v = v ( u ) . The map u = x + i y ↦ ( y , ℑ v ( u ) ) is locally invertible because ℑ v ′ ( 0 ) = B > 0 . It therefore identifies the angular boundary parameters with that geometric branch, rather than with an unrelated constrained family. The Schur-complement identity for the linear constraints is − D 2 V ¯ = ( P K ( ξ ) − 1 P T ) − 1 . (16.42) Set T = v ′ ( u ) = A 0 + i B 0 , with B 0 > 0 near the complete point. Solving these two linear differential equations yields − D 2 V ¯ = 1 2 B 0 ( | T | 2 − A 0 − A 0 1 ) , det ⁡ ( − D 2 V ¯ ) = 1 4 . records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: 17.1 What a volume computation determines
records.text: The problem is to integrate a sum over curves while the underlying surface also varies. Directly, this asks us to keep track of all the curves on every surface in moduli space. Unfolding changes the order of description: we integrate over surfaces equipped with one chosen curve, and evaluate just the term belonging to that curve. The sum disappears because the choice of curve has become part of the integration domain. An elementary example shows exactly how this trade works.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A toy model: unfolding the circle to the line.
records.text: A toy model: unfolding the circle to the line.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A toy model: unfolding the circle to the line.
records.text: Let f : ℝ → [ 0 , ∞ ) be integrable, and form the periodic sum P f ( x ) = ∑ n ∈ ℤ f ( x + n ) . Shifting x by one merely reindexes the sum, so P f is a function on the circle ℝ / ℤ . A fundamental interval for that circle is [ 0 , 1 ) : each point of the circle has one representative there. By nonnegativity, Tonelli’s theorem allows us to interchange sum and integral: ∫ 0 1 P f ( x ) ⁡ d x = ∑ n ∈ ℤ ∫ 0 1 f ( x + n ) ⁡ d x = ∑ n ∈ ℤ ∫ n n + 1 f ( u ) ⁡ d u = ∫ ℝ f ( u ) ⁡ d u . In the second line we used u = x + n . The translated intervals [ n , n + 1 ) tile the real line, so they join into a single integration domain. This is unfolding: one integral of a sum on a quotient becomes one integral of a single function on a larger space. For a signed or complex-valued f , the same argument works if ∫ ℝ | f | < ∞ .

records.text: Take f ( u ) = e − | u | . For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 , separate n ≥ 0 from n ≤ − 1 and sum the two geometric series: P f ( x ) = e − x + e x − 1 1 − e − 1 , ∫ 0 1 P f ( x ) ⁡ d x = 2 . Knowing the integral has not determined the function: P f ( 0 ) = 1 + e − 1 1 − e − 1 , P f ( 1 2 ) = 2 e − 1 / 2 1 − e − 1 , and these values differ by ( 1 − e − 1 / 2 ) 2 / ( 1 − e − 1 ) > 0 . Thus unfolding computes the mean, here 2 , without making the periodic sum constant.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A toy model: unfolding the circle to the line.
records.text: A contrasting example is the tent function f ( u ) = max ⁡ ( 1 − | u | , 0 ) . For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 only the terms with n = 0 , − 1 can be nonzero, and their sum is ( 1 − x ) + x = 1 . Its translates form a partition of unity : their values add to one at every point. This extra pointwise fact explains constancy; integrating it also gives the value of the integral. McShane’s identity will supply a geometric partition playing a comparable role.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: What replaces the circle and the line?
records.text: Fix an oriented surface and its boundary lengths. Teichmüller space 𝒯 consists of its marked hyperbolic structures: the marking identifies curves with curves on a fixed reference surface. The mapping class group Γ consists of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms modulo isotopy, with the prescribed boundary conventions. Its action changes the marking. The quotient Γ ∖ 𝒯 is moduli space, where the marking has been forgotten.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: What replaces the circle and the line?
records.text: Choose an essential, nonperipheral curve class γ : it cannot be contracted to a point or moved into a puncture or boundary. Its orbit Γ γ consists of all classes obtained by changing the marking, each counted once. Write ℓ δ ( X ) for the length of the geodesic representative of δ on X . The subgroup Stab ⁡ ( γ ) preserves γ . Consequently Stab ⁡ ( γ ) ∖ 𝒯 remembers a surface together with a distinguished curve in this orbit . The map to Γ ∖ 𝒯 forgets that curve. The different choices over a surface are precisely what the orbit sum counts, with automorphisms handled by orbifold integration. Curves of equal length are still distinct summands when their classes are different.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: What replaces the circle and the line?
records.text: Use the same Weil–Petersson (WP) orbifold measure ⁡ d V W P on both quotients. For a measurable nonnegative function F , or one for which ∫ Γ ∖ 𝒯 ∑ δ | F ( ℓ δ ) | ⁡ d V W P < ∞ , the basic unfolding identity is ∫ Γ ∖ 𝒯 ∑ δ ∈ Γ γ F ( ℓ δ ( X ) ) ⁡ d V W P ( X ) = ∫ Stab ⁡ ( γ ) ∖ 𝒯 F ( ℓ γ ( X ) ) ⁡ d V W P ( X ) . (17.1) To prove it, take a fundamental domain for Γ and integrate each summand over that domain. Change the marking in each term so that the chosen curve becomes γ . The resulting translates assemble into a fundamental domain for Stab ⁡ ( γ ) , just as the translated unit intervals assembled into ℝ . The stabilizer identifies exactly the repetitions that would otherwise count the same chosen curve again. Ineffective isotropy is retained on both sides: even symmetries that act trivially contribute the reciprocal of their group order. For nonnegative functions either integral may be infinite.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: What replaces the circle and the line?
records.text: The same argument applies to a specified multicurve, with Stab ⁡ ( γ ) preserving its entire decoration, including any orientation, ordering or component weights, and with the same length statistic on both sides. Simplicity is not needed for this change of integration domain.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: Why remembering a simple curve helps.
records.text: If the chosen curve is simple, meaning it has no self-intersections, cutting along it produces two geodesic boundary circles of the same length x . To reconstruct the surface we must specify the cut surface and how far one boundary is shifted before regluing it to the other. That shift is the Fenchel–Nielsen twist τ , measured in length units. A full Dehn twist changes τ to τ + x , so a fundamental twist interval is 0 ≤ τ < x . The WP length–twist factor is ⁡ d x ⁡ d τ ; integrating out the twist therefore gives ∫ 0 x ⁡ d τ ⁡ d x = x ⁡ d x . This is the origin of the length factor in the unfolded integral. It is the size of the gluing parameter, rather than an extra weight chosen for the curve.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: Why remembering a simple curve helps.
records.text: For a disjoint simple multicurve, repeat this construction along each component. The result has factors ∏ j x j ⁡ d x j and the WP volumes of the cut components. For example, cutting a nonseparating curve on a genus- g surface with n boundaries leaves a genus- ( g − 1 ) surface with n + 2 boundaries, the two new lengths both being x . A separating cut leaves two surfaces, so their volume factors multiply. Finite symmetries must still be accounted for: unoriented cuffs or indistinguishable components must not be accidentally counted twice. Mirzakhani’s integration formula makes these factors precise [ 75 , Theorem 7.1 and Lemma 7.3] . Its symmetry and one-handle factors must be converted using the volume convention for each component; they are not extra factors to append to an already stack-normalized quotient.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: An integral is an average; an identity needs more.
records.text: Suppose a series S ( X ) is independently known to be constant, say C , and 0 < V g , n < ∞ in the chosen normalization. Then C = 1 V g , n ∫ ℳ g , n S ( X ) ⁡ d V W P ( X ) , (17.2) and unfolding can calculate its value. Without an independent constancy argument the same quotient is only the mean of S , as the exponential toy example shows. Conversely, if a pointwise identity supplies a known nonzero C , evaluating its integral can determine the unknown volume V g , n . This second use is the starting point of Mirzakhani’s volume recursion.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A complete surface example: the punctured torus.
records.text: Let X be a complete finite-area hyperbolic torus with one cusp. All essential unoriented simple closed curves belong to a single mapping class group orbit. Cutting along a chosen one, of length x , leaves a pair of pants with boundary lengths ( 0 , x , x ) , where length zero denotes the cusp. A hyperbolic pair of pants is determined by its three boundary lengths. There is therefore no further moduli integral for the cut surface: the remaining continuous parameters are just x > 0 and the regluing twist τ .

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A complete surface example: the punctured torus.
records.text: The effective stabilizer quotient has coordinates x > 0 and 0 ≤ τ < x . In the stack convention of Section 6 , the torus’s generic elliptic involution has order two and acts trivially on Teichmüller space. Orbifold integration retains its weight 1 / 2 . Thus the unfolded integral is 1 2 ∫ 0 ∞ ∫ 0 x f ( x ) ⁡ d τ ⁡ d x , giving ∫ ℳ 1 , 1 ∑ α simple f ( ℓ α ) ⁡ d V W P = 1 2 ∫ 0 ∞ x f ( x ) ⁡ d x . (17.3) The sum is over unoriented, nonperipheral simple curve classes. The factor 1 / 2 occurs once; it is not a second quotient by cuff exchange.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A complete surface example: the punctured torus.
records.text: Choose f ( x ) = ( 1 + e x ) − 1 . The many-curve integral has become an elementary one-variable integral: ∫ 0 ∞ x ⁡ d x 1 + e x = ∑ m ≥ 1 ( − 1 ) m − 1 ∫ 0 ∞ x e − m x ⁡ d x = ∑ m ≥ 1 ( − 1 ) m − 1 m 2 = π 2 12 . Here ( 1 + e x ) − 1 = ∑ m ≥ 1 ( − 1 ) m − 1 e − m x for x > 0 . Termwise integration is justified by ∑ m ∫ 0 ∞ x e − m x ⁡ d x = ∑ m m − 2 < ∞ . For a finite numerical check, the integral beyond R is at most ( R + 1 ) e − R , and the alternating sum through m = M has error at most ( M + 1 ) − 2 . Equation (17.3) therefore gives π 2 / 24 for the integral over moduli space.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A complete surface example: the punctured torus.
records.text: Why choose this particular f ? Because McShane’s theorem says that its curve sum is pointwise constant [ 73 ] : ∑ α simple, unoriented 1 1 + e ℓ α ( X ) = 1 2 . (17.4) The geometric idea is a partition at the cusp on a single fixed surface . Take a small horocycle around the cusp and normalize its length measure to have total mass one. Its points specify geodesic rays leaving the cusp. The gap construction groups the complementary intervals by simple curves; the exceptional set has measure zero. For a curve of length x , the associated gaps have combined normalized measure 2 / ( 1 + e x ) . This width is computed in the pair of pants obtained by cutting along that curve. Adding the gap widths gives one, hence (17.4) . This describes the mechanism, not a proof of the required gap classification or null-set theorem; see [ 74 , Sections 3, 5, and 9] . As with the tent function, the partition supplies the pointwise statement that integration alone cannot supply.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: A complete surface example: the punctured torus.
records.text: We can now use the two ingredients in either direction. Integrating McShane’s identity and using the computed integral gives 1 2 V 1 , 1 = π 2 24 , V 1 , 1 = π 2 12 . Alternatively, if the volume is already known from the tetrahedral calculation and torus–sphere correspondence, unfolding checks that the mean of the McShane sum is 1 / 2 . Its constancy still comes from McShane’s theorem. The cusp partition and unfolding do different jobs: one sums gaps on one surface; the other integrates a curve sum over all surfaces.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: How the example becomes a volume recursion.
records.text: How the example becomes a volume recursion.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: How the example becomes a volume recursion.
records.text: For a surface with positive boundary lengths, Mirzakhani’s generalized McShane identity partitions a distinguished boundary of length L 1 by gap functions associated with embedded pairs of pants. Its right-hand side is L 1 . Integration makes that side L 1 V g , n ( L ) . On the other side, group the pants by topological type and unfold each orbit sum. Removing the chosen pants leaves surfaces of smaller complexity. Their volumes, together with the explicitly known gap kernels and the length–twist factors, evaluate the unfolded terms. Consequently the unknown volume is related to lower-complexity volumes; this is a recursion, not just another integral representation [ 75 , Section 8] . The punctured-torus example is especially simple because its cut surface is already a pair of pants, whose fixed-boundary moduli space is a point.

records.title: 17.2 Operations that preserve constancy
records.text: 17.2 Operations that preserve constancy

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: 17.2 Operations that preserve constancy
records.text: Finite linear combinations of constant series preserve constancy. Parameter integrals do too when the constant is integrable and Fubini’s theorem applies to the joint sum and integral, or when all terms are nonnegative and Tonelli’s theorem applies. For differentiation on an identified parameter family, one sufficient hypothesis is local uniform absolute convergence of both the series and its first derivatives. Uniform convergence of the original series alone is insufficient. Products give constant double series when Tonelli’s theorem or absolute convergence applies. These operations construct kernels together with their required convergence hypotheses.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: 17.2 Operations that preserve constancy
records.text: Their geometric interpretation needs to be retained. A product usually indexes pairs of curves that may intersect; it is not automatically a disjoint-multicurve sum. A parameter derivative also differentiates lengths if the metric varies with that parameter. In particular, differentiating a constant series with respect to the metric gives the one-form identity ∑ γ F ′ ( ℓ γ ) ⁡ d ℓ γ = 0 , (17.5) under the stated local C 1 control, for a kernel with no additional explicit metric dependence. It does not generally give another scalar identity by differentiating only the displayed weight.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: 17.2 Operations that preserve constancy
records.text: Two possible tests for a proposed constant series follow. One can try to show that (17.5) vanishes on a spanning set of tangent directions at every point; a C 1 series is then constant on each connected component. Alternatively, for real-valued S ∈ L 2 on a finite positive-volume moduli space, let S ¯ be its mean. Then ∫ ℳ ( S − S ¯ ) 2 ⁡ d V W P = 0 (17.6) proves constancy almost everywhere, and everywhere if S is continuous, since WP measure has full support. For a complex-valued series use | S − S ¯ | 2 instead of the square. The second-moment calculation involves pairs of curves, including their intersection patterns. It can be substantially harder than the first unfolding integral.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: 17.2 Operations that preserve constancy
records.text: Thus a useful search for further identities should ask for more than formal closure: a natural index set, a manageable positive weight, a geometric partition or telescoping mechanism, and a convergence proof. The constructions in Sections 18 and 20 illustrate these requirements.

records.text: There are also constant series with substantially different kernels. For example, write ℒ ( x ) = Li ⁡ 2 ( x ) + 1 2 log ⁡ x log ⁡ ( 1 − x ) for the Rogers dilogarithm on ( 0 , 1 ) , extended continuously to its endpoints, and define D ( r ) = ℒ ( sech ⁡ 2 ( r / 2 ) ) + 2 ℒ ( 1 + e − r 2 ) − 2 ℒ ( 1 − e − r 2 ) . On a complete finite-area once-punctured torus, Hu–Tan’s identity is ∑ α simple, unoriented D ( ℓ α ) = π 2 2 . (17.7) Here the index set is the nonperipheral simple spectrum with its curve multiplicities [ 63 , Theorem 2, equation (2)] . Their Theorem 1 treats a positive geodesic boundary with a different, boundary-dependent kernel; the displayed D is the cusped specialization.

records.source: 17 Unfolding and the problem of finding constant series
records.title: 17.3 Other established constant series
records.text: For a closed oriented surface of genus g ≥ 2 , Luo–Tan give explicit dilogarithmic weights f ( P ) , g ( T ) on properly embedded geometric pairs of pants and one-holed tori, each subsurface counted once, such that ∑ P f ( P ) + ∑ T g ( T ) = 8 π 2 ( g − 1 ) = Vol ⁡ ( T 1 X ) . (17.8) Their construction partitions unit tangent directions up to a null set [ 70 , Theorem 1.1 and Section 1.2] . Angular measure 2 π on each unit tangent circle, together with area 4 π ( g − 1 ) , explains the normalization on the right. It illustrates another source of constant series: the invariant measure being partitioned need not live only on a horocycle or a geodesic boundary. The precise, longer subsurface weights are given in that reference.

records.source: 18 Figure-eight curves and simple lifts
records.title: 18.1 The pants trace relation
records.text: Let γ be a closed geodesic with exactly one transverse self-intersection, not a proper iterate. Its two-lobed regular neighborhood is a pair of pants: the two ends of each lobe are adjacent in the cyclic order at the crossing. Its cuffs are essential or peripheral; a compressing disk would give a geodesic monogon or bigon, or make the curve an iterate. After tightening the cuffs, allow coincident cuff images in the ambient surface; this occurs on a one-holed torus. If the three cuff lengths are a , b , c , write t a = 2 cosh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) , t b = 2 cosh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) , t c = 2 cosh ⁡ ( c / 2 ) . A cusp has positive geometric trace 2 , regardless of the sign of a chosen S L 2 lift. For the figure-eight that wraps the a and b cuffs, the trace identity is t γ = t a t b + t c . (18.1) This is Rivin’s pants relation [ 90 , Theorem 1.3] . It also follows directly from tr ⁡ ( A B − 1 ) = tr ⁡ A tr ⁡ B − tr ⁡ ( A B ) with the consistent signs of pants holonomies: choose tr ⁡ A = t a , tr ⁡ B = t b , and tr ⁡ ( A B ) = − t c . Rewriting in positive geometric traces produces the plus sign in (18.1) . One cannot make this replacement in an arbitrary character identity; Section 23 retains signed traces and therefore has a different sign.

records.source: 18 Figure-eight curves and simple lifts
records.title: 18.1 The pants trace relation
records.text: For pants with lengths ( a , b , 0 ) , the two figures that use the cusp as one lobe have traces u = 2 t a + t b , v = t a + 2 t b , t a = 2 u − v 3 , t b = 2 v − u 3 . (18.2) Consequently any weight assigned to this pair of cuffs can be rewritten as a weight in the two associated figure-eight lengths. This gives a direct reindexing of a pants identity. It produces a paired-curve weight; it does not automatically produce a universal function of one figure-eight length.

records.text: Use pants generators a , b , with third cuff c = ( a b ) − 1 and figure γ = a b − 1 . Consider the connected double cover given by χ ( a ) = χ ( b ) = 1 ∈ ℤ / 2 ℤ . Then χ ( c ) = χ ( γ ) = 0 . The a , b cuffs each lift with degree two, while c has two degree-one lifts. The upstairs surface is a four-holed sphere with cuff lengths ( 2 a , 2 b , c , c ) . (18.3) The figure-eight has two closed degree-one lifts, each of which is simple. One way to see this is to lift its two-loop spine: the lifted graph has two vertices, and either lift uses one a edge and one b edge to form a simple cycle.

records.source: 18 Figure-eight curves and simple lifts
records.title: 18.2 What the local double cover accomplishes
records.text: The two lifted cycles meet at both vertices of that graph. Geometrically, the two simple lifts intersect each other twice, once over each lift of the original crossing. Thus two components of the lifted domain do not mean a disjoint multicurve upstairs.

records.source: 18 Figure-eight curves and simple lifts
records.title: 18.2 What the local double cover accomplishes
records.text: There is a further global issue: this particular character of the pants group need not extend to the whole surface. A lobe that is zero in H 1 ( S ; ℤ / 2 ℤ ) —for example, a separating lobe on a closed surface— cannot be assigned value one by an ambient character. Rivin proves a global substitute: a one-double-point geodesic has a simple lift in a fourfold cover [ 90 , Theorem 4.2] .

records.source: 18 Figure-eight curves and simple lifts
records.title: 18.2 What the local double cover accomplishes
records.text: Even when a suitable cover exists, applying an entire simple-curve identity upstairs and projecting downstairs introduces other projected topological types, covering degrees, and multiplicities. Desingularization supplies an important geometric tool, but selecting just the desired downstairs curves requires additional accounting.

records.source: 18 Figure-eight curves and simple lifts
records.title: 18.3 The two types on a punctured torus
records.text: On a once-punctured torus, a figure-eight has a unique essential simple curve α disjoint from it. To see the topological restriction, truncate the cusp and consider the complement of its incompressible pants neighborhood in the resulting compact torus. That complement has Euler characteristic zero and no disk components, so it consists of two annuli. One joins a pants cuff to the cusp boundary; the other joins the remaining two cuffs, which are therefore parallel essential curves. Conversely, any essential simple curve disjoint from the figure can be pushed out of its regular neighborhood and is parallel to these cuffs. Thus its pants neighborhood has one peripheral cuff and two essential cuffs that tighten to α . Cutting along α gives pants of lengths ( a , a , 0 ) , where a = ℓ α and t = 2 cosh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) > 2 .

records.text: There are exactly three unoriented figure-eight classes in these cut pants. Indeed, splitting at the unique crossing gives two simple based lobes; their two distinct peripheral classes determine a choice of two of the three pants cuffs. Traversing them with opposite boundary orientations is the one-crossing class; traversing their product with the other relative orientation is the third cuff. This gives the three choices below:

records.text: The first two are exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution; call their family 𝒩 . The third is hyperelliptic; call its family ℋ . Equal lengths in the first row do not identify the two free-homotopy classes. In torus homology the first family has a primitive class up to sign and the second twice a primitive class, although its geodesics are not proper iterates.

records.text: For a word check, glue pants generators by b = s a − 1 s − 1 . The first two figures can be represented by a 2 b and a b 2 , while the third is a b − 1 = a s a s − 1 . The last word is not a square. The common disjoint class α is recoverable from the figure’s pants neighborhood, so grouping all figure-eights by α has no duplication. More explicitly, the first two words become a 2 s a − 1 s − 1 and a s a − 2 s − 1 in the free basis a , s . Their cyclic words are neither conjugate nor inverse-conjugate. Their homology classes are [ a ] and − [ a ] ; the third has class 2 [ a ] and cyclic word a s a s − 1 , which is not a power of a shorter cyclic word. This also checks primitivity.

records.source: 19 Cutting into pants and varying twists

records.text: Fix an oriented hyperbolic surface of finite type, without cone points, and a pants decomposition with internal cuff lengths a 1 , … , a N > 0 , where N = 3 g − 3 + n . Boundary lengths, including cusps, are fixed. Apart from components parallel to a cutting cuff, cutting a simple multicurve gives disjoint essential arcs in each pair of pants. Cutting a general immersed curve, even a filling one, need not give disjoint arcs: self-intersections may remain inside a pair of pants. Nor are the actual segments generally orthogonal to the cuffs.

records.source: 19 Cutting into pants and varying twists
records.title: 19.1 What data a cut curve retains
records.text: Boundary intersection counts alone lose the relative homotopy classes of the arcs, their cyclic joining pattern, and winding information. For simple multicurves this information is organized by Dehn–Thurston coordinates. For a general immersed curve one must retain a fuller itinerary. Once this topological data is fixed, varying the metric twist is a well-defined and tractable problem.

records.source: 19 Cutting into pants and varying twists

records.text: There are two complementary exact descriptions. One uses arc lengths as generating functions in endpoint positions. The other uses products of holonomy matrices. Both keep the information that intersection counts alone discard.

records.text: Take two distinct ultraparallel geodesic lifts of positive-length cuffs in ℍ 2 , at common perpendicular distance d > 0 . Let u , v be signed distances on the two lines from the perpendicular feet, with compatible orientations. Then D d ( u , v ) = arcosh ⁡ ( cosh ⁡ d cosh ⁡ u cosh ⁡ v − sinh ⁡ u sinh ⁡ v ) . (19.1) For example, in the hyperboloid model use p ( u ) = ( cosh ⁡ u , sinh ⁡ u , 0 ) , q ( v ) = ( cosh ⁡ d cosh ⁡ v , sinh ⁡ v , sinh ⁡ d cosh ⁡ v ) . Then cosh ⁡ D = − ⟨ p , q ⟩ for the Lorentz form of signature ( − , + , + ) , and arcosh is its nonnegative real branch. Reversing one endpoint coordinate changes the sign of the mixed term.

records.source: 19 Cutting into pants and varying twists

records.text: For the ordinary seam between cuffs a , b > 0 of pants with third cuff c ≥ 0 , the right-angled-hexagon relation gives cosh ⁡ d = cosh ⁡ ( c / 2 ) + cosh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) cosh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) sinh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) sinh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) . (19.2) It can also be checked from pants holonomy: translations of lengths a , b on axes at distance d , with the opposed boundary directions, have product trace 2 cosh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) cosh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) − 2 cosh ⁡ d sinh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) sinh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) . Equating this to − 2 cosh ⁡ ( c / 2 ) gives (19.2) , with the same lift signs as (18.1) . For a returning or winding arc, choose the boundary lifts appropriate to its relative homotopy class and use their common perpendicular instead. There is no single seam length that describes all relative arc classes.

records.source: 19 Cutting into pants and varying twists

records.text: For the reduced itinerary of a fixed nonperipheral closed curve, fix the boundary lifts for each segment and retain its integer winding data. Cuff gluing then imposes affine relations on the real endpoint positions, involving the twists τ i . Minimize the sum of the corresponding functions (19.1) over the crossing positions. Every competitor is a piecewise geodesic in the fixed free-homotopy class, so its length is at least the closed geodesic length. The geodesic representative realizes equality: geodesics have no bigons with the cutting cuffs and therefore realize the same reduced itinerary. At the minimum, first variation imposes smooth tangent matching at every crossing. A curve contained entirely in one pair of pants is handled directly by its holonomy; it has no endpoint variables.

records.text: The endpoint Hessian will also control variation in a twist. Put z = cosh ⁡ D d ( u , v ) and S = z 2 − 1 > 0 . Direct differentiation gives ∇ 2 D d = sinh ⁡ 2 d S 3 ( z cosh ⁡ 2 v − cosh ⁡ u cosh ⁡ v − cosh ⁡ u cosh ⁡ v z cosh ⁡ 2 u ) , det ⁡ ∇ 2 D d = sinh ⁡ 4 d cosh ⁡ 2 u cosh ⁡ 2 v S 4 > 0 . (19.3) For example, z u u = z and z 2 − z u 2 − 1 = sinh ⁡ 2 d cosh ⁡ 2 v , while z u v ( z 2 − 1 ) − z z u z v = − sinh ⁡ 2 d cosh ⁡ u cosh ⁡ v . These identities give the displayed matrix. Its positive diagonal and determinant prove strict joint convexity in the two endpoint coordinates. Reversing an endpoint orientation conjugates the Hessian by a sign matrix and preserves positive definiteness.

For a fixed nonperipheral curve word γ , insert these matrices and their inverses into the fixed pants holonomies. The resulting product W γ satisfies 2 cosh ⁡ ( ℓ γ / 2 ) = | tr W γ ( 𝒂 , T 1 ( τ 1 ) , … , T N ( τ N ) ) | . (19.4) With the cuff lengths fixed, its trace is a finite Laurent polynomial in e τ i / 2 . Its coefficients need not all be positive in an arbitrary choice of lifts and coordinates.

records.text: The twist derivative has the cosine formula ∂ ℓ γ ∂ τ i = ∑ p ∈ γ ∩ α i cos ⁡ ϑ p , | ∂ ℓ γ ∂ τ i | ≤ i ( γ , α i ) . (19.5) Angles and twist orientation are chosen consistently, and intersections are counted by passages, including repeated passages for an iterate. Cutting at each crossing proves the cosine formula: endpoint variations inside a segment cancel by stationarity, while the relative displacement across the cuff contributes the tangential projection cos ⁡ ϑ p [ 24 ] . The same argument applies to immersed geodesics. If γ is a power of a cuff, the intersection sum is empty and the derivative is zero.

records.text: Length is strictly convex in one twist τ i whenever i ( γ , α i ) > 0 . Here is a proof that includes nonsimple curves. Hold all pants lengths and the other twists fixed, and use the fixed reduced itinerary above. The segment distances d remain positive and fixed. For two twist values choose the minimizing endpoint configurations. Their affine interpolation is admissible for the interpolated twist. The two full endpoint vectors cannot coincide: at a crossing of α i , the gluing equation contains τ i with coefficient 1 or − 1 , with fixed winding data. Thus a change of this twist cannot be absorbed while leaving all segment endpoints fixed. Strict convexity of the sum in (19.3) , followed by minimization, gives the strict convexity inequality for the geodesic length. This also explains why the conclusion excludes a disjoint cuff, whose twist leaves the length constant. The simple-curve earthquake theorem provides a broader context [ 65 , Theorem 1] ; no extension of that cited statement is needed for the local argument here.

records.text: These ideas overlap with several parts of Mirzakhani’s work, but serve different roles there. Dehn–Thurston coordinates and the definition of combinatorial length for simple multicurves are given in [ 77 , Theorem 3.4 and equation (3.6)] . The comparison with geometric length for an L -bounded pants decomposition is [ 77 , Proposition 3.5 and equation (3.7), p. 107] . The work on general curve orbits studies asymptotically piecewise-linear length, including filling curves and length sublevel volumes [ 78 , Theorem 4.1 and Section 8] . In the basic volume recursion, the cutting curves are simple and the kernel depends on their lengths, so the twist integral itself is just the period a i .

For a nonnegative function F , Tonelli’s theorem gives ∫ ∏ i [ 0 , a i ) ∑ 𝒌 ∈ ℤ N F ( ℓ D 1 k 1 ⋯ D N k N γ ( 𝒂 , 𝝉 ) ) ⁡ d 𝝉 = ∫ ℝ N F ( ℓ γ ( 𝒂 , 𝒖 ) ) ⁡ d 𝒖 . (19.6) As written, the sum is over lattice elements, so the nonnegative equality is valid even if both sides are infinite. For signed functions, impose absolute integrability on ℝ N . To interpret the sum as one term per curve, first quotient any stabilizer and unfold the corresponding nonredundant twist directions; twisting about a disjoint cuff must not produce infinitely many copies of one curve. This quotient may change the lattice and its fundamental domain, so one cannot simply divide an infinite multiplicity out of the displayed formula.

The accompanying WP measure is ∏ i ⁡ d a i ⁡ d τ i . However, the positive cuff orthant times one twist box is the quotient by this particular twist subgroup, not a fundamental domain for the full mapping class group. A further full-moduli integration needs the appropriate orbit unfolding.

records.text: Let X be an oriented one-holed hyperbolic torus with geodesic boundary length b > 0 , or a complete finite-area once-punctured torus when b = 0 . Cut along an essential simple curve α of length a > 0 , and choose an essential simple curve β crossing α once. Normalize the twist origin so that this crossing curve has minimum length at τ = 0 . Set A 2 = cosh ⁡ a + cosh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) cosh ⁡ a − 1 . (20.1) The exact formula is cosh ⁡ ( ℓ β ( τ ) / 2 ) = A cosh ⁡ ( τ / 2 ) . (20.2) It follows from the right-angled-hexagon description of the cut pants; see also [ 43 , Proposition 3.1, pp. 5–6] . Take the positive square root A > 1 . For b = 0 , A = coth ⁡ ( a / 2 ) . The minimum length is r 0 = 2 arcosh ⁡ A .

Then det ⁡ B u = 1 , tr ⁡ B u = 2 A cosh ⁡ ( u / 2 ) , and direct multiplication gives tr ⁡ [ M , B u ] = 2 − 4 sinh ⁡ 2 ( a / 2 ) ( A 2 − 1 ) = − 2 cosh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) , [ M , B u ] = M B u M − 1 B u − 1 . Solving this boundary equation recovers (20.1) . Differentiating (20.2) , with Q = A 2 cosh ⁡ 2 ( u / 2 ) − 1 > 0 , also gives ℓ β ′ ( u ) = A sinh ⁡ ( u / 2 ) Q , ℓ β ″ ( u ) = A ( A 2 − 1 ) cosh ⁡ ( u / 2 ) 2 Q 3 / 2 > 0 . (20.3) In particular | ℓ β ′ | < 1 , consistent with the single crossing in (19.5) .

(20.4) Indeed, differentiating cosh ⁡ ( r / 2 ) = A cosh ⁡ ( u / 2 ) gives ⁡ d u / ⁡ d r = sinh ⁡ ( r / 2 ) / cosh ⁡ 2 ( r / 2 ) − A 2 for u > 0 . The two signs of u explain the factor 2 . (20.9) The second expression telescopes under translation by a , so ∑ n ∈ ℤ H a ( τ + n a ) = 1 . (20.10) All terms are positive and the convergence is exponential on compact twist intervals. More precisely, for N ≥ 0 put L N = ( N + 1 / 2 ) a and P N ( τ ) = ∑ n = − N N H a ( τ + n a ) . Finite telescoping gives P N ( τ ) = 1 2 [ tanh τ + L N 2 − tanh τ − L N 2 ] , 1 − P N ( τ ) = 1 1 + e L N + τ + 1 1 + e L N − τ ≤ 2 cosh ⁡ τ e − L N . (20.12) For r ≥ r 0 , this satisfies K a , b ( r ) = H a ( u ) at the two twists with length r . For r n = ℓ D α n β ( X ) we obtain the pointwise identity ∑ n ∈ ℤ K a , b ( r n ) = 1 . (20.13) This is a constant series proved by telescoping, rather than inferred from its average. Its kernel depends on the distinguished cuff length a and the boundary length b , and its index set is one twist orbit. It is not an unrestricted universal sum over every curve on the surface. The classes D α n β are all distinct as unoriented simple classes, since they cross α once and have distinct integral twist coordinates. Equal lengths, which occur at symmetric twist values, do not merge their labels. Equation (20.11) is also the tail estimate for this K -series.

records.text: The pants viewpoint suggests that orthogeodesic pieces should glue when their boundary data match. There are two levels of matching.

records.source: 21 Matching across cuffs: positions and directions
records.title: 21 Matching across cuffs: positions and directions
records.text: First consider a positive-length cuff a > 0 , with m ≥ 1 distinct endpoint positions x 1 , … , x m and y 1 , … , y m on the two sides. Choose compatible coordinates in ℝ / a ℤ , reversing one induced boundary orientation as needed. For a prescribed cyclic matching σ , a twist τ must satisfy y σ ( j ) − x j ≡ τ ( mod ⁡ a ) ( 1 ≤ j ≤ m ) . (21.1) One endpoint determines τ modulo a ; the remaining m − 1 equations require the cyclic spacings to agree. Integer winding data must also be retained if the curve is marked, rather than only considered modulo a twist. These congruences are necessary and sufficient for the prescribed position matching. They do not supply the direction data of the pieces.

records.source: 21 Matching across cuffs: positions and directions
records.title: 21 Matching across cuffs: positions and directions
records.text: Second, orient a chain by its direction of travel and measure all tangential components in the common cuff coordinate just chosen. A transverse unit-speed geodesic segment has a signed tangential velocity component p ∈ ( − 1 , 1 ) at an endpoint. If S is the sum of segment lengths, the first variation at a glued endpoint has the form ∂ S ∂ x = p i n − p o u t . (21.2) Here p i n is the terminal tangential component of the incoming segment and p o u t the initial component of the outgoing segment. The pieces must approach and leave on the opposite sides of the cut. Equality of their tangential components then also matches the normal components, whose magnitudes are 1 − p 2 and whose signs are fixed by this crossing condition. Stationarity therefore imposes full tangent matching as well as position matching. For orthogonal segments the tangential components vanish, so smooth gluing is automatic once the endpoints match. A generic closed geodesic does not satisfy this orthogonality condition along an arbitrarily chosen pants decomposition.

records.source: 21 Matching across cuffs: positions and directions
records.title: 21 Matching across cuffs: positions and directions
records.text: Equivalently, boundary data live in a phase space ( s , p ) : endpoint position and tangential component. The length of an arc is a generating function, with ⁡ d L = − p s ⁡ d s + p t ⁡ d t , and cuff gluing acts by ( s , p ) ↦ ( s + τ , p ) . A nonperipheral periodic chain with these position and direction matches is smooth and locally geodesic, hence is its closed geodesic representative. Conversely, cutting a transverse closed geodesic gives such a chain. Tangent segments lying on a cuff require separate treatment and are not included in the transverse phase space. The orthospectrum records the special p = 0 representatives. It is excellent input for gap identities and local geometry, but endpoint positions and directions are needed to reconstruct arbitrary glued curves.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.1 Which geodesics enter a cusp?
records.text: Throughout, the surface is oriented, hyperbolic of curvature − 1 , and has no cone points. The statements that simple closed geodesics avoid a sufficiently deep cusp and that simple cusp-ended geodesics enter the cusp are compatible. The first concerns a returning excursion; the second concerns an actual end.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.1 Which geodesics enter a cusp?
records.text: Here is an elementary version of the distinction. Normalize a cusp stabilizer in the upper half-plane to z ↦ z + 1 . A geodesic with two finite ideal endpoints u < v is a semicircle of radius ( v − u ) / 2 . If v − u > 1 , its endpoints interlace those of its translate: u < u + 1 < v < v + 1 . The two geodesics intersect, so the projected geodesic is not simple. Therefore a simple geodesic with two finite endpoints cannot reach height greater than 1 / 2 . A geodesic reaching farther into this lifted cusp while remaining simple must have ∞ as an endpoint, and is vertical. It is perpendicular to every horocycle based at that endpoint.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.1 Which geodesics enter a cusp?
records.text: Choose Y > 1 / 2 large enough that the horocycle H = { y = Y } / ⟨ z ↦ z + 1 ⟩ bounds an embedded sufficiently deep cusp. Simple closed geodesics never cross H . Complete simple geodesics with a cusp end do cross it, normally, and continue indefinitely toward that end.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum

records.text: 22.2 The family used in the gap argument

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.2 The family used in the gap argument
records.text: For this gap discussion assume that the surface is complete, has finite area and at least one cusp, and has no geodesic boundary. A surface with geodesic boundary has additional families of cusp-issued rays that exit through it, and needs the corresponding boundary gap terms.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.2 The family used in the gap argument
records.text: At a point x ∈ H , take the normal geodesic directed away from the cusp. A lift is γ ̃ x ( t ) = x + i Y e − t . (22.1) Its backward end tends to the cusp. Its forward continuation enters the rest of the surface. The relevant question is whether that whole continuation remains simple; the short portion inside the cusp is automatically simple.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.2 The family used in the gap argument
records.text: McShane’s gap argument partitions the horocycle using the behavior of these cusp-issued geodesics. Almost every direction eventually develops the relevant intersection pattern. The exceptional simple directions have measure zero and include cusp-to-cusp arcs and rays spiraling toward closed geodesics or minimal laminations [ 73 ] [ 74 , Theorem 3, p. 4, and the paragraph after Corollary 5, p. 5] . In some conventions a gap contains an isolated simple cusp-to-cusp direction; its interior is therefore not literally made entirely of nonsimple directions. The measure statement is unaffected.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.2 The family used in the gap argument
records.text: For a cusp pants contribution whose two other cuffs are interior, with lengths a , b (allowing their identification on the torus), the combined normalized gap is 2 1 + e ( a + b ) / 2 . (22.2) For example, this is the limit as L ↓ 0 of the geodesic-boundary combined gap divided by L : 2 L log ⁡ e L / 2 + e ( a + b ) / 2 e − L / 2 + e ( a + b ) / 2 → 2 1 + e ( a + b ) / 2 . The boundary gap is Mirzakhani’s 𝒟 contribution [ 75 , Lemma 3.1, equation (3.1), and Theorem 4.2] . This calculation fixes the normalization; the null-set and pants-indexing arguments are separate external inputs. On the punctured torus the two cuffs are copies of one simple curve α , so a = b = ℓ α . The gap contributions sum to one, which is precisely (17.4) . The simple closed curve occurring in the formula labels the pants and their gap. It is not the geodesic crossing the deep horocycle.

records.title: 22.3 An exact truncated cusp-arc formula
records.text: Fix a sufficiently small embedded cusp horocycle of length H > 0 ; here H now denotes its length rather than the horocycle as a set. In pants with other cuffs a , b , let η be the simple cusp-to-cusp geodesic arc separating those cuffs. Truncate its two ends at the horocycle and let d η be the resulting length. With the convention λ η = e d η / 2 , e d η / 2 = t a + t b H , t a = 2 cosh ⁡ ( a / 2 ) , t b = 2 cosh ⁡ ( b / 2 ) . (22.3) The other cuffs may be geodesic or cuspidal, so a , b ≥ 0 . The formula also holds for signed truncated lengths of decorations before the horocycle has been made small enough; this does not assert that an arbitrarily large decorated horocycle is embedded.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.3 An exact truncated cusp-arc formula
records.text: Proof. Normalize the cusp parabolic and horocycle to P = ( 1 q 0 1 ) , q > 0 , y = Y , H = q / Y . Choose cuff holonomy lifts A , B with A B = P , tr ⁡ A = t a and tr ⁡ B = − t b , and write c A for the lower-left entry of A . Then tr ⁡ ( A − 1 P ) = t a − q c A = − t b , q c A = t a + t b . The image under A of the horizontal horocycle has Euclidean diameter 1 / ( c A 2 Y ) and is based at A ( ∞ ) . The vertical ideal geodesic from ∞ to this point represents the separating return arc. The upper intersection with that image horocycle is at height 1 / ( c A 2 Y ) , so its signed truncated distance is log ⁡ ( c A 2 Y 2 ) and satisfies e d η / 2 = | c A | Y . Substituting H = q / Y proves the formula. ◻

records.text: On the once-punctured torus, essential unoriented simple cusp-to-cusp arc classes correspond to essential unoriented simple closed-curve classes: each is the unique such class disjoint from the other [ 94 , Proposition 14.1(i),(iv)] . Cutting along the closed curve gives ( a , a , 0 ) pants, hence e d α / 2 = 2 t α H = 4 cosh ⁡ ( ℓ α / 2 ) H . (22.4) As a check, each decorated ideal triangle contributes horocyclic corner lengths u / ( v w ) , v / ( u w ) and w / ( u v ) in the convention λ = e d / 2 [ 94 , Section 11, equation (30)] . The two triangles of a torus therefore give H = 2 ( u 2 + v 2 + w 2 ) / ( u v w ) , as in that paper’s Section 12. By (22.4) , the positive trace of the curve disjoint from edge u is H u / 2 . Thus the trace conversion is derived here from the cusp-parabolic calculation, with no additional factor of 2 in the lambda convention.

records.text: Substitute t α = ( H / 2 ) e d α / 2 into ∑ α h ( t α ) = 1 . This gives a literal orthospectral form of McShane’s identity: ∑ η simple, unoriented cusp-to-cusp ( 1 − 1 − 16 e − d η H 2 ) = 1 . (22.5) All square roots use the nonnegative real branch. Indeed, 16 e − d η / H 2 = 4 / t α 2 < 1 , so the summands are real and positive, even when a chosen signed truncated length is negative. The index set retains the topological arc labels. Scaling the horocycle length by k changes each truncated length to d η − 2 log ⁡ k ; therefore e − d η / H 2 and every summand are decoration-independent.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.4 The precise relation to Basmajian’s identity
records.text: For a compact hyperbolic surface with nonempty geodesic boundary, Basmajian’s boundary-length identity is, with oriented orthogeodesics, ℓ ( ∂ X ) = ∑ η oriented 2 log ⁡ coth ⁡ ( ℓ η 2 ) . (22.6) The oriented convention and this normalization are also explicit in [ 84 , Section 4.2, p. 26] . If each unoriented orthogeodesic is counted only once, the coefficient is 4 instead of 2 . This spectrum includes nonsimple arcs. The gap comes from the shadow on a boundary lift of another boundary lift, and hyperbolic trigonometry expresses its length in terms of their common perpendicular. To see the coefficient directly, take one boundary lift to be x = 0 and the other the semicircle with center coth ⁡ d and radius csch ⁡ d , where d = ℓ η > 0 . Its ideal endpoints are tanh ⁡ ( d / 2 ) and coth ⁡ ( d / 2 ) . Their perpendicular projections to x = 0 have these heights, and the shadow length is log ⁡ ( coth ⁡ ( d / 2 ) / tanh ⁡ ( d / 2 ) ) = 2 log ⁡ coth ⁡ ( d / 2 ) . The opposite orientation records the shadow at the other end. For a large d , the equivalent expression 2 log ⁡ ( 1 + 2 e − d / ( 1 − e − d ) ) retains the positive gap without subtracting nearby numbers.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.4 The precise relation to Basmajian’s identity
records.text: Equation (22.5) uses the simple, truncated cuspidal orthospectrum . Generic normal rays in the McShane gaps are not the canonical returning orthogeodesics, and adding all nonsimple cusp arcs would change the identity. Thus the orthospectrum interpretation is exact after the index set, truncation, and weights have been specified.

records.source: 22 Cusps, McShane gaps, and the orthospectrum
records.title: 22.4 The precise relation to Basmajian’s identity
records.text: Parlier’s coherent-marking framework gives a systematic bridge between these boundary and cusp identities [ 84 ] . The common mechanism is a measure decomposition of boundary initial data, with orthogeodesic geometry computing gaps. What differs is the chosen stopping or marking rule and the resulting index set. This is the useful sense in which the pants, McShane, and Basmajian pictures fit together. A finite selection of cusp arcs or orthogeodesics is not a verified approximation to these whole-surface identities unless its omitted classes are also controlled.

records.title: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.text: This section develops a spectral version of the crossing-resolution idea. We work throughout with a marked, closed, oriented hyperbolic surface X of genus g ≥ 2 and curvature − 1 . All closed curves are unoriented, unless conjugacy classes are explicitly being counted with orientation. A multicurve may have parallel components; its length and number of components count those multiplicities. The empty multicurve is included. Cusps and boundary require additional trace terms and are not included in the assertions below.

records.source: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.title: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.text: The inputs are the twisted Selberg formula, the simple-multicurve basis of the character ring, and Dylan Thurston’s sign-coherence theorem for the bracelet basis. We prove the intervening length and coefficient estimates explicitly. The resulting construction is a deduction from these established inputs, with no novelty claim.

records.source: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.title: 23.1 Broken geodesics and the effect of reconnection
records.text: Colin de Verdière’s construction approximates loop space by broken geodesics and applies stationary phase to a complex heat parametrix [ 19 ] . For an equal time subdivision the finite-dimensional energy is E N ( x 0 , … , x N − 1 ) = N ∑ i = 0 N − 1 d ( x i , x i + 1 ) 2 , x N = x 0 , with consecutive points within the injectivity radius. The critical equations match incoming and outgoing velocities; the critical value for a constant-speed closed geodesic is ℓ γ 2 . On a hyperbolic surface every closed geodesic, including a self-intersecting one, has positive transverse length Hessian. For a unit-speed parametrization and a periodic normal variation f ( s ) N ( s ) this is δ 2 L γ ( f , f ) = ∫ 0 ℓ γ ( ( f ′ ) 2 + f 2 ) ⁡ d s . Consequently simplicity cannot be selected by retaining only positive Hessians in the ordinary loop space.

records.source: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.title: 23.1 Broken geodesics and the effect of reconnection
records.text: Reconnection enlarges that space. In a small embedded disk of radius r about a transverse crossing of angle θ ∈ ( 0 , π ) , the two original diameters have total length 4 r . The two noncrossing pairings have lengths L 0 = 4 arsinh ⁡ ( sinh ⁡ r sin ⁡ ( θ / 2 ) ) , L ∞ = 4 arsinh ⁡ ( sinh ⁡ r cos ⁡ ( θ / 2 ) ) . (23.1) Both are strictly less than 4 r . In particular, 4 r − L 0 = 4 r ( 1 − sin ⁡ ( θ / 2 ) ) + O ( r 3 ) . The descent is first order in the surgery radius. Tightening the resolved components to geodesics, and discarding contractible components, cannot increase total length. This is a change of connectivity, not a negative direction of the original Hessian. An unconstrained global minimization would select the empty cycle; we instead keep the different multicurves as algebraic observables.

(23.2) The phrase “unnegated trace basis” refers to this sign convention, not to positivity of the function on S U ( 2 ) . The functions T C are linearly independent on the unitary character variety and form a basis of the complex character ring after complexification; see Charles–Marché [ 20 , Theorem 1.1] . The usual Kauffman convention uses − tr per component, so differs by a basis sign. The relation tr ⁡ A tr ⁡ B = tr ⁡ ( A B ) + tr ⁡ ( A B − 1 ) resolves crossings.
