records.text: Lemma 23.2 (Length ordering of resolutions). If δ is primitive and k ≥ 1 , then a C ( δ k ) ≠ 0 ⇒ ℓ X ( C ) ≤ k ℓ X ( δ ) . Equality can occur only when δ is simple and C = k δ , the multicurve consisting of k parallel copies. Its coefficient in that case is 1 . If δ is nonsimple, the inequality is strict.

records.source: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.title: 23.3 Length triangularity and the first atom
records.text: Proof. For a primitive nonsimple geodesic, completely resolve its crossings. Each state has a representative obtained by reconnecting the original arcs in small disks. Formula (23.1) gives a strict total saving; tightening and removing contractible loops cannot increase length. At a multiple intersection, resolve the endpoints in a small convex disk by a noncrossing pairing. The original pairing uses intersecting diameters, so at least one new chord is shorter than a diameter. The same strict conclusion holds. Coefficient cancellation cannot introduce a state not produced by a resolution.

(23.6) For each fixed C the gap is locally uniform in X , and uniform on compact subsets of marked Teichmüller space. If C has two or more nonparallel support components, every contributing orbit has length strictly greater than ℓ X ( C ) ; this statement does not assert that the resulting signed measure is nonzero.

records.text: Proof. Lemma 23.2 gives the lower support bound. At m ℓ α the only contributing pair is ( δ , k ) = ( α , m ) , with coefficient 1 . This gives the stated mass, whose numerator is the primitive length. Every other contributing pair has strictly greater length. Local finiteness gives a gap at each X .

records.text: For uniformity on a compact set of marked metrics, use uniform bilipschitz comparison with one reference metric. The target lengths are bounded, and only finitely many orbit labels can have lengths within one unit above them somewhere on the compact set. The strictly positive differences for those finitely many labels have a positive minimum; all remaining labels have a gap at least one. The argument also applies to nonparallel C , without requiring a nonzero first mass after cancellation. ◻

Then ℓ X ( α ) = ⟨ σ α X , L χ ( L ) ⟩ ⟨ σ α X , χ ( L ) ⟩ , ⟨ σ α X , χ ⟩ = ℓ α sinh ⁡ ( ℓ α / 2 ) . (23.7) This is an exact localized identity, with no limiting interchange. Figure 7 relates the local reconnections to this separate first-atom statement for a simple support.

records.text: The passage from compactly supported tests to heat kernels needs a growth estimate. A direct crossing count gives an exponential in ℓ γ 2 and only a small-time conclusion. Bracelet positivity gives a stronger estimate.

records.source: 23 Simple multicurve coefficients of a twisted trace formula
records.title: 23.4 An exponential coefficient bound from bracelet positivity
records.text: At skein parameter + 1 , Dylan Thurston proves that every diagram has a sign-coherent expansion in the bracelet basis [ 22 , Theorem 2] . A bracelet supported on a simple curve β with winding n is the Chebyshev element P n ( z β ) [ 22 , Proposition 4.4] . Distinct bracelet support curves are disjoint; their windings are included in the length ℓ X ( D ) = ∑ i n i ℓ X ( β i ) . The canonical twisted Fuchsian evaluation associated to X is positive on bracelet basis elements: B D ( X ) = ∏ i 2 cosh ⁡ ( n i ℓ X ( β i ) / 2 ) > 0 . For a one-component diagram representing γ , its evaluation has absolute value 2 cosh ⁡ ( ℓ X ( γ ) / 2 ) . Sign coherence therefore gives ∑ D | b D ( γ ) | B D ( X ) = 2 cosh ⁡ ( ℓ X ( γ ) / 2 ) . (23.8) A spin structure identifies the + 1 and − 1 skein algebras by signs on diagrams. Changing to (23.2) also changes only basis signs. On a simple generator this replaces z β by ϵ β T β , with ϵ β ∈ { 1 , − 1 } ; the identity P n ( ϵ x ) = ϵ n P n ( x ) shows that the bracelet-to-multicurve coefficient magnitudes are unchanged. All the absolute estimates below are consequently valid in our unnegated trace basis. The positive Fuchsian evaluation is an auxiliary algebraic estimate; the Laplacians defining σ C X still use unitary twists.

The subscript 2 denotes the trace bound | tr ⁡ ρ ( α ) | ≤ 2 ; this is a weighted coefficient norm, not an L 2 norm. The Chebyshev recurrence gives ∑ r | [ x r ] P n ( x ) | 2 r ≤ 2 ( 1 + 2 ) n . A bracelet has at most 3 g − 3 distinct support curves, so ∥ B D ∥ 2 ≤ 2 3 g − 3 e c X ℓ X ( D ) . In (23.8) the nonzero coefficients are integers, and B D ( X ) ≥ e ℓ X ( D ) / 2 . Hence ℓ X ( D ) ≤ ℓ X ( γ ) + 2 log ⁡ 2 for every occurring D , and ∑ D | b D | ≤ 2 e ℓ X ( γ ) / 2 . Therefore ∥ tr ⁡ γ ∥ 2 ≤ C X e ( 1 / 2 + c X ) ℓ X ( γ ) , C X = 2 3 g − 2 e 2 c X log ⁡ 2 . (23.14) Gaussian decay dominates this exponential bound and the orbit count. It follows that Tr ⁡ e − t Δ ρ − 2 I X ( t ) = ∑ C ∈ 𝒞 ( S ) H C X ( t ) T C ( ρ ) , t > 0 , (23.15) where I X ( t ) = Area ⁡ ( X ) 4 π ∫ ℝ r tanh ⁡ ( π r ) e − t ( r 2 + 1 / 4 ) ⁡ d r , ∑ C | H C X ( t ) | 2 # C < ∞ . The series is uniform on the unitary character variety and locally uniform for ℜ t > 0 . It is obtained by taking the limit of the finite length-cutoff expansions; the preceding absolute estimate justifies the rearrangement. For a compact set of such t , ℜ ( 1 / t ) has a positive lower bound, so the same Gaussian majorant proves local uniformity and termwise holomorphy. On the spectral side, smooth cutoffs of the Gaussian converge in the Schwartz topology on the real spectral axis and at the finitely many imaginary spectral parameters; the compact-surface Weyl bound justifies passing to the heat trace for each unitary twist.

records.text: This construction does not assert uniqueness among arbitrary infinite expansions of a continuous function. For example, ∥ tr ⁡ ρ ( α 2 n + 1 ) ∥ ∞ ≤ 2 , while its T α coefficient is ( − 1 ) n ( 2 n + 1 ) . Coefficient extraction is therefore not bounded for the uniform norm on unitary characters. Our coefficients are fixed by the finite spectral tests first; the estimates then justify their heat transform.

records.text: Two concrete further problems are to continue D C ( s ) beyond its proved half-plane, with control of the coefficient operation, and to find combinations of coefficients whose cancellations organize globally over pants. Formula (23.26) provides an exact local model for the second problem. An identity constant in X would require an additional normalization or geometric partition; the existence of these transforms alone does not supply that constancy. Section 24 strengthens the lattice benchmark and gives explicit orbital gaps, uniform recovery estimates, and a conditional counting criterion.

records.source: 24 Quantitative counting and coefficient cancellation
records.title: 24 Quantitative counting and coefficient cancellation
records.text: The preceding construction raises a quantitative question: can explicit crossing resolutions give a counting remainder with a specified exponent and geometric constants? We first give an elementary counting benchmark. We then prove a systole-dependent gap and a uniform recovery estimate, and show on a fixed surface why their exponential separation scale is unavoidable for estimates of individual orbital terms. Finally, a finite support coefficient and a smoothing criterion isolate the additional estimate needed for connected-curve counting.

For a fixed nonzero rational multicurve γ 0 , write N X , γ 0 ( R ) = # { γ ∈ Mod ⁡ ( S ) γ 0 : ℓ X ( γ ) ≤ R } . Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi prove that there exists κ ( g ) > 0 such that N X , γ 0 ( R ) = c X , γ 0 R d + O X , γ 0 ( R d − κ ( g ) ) . (24.1) Their theorem also allows variable negative curvature; the hyperbolic case suffices here [ 14 , Theorem 1.1] . The theorem states the existence of the exponent rather than a numerical value. Its proof uses exponential mixing of the Teichmüller flow. A specified exponent and certified constants for a given surface would therefore be additional quantitative information. This distinction does not diminish the proved power saving or establish that its constants are intrinsically noncomputable.

records.text: Proof. Here is the quantitative lattice estimate needed for the argument. Let Λ ⊂ ℝ d have covolume v and a fundamental cell F ⊂ B ( 0 , ρ ) . Suppose the convex compact body K has volume V and contains B ( x 0 , r ) , where r > 0 . Put a = ρ / r . Then V v ( R − a ) + d ≤ # ( Λ ∩ R K ) ≤ V v ( R + a ) d . (24.3) Indeed, up to null sets the lattice cells tile Euclidean space, so ( R K ) ⊖ B ρ ⊂ ⋃ p ∈ Λ ∩ R K ( p + F ) ⊂ R K + B ρ . Here A ⊖ B ρ = { x : x + B ρ ⊂ A } . Writing K 0 = K − x 0 , we have B r ⊂ K 0 and R K + B ρ ⊂ R x 0 + ( R + a ) K 0 . For R ≥ a , also R x 0 + ( R − a ) K 0 ⊂ ( R K ) ⊖ B ρ . Taking volumes proves (24.3) ; the lower bound is zero when R < a . Notice that the homotheties are centered at R x 0 , since the origin can be a boundary point of K . For R ≥ a this gives the explicit bound | # ( Λ ∩ R K ) − V v R d | ≤ d 2 d − 1 V v ρ r R d − 1 . (24.4) The upper increment ( R + a ) d − R d dominates the lower decrement.

records.text: To apply this estimate, use a finite rational polyhedral cone subdivision subordinate to train-track charts, with their actual integral weight lattices. Length is convex in each train-track cone, by the surgery argument in [ 14 , Theorem 5.1] . The finite polyhedral handling of chart overlaps is given in [ 14 , Lemma 5.1 and the end of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in Section 8] ; a further finite subdivision makes the chambers convex and their overlaps faces. In the coordinates of each chamber Q i , the sets K i = Q i ∩ { ℓ X ≤ 1 } are compact convex bodies. Indeed, continuity and positivity of length on the projectivized cone give boundedness, and scaling an interior point of a full-dimensional chamber to length less than one gives an interior ball. Lower-dimensional chambers are handled as faces. Apply (24.3) in every full-dimensional chamber with its own integral lattice. Their normalized volumes sum to B ( X ) . In particular, a coordinate parity condition must be absorbed into the lattice covolume, not silently discarded.

records.text: Shared faces can be assigned to one chamber. Alternatively, count closed chambers and bound the overcount. If a face has dimension 1 ≤ k ≤ d − 1 , its unit-length part lies in a ball of radius A F , and its induced lattice has shortest nonzero vector of length δ F , disjoint-ball packing gives # ( Λ F ∩ R K F ) ≤ ( 1 + 2 R A F δ F ) k . Zero-dimensional faces contribute at most one point each. The finite sum of these bounds is O X ( R d − 1 ) . Removing the zero multicurve changes the answer by one. ◻

records.source: 24 Quantitative counting and coefficient cancellation

records.text: This refines the elementary total-multicurve lattice asymptotic in [ 77 , Proposition 3.1] ; it is a benchmark for the new machinery. Formula (24.4) is explicit once bounds on its geometric inputs are certified. It does not supply numerical values for an unspecified surface. Fixed train-track representatives give linear upper bounds for length, and coordinate length estimates such as [ 15 ] help certify the required geometric bounds. Hyperbolic length itself need not be piecewise linear. For example, choose an interior rational weight vector in a chamber and scale it until a certified linear upper bound for length is less than one. A small coordinate ball then remains both in that chamber and below the upper bound, producing an inradius certificate. For an outer-radius certificate one needs a lower bound for length on the chamber’s unit coordinate sphere. A finite filling collection of curves, together with collar inequalities and their piecewise-linear intersection functions, supplies such a bound. The constants can deteriorate when the surface degenerates; no uniformity over the entire moduli space is being asserted. On a fixed compact subset of Teichmüller space the same finite coordinate construction and uniform length comparisons give uniform versions of the bounds.

On every closed hyperbolic surface X of genus at least two there are fixed distinct simple curves a , b , and simple curves c n with R n = ℓ X ( c n ) → ∞ , such that a , b , c n bound embedded geodesic pairs of pants. Let γ n be their figure-eight curves with T γ n = T a T b − T c n , and set A = cosh ⁡ ℓ X ( a ) 2 cosh ⁡ ℓ X ( b ) 2 , L n = ℓ X ( γ n ) . records.text: Proof. Choose distinct disjoint nonseparating curves a , b whose complement after cutting is connected, of genus g − 2 with four boundary components. In this cut surface let c bound a pair of pants with one copy of a and one copy of b . Choose an essential interior curve intersecting c . A Dehn twist about that curve fixes the boundary and gives infinitely many distinct curves c n , each bounding a pair of pants with a , b . Straightening preserves this configuration. Finiteness of the closed-geodesic length set below a bound implies R n → ∞ .

The support count is a discrete connectivity statistic, and a general weighted multicurve cannot be assigned that statistic by a continuous function on all of measured-lamination space. Knowing its value for each integral point does not establish its density in expanding regions.

records.source: 24 Quantitative counting and coefficient cancellation

records.text: Connectivity itself is computationally accessible: the Agol–Hass–Thurston interval-pairing algorithm counts components of a normal curve in time polynomial in the triangulation size and the logarithm of its normal weight [ 18 , Theorem 12 and Corollary 13] . For the one-support selector, first pass from C to its primitive integral divisor C 0 : then r ( C ) = 1 if and only if C 0 has one component. This division takes place in an integral-lamination chart before supplying a normal representative to the component algorithm; admissibility and parity must be respected in the chosen coordinates. A coordinate gcd alone is not a substitute for this integral-divisibility test. Counting the components of C without this division would count parallel copies separately and would not compute r ( C ) . The missing quantitative input is an average estimate for this selector, or a cancellation formula that supplies such an estimate. Moreover, (24.16) is a target positive partition function. It has not been identified with an evaluation of the signed coefficient heat expansion. Defining a linear operation T C ↦ z r ( C ) on finite trace polynomials alone does not change an orbital length ℓ γ into the resolved length ℓ X ( C ) , and does not supply that identification.

records.text: The two limiting regimes must be distinguished. The first-atom theorem uses t ↓ 0 for G α ( t ) , or a large positive Laplace parameter. A positive sum over simple curves detects growing lengths through Z X s i m p l e ( s ) as s ↓ 0 . With the denominator Gaussian e − L 2 / ( 4 t ) , lengths of order R correspond to t of order R 2 . These are different asymptotic problems, and the latter positive measure has not been constructed by summing the present signed coefficient measures.

records.source: 24 Quantitative counting and coefficient cancellation
records.title: 24.8 The remaining analytic step
records.text: The support polynomial (24.16) specifies a useful aggregate target. Its finite Fourier extraction is stable, and its primitive inversion is exact. A positive-axis Laplace remainder such as (24.20) does not by itself justify an equally strong sharp counting error; quantitative desmoothing or suitable complex-parameter estimates are still required. Proposition 24.5 gives one sufficient condition with an explicit loss. The unresolved task is to construct and bound that smoothed connected-support observable using the coefficient relations, including their pants cancellations, before taking absolute values. No improved connected-simple-curve exponent is claimed here.

records.text: Continue throughout with a closed hyperbolic surface of genus at least two; the pants cuffs below are essential curves, not specialized peripheral trace constants. There are two concrete ways to advance the preceding construction. First, an explicit bounded coefficient functional cancels every one-self-intersection primitive geodesic together with all its iterates, simultaneously over all pants. Second, a product in the length-convolution algebra gives a unit first atom for every weighted multicurve, including those with disconnected support. Neither result proves a new counting remainder. They also reveal why a fixed linear functional cannot remove every nonsimple primitive curve.

They are nonperipheral cyclically reduced words in the pants group, so their geodesics are nonsimple. Embedded geodesic pants are convex; these intersections persist in the ambient surface. An ambient proper root would traverse the same geodesic image inside the pants and give a root in the pants group, which the homology vectors exclude. Here the word primitive does not assert membership in a free basis of the pants group.

records.text: Proof. Resolve the crossings of the union of geodesics in an input multiset. Every resulting multicurve has total length at most the input length. If some primitive component is nonsimple, or two distinct components intersect, resolving a genuine transverse crossing and tightening gives strict shortening, as in the earlier length-ordering argument. Repeated components can be separated by small perturbations; a transverse crossing already present in a component or between distinct geodesics retains a strict shortening.

records.text: A counting remainder can imply mixing when the counts determine an appropriate operator, or when they retain sufficiently uniform information about both endpoints of orbit segments. The following elementary converses make these hypotheses and their quantitative losses explicit. They do not identify the simple-curve counting function of Section 24 with such an operator.

Its normalized transition chain alternates between two states; the correlation of ( 1 , − 1 ) with itself is ( − 1 ) n . The closed-path count detects what the total path count misses: tr ⁡ ( A n ) = m n + ( − m ) n . Thus a scalar sequence can suffice when it is a complete trace encoding of a suitable operator. records.text: Continuous time introduces a separate return-time issue. The full shift on m symbols has exactly m n fixed points for its n th iterate and is mixing for its Bernoulli measure. Suspend it with constant roof 1 : Y = ( Σ × [ 0 , 1 ] ) / ( ( x , 1 ) ∼ ( σ x , 0 ) ) . For the suspension flow ϕ t , the mean-zero function F ( [ x , u ] ) = e 2 π i u is well defined and satisfies F ∘ ϕ t = e 2 π i t F , ∫ F ¯ F ∘ ϕ t ⁡ d ν = e 2 π i t . The flow is therefore not mixing. Its physical periods lie in a lattice, so this is not an example of an unoscillating continuous-time prime-orbit asymptotic. It shows why a discrete-time counting converse does not automatically pass to a suspension. Ruling out arithmetic return times is necessary; quantitative flow estimates also require control of approximate eigenfunctions or high-frequency return-time operators. The role of these additional geometric conditions is discussed in [ 13 ] .

records.text: There is also a simple geometric deduction. In Babillot [ 12 , Theorem 1] , the universal cover is a simply connected complete Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature bounded above by a negative constant, and the acting discrete isometry group is non-elementary. A quasi-product measure means a flow-invariant measure whose geodesic current is in the measure class of a product of its two boundary measures. For such a measure, nonarithmeticity of the closed length spectrum implies mixing. Assume a nonzero finite such measure, normalized to probability, and suppose the full primitive closed-orbit count is finite at each cutoff and satisfies π ( T ) ∼ C e h T T , C , h > 0 , as T → ∞ through all real values. If all periods belonged to a ℤ , a > 0 , then π ( n a + a / 4 ) = π ( n a + 3 a / 4 ) , whereas the ratio of their proposed main terms tends to e h a / 2 > 1 . This contradiction proves nonarithmeticity and hence qualitative mixing under the stated structural hypotheses. No rate follows from this argument. For a polynomial simple-curve main term C T d , the corresponding fixed-shift ratio tends to one, so this argument does not transfer to simple-curve counting.

records.text: The preceding converse criteria suggest retaining two independent sets of curve data. This section carries that proposal through three concrete steps. First, a tensor product of the coefficient construction recovers marked filling pairs, hence square-tiled differentials. Second, an exactly weighted count of Teichmüller orbit segments unfolds into a time integral of correlations. Third, an elementary de-averaging argument converts an assumed counting remainder into a mixing rate. An arithmetic torus calculation illustrates the additional cancellation needed to prove such a remainder. The identities and conditional implications below do not constitute a new proof of Teichmüller mixing.

Here ⊠ is the external product of locally finite discrete measures, and both C and D range over integral weighted multicurves. records.text: For definiteness let S be closed, oriented, and of genus g ≥ 2 . A pair ( A , B ) of nonzero measured foliations is filling if i ( A , C ) + i ( B , C ) > 0 for every nonzero measured foliation C . The condition is stronger than i ( A , B ) > 0 . The realization theorem of Gardiner–Masur, also proved by Wentworth using harmonic maps, identifies filling pairs with marked nonzero holomorphic quadratic differentials [ 1 , Theorem 1.6 and Corollary 1.7] ; see also [ 2 , Theorem 1.6] for the equivariant homeomorphism and its integral interpretation. Use the convention that A = 𝒱 ( q ) is the vertical foliation with transverse measure | d x | , and B = ℋ ( q ) is the horizontal foliation with transverse measure | d y | , in coordinates q = d z 2 . Write q ( A , B ) for the resulting differential. Then Area ⁡ ( q ( A , B ) ) = i ( A , B ) , (27.1) g t q ( A , B ) = q ( e t A , e − t B ) , g t = diag ⁡ ( e t , e − t ) . (27.2) In particular q ̂ ( A , B ) := q ( A i ( A , B ) , B i ( A , B ) ) has unit area. This is a genuine parametrization of points of the flow space; the two foliations are the stable and unstable data of a single differential, rather than two unrelated curves.

records.source: 27 Filling-pair coefficients and a weighted mixing converse
records.title: 27.2 Filling pairs as actual coordinates for the flow
records.text: For an integral pair A = ∑ i a i α i , B = ∑ j b j β j in minimal position, there is a concrete realization. Put a rectangle of horizontal width a i and vertical height b j at each intersection of α i with β j , and glue the sides in the cyclic orders supplied by the embedded curves. The filling condition makes the complementary regions disks. Minimal position excludes bigons. A complementary 2 k -gon yields total angle k π , hence a zero of order k − 2 ; k = 2 gives a regular point. Integral side lengths subdivide the rectangles into unit squares, with edge identifications by translations or half-turns. The total number of squares is ∑ i , j a i b j i ( α i , β j ) = i ( A , B ) . Thus the discrete objects suggested by the pair coefficients are precisely square-tiled half-translation surfaces. Translation surfaces form the subcollection in which the half-translation structure has trivial linear holonomy. Formula (27.2) is then visible by stretching and contracting the rectangles.

Equivariance of the pair parametrization identifies the stabilizer of the measured pair with the finite automorphism group of its differential: Stab ⁡ Γ ( A , B ) = Stab ⁡ Γ ( A ) ∩ Stab ⁡ Γ ( B ) . For integral pairs, finiteness also follows by acting on the finite filling graph A ∪ B and then on its complementary disks; for general measured foliations it follows from the realized conformal automorphism group. It matters here that one fixes the measured foliations, including their scales. Stabilizers of projective foliations can contain nontrivial flow translations.

To obtain a growing family, prescribe the two curve types separately and take the diagonal quotient: ( Γ α × Γ β ) f i l l / Γ . If Γ α = Stab ⁡ Γ ( α ) and Γ β = Stab ⁡ Γ ( β ) , its classes are the relevant double cosets in Γ α ∖ Γ / Γ β , represented by ( α , ϕ β ) . For an orbifold volume comparison the natural weight of such a class is 1 | Γ α ∩ ϕ Γ β ϕ − 1 | . This is the same stabilizer factor appearing in the square-tiled count of [ 2 , Section 1 and Section 3] .

records.text: Fix a connected component 𝒬 of a stratum and put h = dim ⁡ ℂ 𝒬 . The real period-coordinate dimension of its cone is 2 h , and the unit-area locus has real dimension 2 h − 1 . If D r multiplies every period by r , then area is multiplied by r 2 . With the appropriate period lattice and its covolume fixed, Lebesgue measure ν scales by ν ( D r E ) = r 2 h ν ( E ) . Consequently an area cutoff L has natural count exponent h , whereas a common linear scale R = L has exponent 2 h . These conventions must not be interchanged when converting powers into rates in flow time.

records.text: For the closed principal quadratic stratum h = 6 g − 6 . For a quadratic stratum with n specified singularities, including marked regular points, h = 2 g − 2 + n when the differential is not a square; the corresponding square locus has h = 2 g − 1 + n . Lower-dimensional strata require their own period-coordinate lattice and Masur–Veech measure. The ambient product of two full-dimensional Thurston measures cannot serve as their volume form. Likewise, counting all square-tiled surfaces in a stratum does not by itself approximate an arbitrary affine invariant measure on a smaller locus.

records.title: 27.4 The existing square-tiled counting theorem and the new target
records.text: The passage from pairs to square tilings is established mathematics, not a new consequence of the coefficient construction. Arana-Herrera’s effective theorem counts square-tiled surfaces in a fixed connected component with prescribed horizontal and vertical multicurve types, with a power-saving error in the area cutoff [ 3 , Theorem 1.1] . Its proof explicitly passes through Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi orbit counting and effective horosphere equidistribution, using exponential Teichmüller mixing [ 3 , Theorem 3.2 and its proof] . Using that estimate to recover mixing would therefore not provide an independent proof of mixing.

records.text: There is a useful distinction already visible in that paper. When one foliation type is fixed and the other is unrestricted, standard lattice counting replaces the mapping-class-orbit estimate [ 3 , Theorem 3.9] . This provides a tractable elementary benchmark. It does not control arbitrary initial and terminal observables at long times: their weights must still be tracked through the reciprocal scaling in (27.2) .

The first can be effective without implying the second. Here is a precise local calculation. Put A t = diag ⁡ ( e t I d , e − t I d ) , H t ( x ) = F ( x ) G ( A t x ) , where F ∈ C c 1 ( ℝ 2 d ) has support in a fixed compact set K and G ∈ C b 1 ( ℝ 2 d ) . For R ≥ 1 define Q R ( t ) = R − 2 d ∑ k ∈ ℤ 2 d H t ( k / R ) , I ( t ) = ∫ ℝ 2 d H t ( x ) d x . Then, for t ≥ 0 , | Q R ( t ) − I ( t ) | ≤ C K R − 1 e t ∥ F ∥ C 1 ∥ G ∥ C 1 . (27.3) Indeed, partition space into cubes of side R − 1 , compare the value at one corner with the integral on its cube, and use ∥ ∇ H t ∥ ∞ ≤ ∥ ∇ F ∥ ∞ ∥ G ∥ ∞ + e t ∥ F ∥ ∞ ∥ ∇ G ∥ ∞ . Only O K ( R 2 d ) cubes contribute. A fixed smooth density can be absorbed in F . To model unit-area data by an ambient lattice, one can first use a smooth radial cutoff in a compact area shell bounded away from area zero; radial normalization is then smooth. This local argument does not supply uniform estimates across arbitrarily many period-coordinate charts, their boundaries, or the cusp.

records.text: There is a concrete discrete count whose remainder does imply mixing. The necessary weight can be specified exactly, and the passage from a cumulative count to a correlation has an elementary quantitative proof. This construction uses the full unit cotangent bundle, with its Masur–Veech measure supported on the principal stratum; it is not an automatic statement for an arbitrary lower-dimensional stratum or affine invariant measure.

records.text: The exact weight e h t / J x ( q , t ) cannot simply be omitted. To compare normalizations, let μ 0 be the local-product normalization of [ 4 , Section 2.2] and put V 0 = μ 0 ( Y ) . Our probability normalization is μ = μ 0 / V 0 . The conditional probability measures s x are unchanged, whereas m = m 0 / V 0 and J x = J 0 , x / V 0 . Use the canonical Hubbard–Masur factors λ ± belonging to μ 0 . For endpoints in a fixed compact subset of the principal stratum, and for segments spending at least half their time in a suitable larger compact set, [ 4 , Proposition 2.5] then gives J x ( q , t ) = V 0 − 1 e h t λ − ( q ) λ + ( g t q ) + O ( e ( h − α ) t ) . (27.18) If the endpoint factors are bounded away from zero on the sets under consideration, then, uniformly there for sufficiently large t , the relative error in (27.18) is less than 1 / 2 . Taking the reciprocal yields e h t J x ( q , t ) = V 0 λ − ( q ) λ + ( g t q ) + O ( e − α t ) . (27.19) Thus the natural approximation is an ordinary bisector count with the two endpoint observables divided by the corresponding Hubbard–Masur factors, with the factor V 0 . Usual bisector counts often use the direction pointing back from the terminal point; that convention replaces the terminal differential here by its negative and requires the corresponding substitution in G . There are three distinct estimates to check: the weighted bisector remainder, the accumulated error in replacing the exact Jacobian, and the contribution of segments failing the recurrence or compactness conditions. Formula (27.18) is not a global uniform asymptotic.

Suppose cutoffs at height H have this error, the counting constant for cutoff observables grows as e b H , and their k th flow-derivative bounds are uniform. That smoothing proof gives an error of the form ε k + ε − 1 e b H − δ t + e − a H . Balancing the three terms yields η k = δ 1 + b / a + 1 / k . For trigonometric polynomials supported on | m | , | n | ≤ M , the sharper explicit estimate is | D c ( f , g ) − ( ∫ f ) ( ∫ g ) | ≤ τ ( c ) c M φ ( c ) ∥ f ̂ ∥ ℓ 1 ∥ g ̂ ∥ ℓ 1 , M ≥ 1 . For a prime c = p and M < p , the numerator τ ( c ) c M can be replaced by 2 p ; a frequency with exactly one zero coordinate gives the Ramanujan sum − 1 .

records.text: Uniformity cannot be omitted: for f c ( x ) = g c ( x ) = e ( c x ) , both continuous means vanish but D c ( f c , g c ) = 1 . The growth of the test norms in (27.23) correctly prevents a false conclusion. This is the arithmetic counterpart of the expanding-frequency problem. The result is a rigorous benchmark for endpoint-residue decorrelation. A proof of mixing of the modular geodesic flow still requires the appropriate unfolding, radial/time weights, and cusp estimates; no higher-genus analogue of the displayed Kloosterman bound has been established here.

records.text: For comparison, fix two primitive oriented torus curve types. In the corresponding matrix model, with positive oriented intersection c , the remaining residue is a ( mod ⁡ c ) , ( a , c ) = 1 , so there are exactly φ ( c ) possibilities. Thus the unweighted count already has the power-saving asymptotic ∑ c ≤ L φ ( c ) = 3 π 2 L 2 + O ( L log ⁡ L ) . Indeed, substitute φ ( c ) = c ∑ d ∣ c μ ( d ) / d and sum first over c = d k ; the leading term is 1 2 L 2 ∑ d ≤ L μ ( d ) / d 2 and the remainder is O ( L log ⁡ L ) . These constants belong to this oriented matrix model; no unmentioned quotient by signs or orbifold automorphism weight is being included. The exact formula φ ( c ) by itself says nothing about the values of S ( m , n ; c ) for ( m , n ) ≠ ( 0 , 0 ) .

records.source: 27 Filling-pair coefficients and a weighted mixing converse
records.title: The remaining independent estimate
records.text: We have obtained an exact encoding of the filling-pair data, an exact weighted orbit-counting identity, and a quantitative implication from a remainder for that count to mixing. What has not been established is a norm-controlled estimate of the form (27.8) from the coefficient distributions. The tensor product and the first-corner extraction do not by themselves estimate a sum over returning mapping classes. In particular, an exact or quantitative comparison between the resulting square-tiled sums and the bisector kernel has not yet been supplied.

records.source: 27 Filling-pair coefficients and a weighted mixing converse
records.title: The remaining independent estimate
records.text: The next analytic target can now be stated without referring vaguely to a good scalar counting error: construct that comparison and control the nonconstant two-endpoint weights in (27.6) , with the exact inverse Jacobian or with a proved replacement and a controlled discarded contribution. The modular calculation shows what success looks like. Its scalar count determines the zero mode, while the Kloosterman estimate controls the coupled nonzero modes. No analogous estimate for the principal higher-genus kernel is proved here. Section 28 does close a different, explicitly defined return calculation on the exceptional marked-torus model of the nonsquare genus-two ( 2 , 2 ) stratum.

records.source: 27 Filling-pair coefficients and a weighted mixing converse
records.title: The remaining independent estimate
records.text: An independent proof of the displayed remainder would yield a new route to mixing for the specified Masur–Veech measure, with the full rate in (27.13) when derivative endpoint weights are controlled, and the cutoff rate (27.17) . The single-test estimate (27.9) remains an alternative under its weaker hypothesis. It would not by itself classify invariant measures or orbit closures, nor would it establish spectral properties of a separate cocycle. Those require additional information beyond correlations of the base flow.

records.text: The hyperelliptic quotient makes genus two a concrete testing ground for the counting converse. There are two useful reductions. The hyperbolic quotient gives a compact polyhedral model for every conformal base. On the nonsquare stratum with two double zeros, a second, flat quotient identifies the entire stratum flow space, up to finite markings, with the admissible invariant open subset of an affine homogeneous space of marked flat tori. Its complement has measure zero. The latter identification is specific to that stratum.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.1 Six branch points and the compact polyhedron
records.text: 28.1 Six branch points and the compact polyhedron

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.1 Six branch points and the compact polyhedron
records.text: Every genus-two Riemann surface X is hyperelliptic. Its quotient map π : X → ℙ 1 has six branch values: the Riemann–Hurwitz formula reads 2 = 2 ( − 2 ) + 6 . With compatible markings the quotient induces a holomorphic Teichmüller isometry 𝒯 2 , 0 ≅ 𝒯 0 , 6 ; see, for example, [ 101 , Corollary 1.2(3)] . Both sides have complex dimension three. The four-pointed sphere is the corresponding genus-one example.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.1 Six branch points and the compact polyhedron
records.text: The hyperelliptic involution is an isometry of the curvature- − 1 metric on X . The quotient metric is a hyperbolic sphere with six cone angles π , and its area is 2 π . Alexandrov’s hyperbolic realization theorem therefore gives a unique compact convex polyhedron in ℍ 3 whose intrinsic boundary metric is this quotient metric, allowing the usual degenerate case of a doubled convex polygon [ 102 , Theorem 1.1] . There are six vertices, all with intrinsic total angle π . Conversely, take the double cover of such a cone sphere branched at its six vertices. Each cone angle becomes 2 π , so the lifted metric is smooth, complete, and of curvature − 1 . Riemann–Hurwitz identifies its genus as two. Thus this compact-polyhedral realization is an exact model for the genus-two hyperbolic metric, with the appropriate finite labeling and marking conventions.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.1 Six branch points and the compact polyhedron
records.text: This metric must be distinguished from the complete hyperbolic metric on the sphere with the six branch values deleted. The latter has six cusps and area 8 π ; it is the metric to which the ideal-polyhedron realization applies. Passing between them uses uniformization within the same punctured conformal class. It does not identify their lengths, vertex data, or volume forms. In particular, fixed intrinsic cone angles at compact vertices are not automatically linear constraints on the dihedral angles.

records.text: Choose a coordinate with all six branch values finite and write X : y 2 = B 6 ( z ) := ∏ i = 1 6 ( z − a i ) . (28.1) The forms ⁡ d z / y and z ⁡ d z / y form a basis of H 0 ( X , K X ) . Their three symmetric products are linearly independent and, by Riemann–Roch, span H 0 ( X , K X 2 ) . Hence every holomorphic quadratic differential is q X = P 2 ( z ) ⁡ d z 2 y 2 = π * q 0 , q 0 = P 2 ( z ) B 6 ( z ) ⁡ d z 2 , deg ⁡ P 2 ≤ 2 . (28.2) In particular, every such differential is invariant under the hyperelliptic involution. At a branch point the order transforms by ord ⁡ p ( π * q 0 ) = 2 ord ⁡ π ( p ) ( q 0 ) + 2 . (28.3) For a generic polynomial with two distinct roots away from the branch values, this gives 𝒬 2 ( 1 4 ) ↔ 𝒬 0 ( 1 2 , − 1 6 ) , with finite choices of labels understood. This is the genus-two case of the hyperelliptic covering construction in [ 103 , Section 1.1.3] . The descended flat metric has six angles π at its poles and two angles 3 π at its zeros. It is different from the hyperbolic cone metric of the preceding subsection.

It commutes with g t = diag ⁡ ( e t , e − t ) , with no change of the time parameter. Period-lattice covolumes, finite labelings, and orbifold stabilizers must still be tracked when comparing unnormalized Masur–Veech volumes; the area factor alone is not a formula for those volumes.

records.title: 28.3 The nonsquare stratum with two double zeros
records.text: Write 𝒬 2 n s ( 2 , 2 ) for quadratic differentials with two double zeros which are not global squares of Abelian differentials. The superscript is essential: the squares of differentials in ℋ 2 ( 1 , 1 ) have the same quadratic zero orders but form a different locus.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.3 The nonsquare stratum with two double zeros
records.text: Formula (28.2) gives an elementary description. The differential is a global square exactly when P 2 is the square of a polynomial of degree at most one: this follows by writing every Abelian differential as ( a z + b ) ⁡ d z / y . In homogeneous degree-two notation this includes a double root at infinity. A nonzero constant P 2 is therefore a square, while a degree-one P 2 has a simple zero at each of the two unbranched points at infinity and cannot lie in 𝒬 2 ( 2 , 2 ) . For degree two, a simple root at a branch value gives one double zero by (28.3) , and a simple root elsewhere gives two simple zeros. Thus, to obtain two double zeros without a square, the roots must be two distinct branch values, say b 1 , b 2 . After relabeling the remaining four branch values, X : y 2 = B 4 ( z ) ( z − b 1 ) ( z − b 2 ) , B 4 ( z ) = ∏ i = 1 4 ( z − a i ) , q X = c ( z − b 1 ) ( z − b 2 ) ⁡ d z 2 y 2 = π * ( c ⁡ d z 2 B 4 ( z ) ) , c ∈ ℂ * . (28.4) The six values a 1 , … , a 4 , b 1 , b 2 are distinct. Downstairs q 0 = c ⁡ d z 2 / B 4 ( z ) has four simple poles and is regular at the two additionally marked points b 1 , b 2 : 𝒬 2 n s ( 2 , 2 ) ↔ 𝒬 0 ( − 1 4 , 0 , 0 ) . (28.5) The regular marks cannot be discarded. They are branch values of X → ℙ 1 , and their positions supply four real parameters.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.3 The nonsquare stratum with two double zeros
records.text: For each fixed X , choosing the unordered pair of branch values b 1 , b 2 gives ( 6 2 ) = 15 complex lines of nonsquare ( 2 , 2 ) differentials in the three-dimensional cotangent space. Area normalization leaves a phase on each line. Consequently this stratum meets every conformal base, but its unit-area locus has real dimension seven, compared with eleven for the full principal unit cotangent locus. Its Masur–Veech measure is an intrinsic stratum measure, not a conditional probability obtained by restricting the principal measure to a set of measure zero.

records.text: The orientation double cover of the four-pole differential q 0 is the elliptic curve E : w 2 = B 4 ( z ) , ω = c ⁡ d z w , ρ * q 0 = ω 2 . (28.6) Choose one branch point of E → ℙ 1 as the origin. The involution is then v ↦ − v , and its four fixed points are E [ 2 ] . The two marked regular points lift to unordered pairs ρ − 1 ( b 1 ) = { p , − p } , ρ − 1 ( b 2 ) = { q , − q } . Their admissibility conditions are exactly p , q ∉ E [ 2 ] , p ≠ q , p ≠ − q . (28.7) Conversely, a flat torus ( E , ω ) with an origin and such two points gives the sphere E / { ± 1 } with its four poles and two regular marks. The unique connected double cover of this sphere branched at all six marked values is X , and pullback of q 0 gives (28.4) . The cover is connected because its monodromy is the nontrivial homomorphism to ℤ / 2 ℤ on every small loop around a branch value; six such loops satisfy the sphere relation. It is unique because those loops generate the fundamental group of the punctured sphere.

Both covers have degree two, but their branch sets differ: the former is branched at the four a i , the latter also at b 1 , b 2 . Equivalently, the square root of B 4 is not in the function field ℂ ( z , B 4 ( z ) ( z − b 1 ) ( z − b 2 ) ) .

(28.8) Thus the unit-area marked torus corresponds directly to the unit-area genus-two differential, with no further area scaling. The entire construction commutes with the S L 2 ( ℝ ) action on flat charts. In particular its time parameter is exactly the Teichmüller time used above. records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.5 A homogeneous finite cover
records.text: Choose a full symplectic level-two structure on the torus and choose an ordering and one lift from each of the two pairs { ± p } , { ± q } . Together with the origin, level two labels the four two-torsion points and hence the four poles. Set Γ 2 = ker ⁡ ( S L 2 ( ℤ ) → S L 2 ( ℤ / 2 ℤ ) ) , G 2 = S L 2 ( ℝ ) ⋉ ( ℝ 2 ⊕ ℝ 2 ) , where S L 2 ( ℝ ) acts in the standard way on both vector factors. Our group law and right-quotient convention are ( A , u 1 , u 2 ) ( B , v 1 , v 2 ) = ( A B , u 1 + A v 1 , u 2 + A v 2 ) , (28.9) Y 2 = G 2 / ( Γ 2 ⋉ ( ℤ 2 ⊕ ℤ 2 ) ) . (28.10) A representative ( A , u 1 , u 2 ) describes the area-one torus ℝ 2 / A ℤ 2 with marked points [ u 1 ] , [ u 2 ] . Right multiplication by ( γ , n 1 , n 2 ) changes the representative to ( A γ , u 1 + A n 1 , u 2 + A n 2 ) , which is exactly change of the lattice basis preserving level two and change of the two point lifts. The presence of − I in Γ 2 causes no singularity in this homogeneous quotient: right translation by a discrete subgroup on a Lie group is free. Here A and − A give the same physical lattice and the same level-two data. A finer congruence level gives an additional finite cover. The spectral argument below uses level two specifically; its conclusion about the base spectrum is not automatically inherited by further covers.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.5 A homogeneous finite cover
records.text: Delete the locus where one of the points is two-torsion or where [ u 1 ] = ± [ u 2 ] , and call the resulting open set Y 2 ∘ . In each torus fiber the deleted set is a finite union of real codimension-two subtori. It has Haar measure zero and its complement is connected. Since the base S L 2 ( ℝ ) / Γ 2 is connected, so is Y 2 ∘ . Forgetting the finite marking choices gives a finite equivariant local parameterization of 𝒬 2 n s , 1 ( 2 , 2 ) . The finite choices include the distinguished origin over a pole, the level structure, the ordering of the two regular marks, and their signs. Their changes preserve Haar measure and commute with the S L 2 ( ℝ ) action; the stratum is their finite quotient. Over the coarse-moduli locus without additional automorphisms this is an ordinary finite covering. If one retains the ubiquitous genus-two hyperelliptic involution in the orbifold stabilizers, its fixed order-two contribution must also be included in unnormalized volume conventions. No infinite marking choice is being discarded in this finite-cover statement.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.5 A homogeneous finite cover
records.text: The flow is left multiplication: g t [ A , u 1 , u 2 ] = [ a t A , a t u 1 , a t u 2 ] , a t = diag ⁡ ( e t , e − t ) . (28.11) The admissible set Y 2 ∘ is invariant under this action. Although the coordinates ξ i = A − 1 u i ( mod ⁡ ℤ 2 ) are unchanged in a fixed lattice chart, a change A ↦ A γ changes them by ξ i ↦ γ − 1 ξ i . Therefore they are not globally fixed torus coordinates on the quotient. This monodromy is essential in the later Fourier calculation.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.6 Haar measure and the period lattice
records.text: The group G 2 is unimodular, and its Haar measure is ⁡ d A ⁡ d u 1 ⁡ d u 2 , where ⁡ d A is Haar measure on S L 2 ( ℝ ) . In a local lattice chart, u i = A ξ i and det ⁡ A = 1 , so its quotient measure is the product of modular Haar measure and Lebesgue probability on ( ℝ 2 / ℤ 2 ) 2 . The modular quotient has finite Haar volume and each torus fiber has volume one, hence Y 2 has finite volume.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.6 Haar measure and the period lattice
records.text: Before area normalization, local coordinates are the two complex lattice periods and the two complex positions of the marked points. These are four complex coordinates, agreeing with dim ⁡ ℂ 𝒬 2 n s ( 2 , 2 ) = 4 . The covering construction transports these coordinates to quadratic-differential period coordinates by a fixed linear map on each marked chart. This can be seen without a global classification theorem. The orientation cover of q X is the fiber product X ̂ : w 2 = B 4 ( z ) , t 2 = ( z − b 1 ) ( z − b 2 ) , y = w t , ω ̂ = c ⁡ d z w . Its map to E is a double cover branched at { p , − p , q , − q } . Thus its relative periods are integral linear combinations of torus periods and marked-point positions, after paths and lifts have been fixed. Transfer on absolute cycles and paths between p and − p , or between q and − q , recover the torus periods and twice the point positions, up to periods. Consequently the inverse change of coordinates is rational linear. The integral period lattices are commensurable; factors of two can occur, so the map need not be unimodular. This is the period-coordinate construction underlying the stratum measure [ 103 , Sections 1.1.1–1.1.2] .

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.6 Haar measure and the period lattice
records.text: It follows that the transported Masur–Veech measure is a constant multiple of Lebesgue measure in these cone coordinates. More explicitly, write the torus area as s > 0 , put A = s B with det ⁡ B = 1 , and use the point coordinates ξ i = A − 1 u i . Up to a fixed positive constant the cone measure is s 3 ⁡ d s ⁡ d B ⁡ d ξ 1 ⁡ d ξ 2 . Restricting by area as in (28.8) therefore makes the unit-area measure a constant multiple of Haar measure on Y 2 . After normalizing to probability and accounting for the finite covering, the measures agree. No numerical identity between unnormalized volumes is asserted without a choice of lattice and labeling conventions. The measure-zero exclusions in Y 2 \ Y 2 ∘ do not affect this probability identification.

records.text: For observables compactly supported inside Y 2 ∘ , extension by zero gives smooth observables on the homogeneous space. Thus estimates proved there pass to the stratum after lifting the observables and, if necessary, averaging over the finite markings. For observables which grow near collisions, extension and norm control require additional estimates; a null collision set alone is not a bound on such observables.

records.text: The affine homogeneous model admits a direct calculation which does not use a general Teichmüller mixing theorem. Let G = SL ⁡ 2 ( ℝ ) , 𝖠 = G ⋉ Mat ⁡ 2 × 2 ( ℝ ) , Λ = Γ ⋉ Mat ⁡ 2 × 2 ( ℤ ) , where Γ = Γ ( 2 ) initially. The group law is ( g , v ) ( g ′ , v ′ ) = ( g g ′ , v + g v ′ ) . Set Y 2 = 𝖠 / Λ , with Haar probability measure μ , and let a t = diag ⁡ ( e t , e − t ) act by left translation. A point is a unit-area lattice together with two marked vectors modulo that lattice. If one counts the origin as a marked point, this is a torus with three ordered marked points. Coincidence loci have measure zero and may be removed. Any application to a particular quadratic stratum uses its separately established geometric identification with this model or a finite quotient; an arbitrary finite cover cannot be discarded without checking its base spectrum.

For F ∈ L 2 ( Y 2 ) expand, in the L 2 sense, F ( g , u ) = ∑ M ∈ Mat ⁡ 2 × 2 ( ℤ ) F M ( g ) e 2 π i tr ⁡ ( M T u ) . (28.12) The equivariance relation is F M ( g γ ) = F γ − T M ( g ) . (28.13) Consequently each Γ -orbit of frequency matrices contributes a G -invariant summand isometric to L 2 ( G / Γ M ) , Γ M = { γ ∈ Γ : γ T M = M } . (28.14) Indeed, Parseval followed by unfolding the orbit sum gives ∫ G / Γ ∑ M ′ ∈ Γ ⋅ M | F M ′ ( g ) | 2 ⁡ d g = ∫ G / Γ M | F M ( g ) | 2 ⁡ d g .

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: Fiber Fourier coefficients and their stabilizers
records.text: The stabilizers are elementary. If M = 0 , the summand is L 2 ( G / Γ ) . If M has rank two, Γ M = { 1 } . If M has rank one, write M = v w T , with v a primitive integral column vector and w ≠ 0 an integral column vector. Then Γ M fixes v under the transpose action. It is a subgroup conjugate to a discrete unipotent group, hence is amenable. For example, if v = ( 1 , 0 ) T and Γ = Γ ( 2 ) , Γ M = { ( 1 0 2 n 1 ) : n ∈ ℤ } . No transitivity assertion about primitive vectors under Γ ( 2 ) is required: one simply sums over all its frequency orbits. The same rank distinction appears in the fiber Fourier analysis of [ 104 , Section 4, especially Lemma 4.3] .

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: Fiber Fourier coefficients and their stabilizers
records.text: The trivial representation of an amenable group is weakly contained in its regular representation. Induction preserves weak containment and takes the regular representation of a closed subgroup to that of G . Thus every nonzero-frequency summand in (28.14) is tempered. See [ 105 , Lemma 2.3 and Remark 2.4] . The whole orthogonal complement of the fiber average is tempered, including its countably many frequency orbits. This gives uniform control of their sum; there is no frequency-dependent implied constant left to sum. Explicitly, for every f ∈ C c ( G ) , all summands satisfy ∥ π [ M ] ( f ) ∥ ≤ ∥ λ G ( f ) ∥ ; their Hilbert direct sum satisfies the same inequality.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: Fiber Fourier coefficients and their stabilizers
records.text: This simple stabilizer argument is enough for the present rate estimate. It does not claim a complete irreducible spectral decomposition. The corresponding finer decomposition for one relative marked vector is developed in [ 108 ] ; in particular, that paper’s genuine part contains no complementary series.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: The base spectrum at level two
records.text: The quotient Γ ( 2 ) ∖ ℍ is the thrice-punctured sphere. The finite-area theorem of [ 107 , Theorem 2] states that the discrete eigenvalue λ 2 g − 2 + n exceeds 1 / 4 , counting λ 0 = 0 and including residual as well as cuspidal eigenvalues. For ( g , n ) = ( 0 , 3 ) , there is therefore no positive discrete eigenvalue at or below 1 / 4 . The continuous spectrum starts at 1 / 4 . Since − I ∈ Γ ( 2 ) , the base representation factors through PSL ⁡ 2 ( ℝ ) . All non-tempered nontrivial representations of PSL ⁡ 2 ( ℝ ) in this setting are spherical complementary-series representations and would produce a Laplacian eigenvalue in ( 0 , 1 / 4 ) ; this is the d = 1 specialization of the unitary-dual description in [ 9 , Section 1] . It follows that L 0 2 ( G / Γ ( 2 ) ) is tempered. The same conclusion holds for Γ = SL ⁡ 2 ( ℤ ) , by pullback from that quotient to the level-two cover.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.10 What the marked-torus calculation settles
records.text: The compact polyhedron encodes the genus-two hyperbolic base, whereas the marked flat torus encodes the nonsquare ( 2 , 2 ) differential and its flow. They use different intrinsic metrics and are linked by the same six branch values. The affine model gives an exact Fourier decomposition, an explicit global correlation bound, and the finite weighted return sum with remainder (28.22) . These are conclusions of the calculation, not hypotheses imported from general Teichmüller mixing. The inputs are classical: amenability and induction, the Cowling–Haagerup–Howe bound, the elementary S L 2 spherical function, and the absence of positive small spectrum on the thrice-punctured sphere. Related marked-torus harmonic analysis is already developed in [ 104 ; 108 ] ; no novelty claim for that machinery is intended.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.10 What the marked-torus calculation settles
records.text: The derivative identity (28.23) also makes the counting converse exact in this model. After subtracting the product of means, a bound for the terminal test ( 4 + V ) G recovers the correlation at T with the same exponential saving. In the proof here the direction is Fourier/representation theory to correlations and hence to counts. The identity identifies the reverse implication as well, without making the proof circular.

records.source: 28 Genus two: compact polyhedra and a marked-torus model
records.title: 28.10 What the marked-torus calculation settles
records.text: The restriction to the chosen stratum remains substantial. Although it meets every genus-two conformal base, its unit-area dimension is seven; the principal unit stratum has dimension eleven. The affine expanding Jacobian is e 4 t , whereas the full genus-two Teichmüller polar kernel in Section 27 has exponent 6 . The two kernels cannot be substituted for one another. Section 29 constructs selected primitive-arc observables from the coefficient data with controlled geometric norms. A comparison with the full orbit kernel, and uniform stability of the nonlinear coefficient extraction, remain open. In particular, the O ( R 3 log ⁡ R ) estimate above is not an error term for the unweighted count of connected simple closed geodesics. A comparison with that count, or an extension to the principal stratum 𝒬 2 1 ( 1 4 ) , is a further problem.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.text: The preceding section supplies an explicit analytic norm for its mixing estimate. We now connect that norm to a selected family of simple curves and their coefficient distributions. The genus-one norm-ball obstruction first fixes the attainable scale of sharp remainders. Primitive pole-to-pole arcs then give geometric coefficient observables with uniform rotation and terminal-derivative bounds. Exact affine Gaussian calculations provide independent tests of the analytic estimates. Throughout, a fixed-surface sharp count, a moduli-averaged covariance, and the conditioning of coefficient extraction remain separate problems.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.1 The norm-ball obstruction and the correct error scale
records.text: The genus-one length norm gives a necessary benchmark for any passage from smooth return estimates to sharp simple-curve counting. Let X be a fixed complete hyperbolic once-punctured torus, and let B X be the unit ball of the McShane–Rivin length norm on H 1 ( X ; ℝ ) ≃ ℝ 2 . Put A X ( L ) = # ( L B X ∩ ℤ 2 ) , P X ( L ) = # ( L B X ∩ ℤ p r i m 2 ) . The first count includes the origin and nonprimitive classes. The second counts oriented primitive classes; the count of unoriented simple closed geodesics is N X ( L ) = 1 2 P X ( L ) . Elementary planar lattice counting and Möbius inversion give A X ( L ) = Area ⁡ ( B X ) L 2 + O X ( L ) , (29.1) P X ( L ) = Area ⁡ ( B X ) ζ ( 2 ) L 2 + O X ( L log ⁡ L ) . (29.2) Indeed, P X ( L ) = ∑ d μ ( d ) ( A X ( L / d ) − 1 ) , with d ≪ X L ; the boundary errors sum as L ∑ d ≪ X L d − 1 . These are the upper estimates behind [ 16 , Theorem 4.1] , with the orientation factor made explicit here.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.1 The norm-ball obstruction and the correct error scale
records.text: The next theorem in that paper concerns a dense set of hyperbolic structures. Its mechanism is an infinitely flat boundary point whose supporting normal is rational with respect to the homology lattice. The subsequent Conjecture 4.3 proposes an O ( L 1 / 2 + ε ) error for the modular torus; thus the obstruction is not asserted there for every individual surface. The phrase “at least O ( L ) ” in Theorem 4.2 should be separated from the literal modern assertion limsup ⁡ | E X ( L ) | / L > 0 . The elementary argument below proves the precise consequence needed here: no fixed improvement of the exponent below one is possible under the stated flat-point hypothesis. We do not use it to claim a literal Ω ( L ) bound.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.1 The norm-ball obstruction and the correct error scale
records.text: Proposition 29.1 (A primitive-row obstruction). Let B ⊂ ℝ 2 be a strictly convex compact body with the origin in its interior. Suppose that p ∈ ∂ B has irrational radial direction, a rational supporting normal, and infinite graph-flatness. Then, for E B ( L ) = # ( L B ∩ ℤ p r i m 2 ) − Area ⁡ ( B ) ζ ( 2 ) L 2 , and every ε > 0 , there are c ε > 0 and arbitrarily large L such that | E B ( L ) | ≥ c ε L 1 − ε . (29.3) In particular E B ( L ) = O ( L 1 − η ) fails for every fixed η > 0 .

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.1 The norm-ball obstruction and the correct error scale
records.text: Proof. An integral unimodular change of coordinates makes the supporting normal vertical. Write p = ( α , h ) , with h > 0 and α / h irrational. Near p , the upper boundary has the form y = h − f ( x − α ) , f ( 0 ) = 0 , where f ≥ 0 is convex. Infinite graph-flatness means that for every integer N > 2 there are C N , ρ N > 0 such that 0 ≤ f ( s ) ≤ C N | s | N ( | s | ≤ ρ N ) . Fix N , let n run through primes, and set L n = n h , δ n = L n − 1 , L n + = L n + δ n . The line y = n supports L n B at the single point ( L n α , n ) . Its first coordinate is irrational, so this row contains no lattice point of L n B .

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.1 The norm-ball obstruction and the correct error scale
records.text: In L n + B , the same row lies a normalized depth h δ n / L n + below the supporting line. Therefore it contains the horizontal interval centered at L n + α with half-width r n = min ⁡ { ( h 2 C N ) 1 / N ( L n + ) 1 − 1 / N δ n 1 / N , n 4 } . For sufficiently large n the local graph description applies, the first quantity realizes the minimum, and r n ≍ B , N L n 1 − 2 / N . The interval has length at most n / 2 . Among its integer points ( k , n ) , at most one has n ∣ k ; every other point is primitive because n is prime. Thus P B ( L n + ) − P B ( L n ) ≥ 2 r n − O ( 1 ) . The change in the quadratic main term is bounded, since ( L n + ) 2 − L n 2 = 2 + L n − 2 . It follows that max ⁡ { | E B ( L n ) | , | E B ( L n + ) | } ≥ c B , N L n 1 − 2 / N for all sufficiently large primes n . Choose N > 2 / ε to obtain the assertion. To rule out a proposed O ( L 1 − η ) estimate, apply the assertion with 0 < ε < η . ◻

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.1 The norm-ball obstruction and the correct error scale
records.text: The proof works directly with primitive classes, so no cancellation in a Möbius sum needs to be controlled. The short interval [ L n , L n + L n − 1 ] acquires many new primitive points along a nearly flat supporting row, while its predicted main-term increment stays bounded. Infinite flatness alone does not force the row length to be a positive fraction of L n ; that is why the proof gives an exponent-one barrier, not a literal linear lower bound. The distinction between a fixed-surface estimate, an estimate uniform over moduli, and a smoothed estimate must be retained.

records.text: The flatness obstruction has a direct oscillatory-integral interpretation. For illustration, suppose a localized smooth boundary arc has graph y = h − f ( x ) , f ( x ) = a x k + O ( x k + 1 ) , a > 0 , where k ≥ 2 is even. Apply smooth cutoffs supported near this arc and equal to one at the supporting point. Integrating the localized indicator in the normal coordinate first gives, up to rapidly decreasing terms, − e − 2 π i r h 2 π i r ∫ χ ( x ) e 2 π i r f ( x ) ⁡ d x . The substitution x = r − 1 / k u in the stationary-phase calculation gives χ 0 𝟏 B ̂ ( r ν ) = c a , k e − 2 π i r h r − 1 − 1 / k + o ( r − 1 − 1 / k ) , c a , k ≠ 0 . (29.4) where ν is the chosen normal direction and χ 0 is the localized cutoff. The familiar nondegenerate exponent is r − 3 / 2 when k = 2 ; larger contact order weakens it toward r − 1 . Localization matters: the contributions of different supporting points can interfere in the Fourier transform of the whole ball. No global lower bound follows from discarding those phases.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.2 The Fourier and spectral meaning of the obstruction
records.text: Under dilation, 𝟏 L B ̂ ( m ) = L 2 𝟏 B ̂ ( L m ) . Thus a finite-type flat point with a lattice-rational normal contributes on the scale L 1 − 1 / k to the corresponding localized Poisson terms. For an infinitely flat point there is no fixed finite type to insert in this formula. Proposition 29.1 supplies a direct counting argument in that case, without assuming smooth boundary regularity at all nearby points or invoking a formal stationary-phase expansion there.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.2 The Fourier and spectral meaning of the obstruction
records.text: There is also an exact elementary spectral model. On an auxiliary flat torus ℝ 2 / ℤ 2 , define the positive self-adjoint Fourier multiplier 𝖯 X e 2 π i ⟨ m , x ⟩ = ∥ m ∥ X e 2 π i ⟨ m , x ⟩ . Norm equivalence gives a discrete spectrum tending to infinity. Its counting function is A X ( L ) , and restriction to the closed span of primitive Fourier modes has counting function P X ( L ) . Restricting further to the even part identifies m and − m and gives N X ( L ) . This multiplier is defined spectrally; the nonsmooth length norm is not being asserted to be a classical smooth pseudodifferential symbol. At a differentiable point p of its unit ball, a supporting covector ν satisfies ∇ ∥ ⋅ ∥ X ( p ) = ν ⟨ ν , p ⟩ . Thus a lattice-rational normal is exactly a rational direction for the translation velocity of the associated Hamiltonian. This explains the periodic-phase interpretation, without assuming that a global smooth trace formula applies to the length norm.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.2 The Fourier and spectral meaning of the obstruction
records.text: The norm-ball discrepancy is therefore a spectral-projector remainder for this particular length multiplier. Its flat normal directions produce degenerate phases in a regularized Poisson or trace calculation. This is distinct from complementary-series spectrum for the S L 2 ( ℝ ) action on the marked-torus moduli space. In particular, it does not contradict the temperedness statement or the smooth correlation estimate in Section 28 . The rotation-Sobolev issue depends on what is held fixed. A sharp indicator of a nonradial region in fixed physical vector coordinates generally has rotational jumps, so smoothing it introduces growing derivative norms. By contrast, hyperbolic length is unchanged when the flat charts are rotated while the underlying conformal surface stays fixed. A sharp cutoff in that invariant length can therefore lie in the rotation generator’s domain, and a radial flat cutoff can be rotation invariant as well. Sharpness alone is not an obstruction to the stated mixing bound. For those invariant observables, the remaining boundary and regularity issues enter when taking flow derivatives or passing from an averaged correlation to a fixed-surface counting remainder.

Outside a Haar-null invariant subset of Y 2 , the preceding segment projects to an embedded arc avoiding the two regular marked points. Its lift to the genus-two double cover is a nonseparating simple closed regular flat geodesic α m , with ℓ q X ( α m ) = | g m | . records.text: Proof. If two parameters 0 < s , t < 1 on the segment identify on the pillowcase, then ( s − t ) m ∈ 2 ℤ 2 or ( s + t ) m ∈ 2 ℤ 2 . Primitivity forces the corresponding scalar to be an even integer. The first case gives s = t , and the second is impossible. Likewise the interior contains no two-torsion point. The segment hits one of the additional regular marks only if one of its lifts p , q lies on the closed rational circle ℝ g m / g ℤ 2 . For each m this is a null condition in the point fiber. The union over the countable set of primitive m is still null and is invariant under the entire S L 2 ( ℝ ) action.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables

records.text: The preimage of an embedded arc joining two branch values of a double cover is a circle. Removing it leaves a connected cover, since the four other branch values still have nontrivial monodromy; thus the circle is nonseparating. At its endpoints the sphere flat angle π doubles to 2 π , so the two lifted segments join to a regular flat geodesic. Its length is twice | g m | / 2 . Different directions give intersecting regular geodesics with distinct tangents at the Weierstrass point over the origin. Freely homotopic regular geodesics in a nonpositively curved flat metric lie in a flat cylinder and cannot intersect transversely. This proves the last assertion. ◻

records.text: Proof. Two nonparallel lattice vectors u , v have | det ⁡ ( u , v ) | ≥ 1 . If both have length at most R , their unoriented angular separation therefore has sine at least R − 2 . For R < 1 there is at most one primitive direction. For R ≥ 1 , placing the directions on the circle of length π shows that their number is at most π / arcsin ⁡ ( R − 2 ) ≤ π R 2 . Each direction contributes only the two opposite primitive vectors. The displayed bound covers both cases without rounding conventions. ◻

records.text: Rotation of the flat charts fixes the underlying conformal surface and the intrinsic pole-to-pole arcs. Consequently Θ ℓ m = 0 , and differentiation of (29.7) under rotation only replaces f by D J f . Set C * = 1 + π , N f , h = C * ∥ h ∥ ∞ ( ∥ f ∥ ∞ 2 + ∥ D J f ∥ ∞ 2 ) 1 / 2 . The primitive-vector bound proves, uniformly in R ≥ 1 and L > 0 , 𝒮 1 ( ℱ δ ; f , h R , L ) ≤ N f , h . (29.9) This is global, including the modular cusp. Although the curve labels can jump as a regular mark crosses a selected arc, the exceptional walls are S L 2 -invariant. Along almost every group orbit the labels are fixed under the natural marking, and the preceding derivatives are legitimate. Uniform bounds on the difference quotients give the corresponding strong L 2 generator statements.

It is a fiber Fourier projection, not a positivity-preserving deletion of physical segments. It is defined fiberwise before global integrability has been proved; no orthogonal projection on the global L 2 space is being applied to the raw product.

(29.22) To see this, the product of the Fourier coefficients is exp ⁡ [ − π tr ⁡ ( Z T C t Z ) ] , C t = I + a − 2 t , det ⁡ Z = k . Since det ⁡ C t = 2 cosh ⁡ t , an S L 2 change of variables reduces this to the radial Gaussian integral with α = 2 π cosh ⁡ t . Summing the positive and negative determinant orbits gives (29.22) . records.title: 29.10 Sharp boundaries and the rotation norm
records.text: The exact isometry also displays a regularity cost of sharp cutoffs. For a bounded convex body B ⊂ ℝ 2 , ∥ F 𝟏 B , j ∘ k θ − F 𝟏 B , j ∥ 2 2 = area ⁡ ( B △ k θ B ) . The first variation of area under rotation, interpreted using the almost-everywhere outer normal of a convex boundary, gives area ⁡ ( B △ k θ B ) = | θ | ∫ ∂ B | J x ⋅ n ( x ) | ⁡ d s + o ( | θ | ) . Unless B is rotationally invariant, this rules out a finite L 2 rotation derivative. Equivalently, the sharp transform has angular Sobolev regularity of order s < 1 / 2 , but not s ≥ 1 / 2 . The direct summation of tempered K -type estimates requires an order greater than 1 / 2 ; the earlier theorem uses order one.

records.source: 29 From simple-curve coefficients to controlled observables
records.title: 29.10 Sharp boundaries and the rotation norm
records.text: This is a generic boundary-regularity phenomenon. It is not by itself the more specific arithmetic obstruction from the unusually flat McShane–Rivin norm ball. It explains why a smooth correlation bound cannot be applied to a sharp norm-ball count while leaving the observable norm unchanged. Here the body B is held fixed in physical Euclidean coordinates. A cutoff depending only on the hyperbolic length ℓ X ( α ) is unchanged when the quadratic differential is rotated over the same conformal surface X , and does not incur this particular rotation loss. These two kinds of cutoffs must be distinguished. The fixed-surface primitive-lattice count, its Möbius inversion, and its unsmoothing error remain distinct from the affine mean-square identities proved here.

records.text: The alternatives for the sharp primitive remainder are not exhausted by L and L log ⁡ L . Strict convexity already gives the qualitative improvement o ( L log ⁡ L ) , proved below, but supplies no effective intermediate rate. A normalized Möbius formula identifies a sufficient criterion for O ( L ) . An exact dyadic inversion removes the leading area constant from the numerical test, and an inverse-flatness formula measures the contribution of a particular supporting row. Finally we describe the dyadic diagnostic using hyperbolic trace recursion on two tori. A new full campaign reproduces the supplied draft’s counts and rounded block values through length 8192 , with its own precision and provenance records; the historical implementation remains unrecovered. The proofs and the exploratory numerical observations are stated separately.

records.text: Let B be a fixed convex body containing the origin in its interior. Rescale its gauge so that the shortest nonzero integer vector has gauge one; central symmetry is not needed in this subsection. Write a = Area ⁡ ( B ) , A 0 ( u ) = # ( u B ∩ ( ℤ 2 \ { 0 } ) ) , D B ( u ) = A 0 ( u ) − a u 2 , and let P B ( L ) count primitive vectors. For M = ⌊ L ⌋ , Möbius inversion gives the exact identity P B ( L ) − a L 2 / ζ ( 2 ) L = ∑ d ≤ M μ ( d ) d D B ( L / d ) L / d − a L ∑ d > M μ ( d ) d 2 . (30.1) The cutoff is exact because A 0 ( u ) = 0 for u < 1 ; boundary points at u = 1 are included. Moreover L ∑ d > M d − 2 ≤ L / M ≤ 2 for L ≥ 2 , so the final term is bounded uniformly. Thus the linear remainder problem is precisely a boundedness problem for the displayed Möbius-weighted harmonic sum. The prime number theorem alone does not bound it: the geometric weight D B ( L / d ) / ( L / d ) varies with both L and d .

records.text: For a convenient sufficient condition, put ω B ( u ) = sup v ≥ u | D B ( v ) | v , u ≥ 1 . The elementary boundary estimate makes ω B bounded, and it is nonincreasing. Absolute values in (30.1) give | P B ( L ) − a L 2 / ζ ( 2 ) | ≤ C B L ( 1 + ∫ 1 L ω B ( u ) d u u ) . (30.2) Indeed, for d ≤ M , ∫ L / ( d + 1 ) L / d ω B ( u ) d u u ≥ ω B ( L / d ) log ⁡ ( 1 + 1 / d ) ≥ ω B ( L / d ) 2 d , with the harmless interval below 1 treated separately. Consequently the Dini condition ∫ 1 ∞ ω B ( u ) d u u < ∞ implies an O B ( L ) primitive remainder without any Möbius cancellation. With the prime number theorem, this improves to o B ( L ) ; see (31.4) below. In particular any all-point power saving D B ( u ) = O B ( u 1 − η ) , η > 0 , suffices. Infinite graph-flatness does not logically exclude this route: for example a bound u exp ⁡ ( − log ⁡ u ) has no fixed power saving but has an integrable normalized modulus.

records.text: Proposition 30.1 (A qualitative strict-convexity improvement). For every fixed strictly convex compact body B ⊂ ℝ 2 containing the origin in its interior, D B ( L ) = o B ( L ) , P B ( L ) − a ζ ( 2 ) L 2 = o B ( L log ⁡ L ) . These statements supply no quantitative rate of little-oh convergence.

records.text: Proof. Fix a unit vector ν and let w ν ( s ) be the length of the chord B ∩ { x : x ⋅ ν = s } . Its support is an interval [ a ν , b ν ] . Convexity makes w ν concave, and strict convexity makes both extreme supporting chords singletons, so w ν ( a ν ) = w ν ( b ν ) = 0 . A finite continuous concave function on a compact interval is absolutely continuous. Indeed, it is locally absolutely continuous, is monotone on either side of a maximum, and the integral of the absolute value of its monotone one-sided derivative on exhausting interior intervals tends to its total variation. Continuity at the endpoints then extends the fundamental theorem there. The zero extension therefore belongs to W 1 , 1 ( ℝ ) . Moreover ∥ w ν ′ ∥ 1 = 2 max s w ν ( s ) ≤ 2 diam ⁡ ( B ) . Fubini and integration by parts give 𝟏 B ̂ ( r ν ) = w ̂ ν ( r ) , r 𝟏 B ̂ ( r ν ) = 1 2 π i w ν ′ ̂ ( r ) → 0 by the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma. The same formula gives the uniform bound | 𝟏 B ̂ ( ξ ) | ≤ C B / | ξ | .

records.text: Fix a nonnegative smooth function ρ ϵ of integral one, supported in the Euclidean disk of radius ϵ . Choose r 0 > 0 with r 0 𝔻 ⊂ B , and put δ = ϵ / r 0 . Convexity gives the pointwise sandwich 𝟏 ( L − δ ) B * ρ ϵ ≤ 𝟏 L B ≤ 𝟏 ( L + δ ) B * ρ ϵ . For this fixed ϵ , Poisson summation shows that either smoothed lattice count equals its area plus o B , ϵ ( L ) : after division by L , each nonzero-frequency term tends to zero, and the summable majorant is a constant times | m | − 1 | ρ ̂ ϵ ( m ) | . The two areas differ from a L 2 by O B ( ϵ L ) + O B ( ϵ 2 ) . Thus limsup L → ∞ | D B ( L ) | / L ≤ C B ϵ . Letting ϵ ↓ 0 proves the first claim. It implies ω B ( u ) → 0 , and logarithmic Cesàro averaging in (30.2) proves the second. ◻

records.source: 30 Diagnosing the sharp remainder without fitting its main term
records.title: 30.2 A rational-polygon comparison
records.text: The intermediate scales cannot be dismissed merely because the O ( L log ⁡ L ) proof takes absolute values. For a rational polygon 𝒜 that is star-shaped about the origin, Bárány, Martin, Naslund, and Robins prove E 𝒜 ( L ) = Ω ± ( L log ⁡ log ⁡ L ) , while their upper bound for every rational polygon is E 𝒜 ( L ) = O 𝒜 ( L ( log ⁡ L ) 2 / 3 ( log ⁡ log ⁡ L ) 4 / 3 ) . These are Theorems 1.4 and 1.2, respectively, on page 2 of the 31 July 2019 version (arXiv:1509.02201v2) of Primitive points in rational polygons [ 111 ] . The polygons have genuine straight sides. These results do not transfer to a strictly convex McShane–Rivin norm ball; they show why an unspecified arithmetic cancellation is not a proof of a linear error. Even the elementary square illustrates the relevant arithmetic: at integer N ≥ 1 , # ( [ − N , N ] 2 ∩ ℤ p r i m 2 ) = 8 ∑ n = 1 N φ ( n ) . There is also a numerical warning. Freezing a rational polygonal approximation to a strictly convex ball can introduce the polygon’s own totient fluctuations. A fixed area error δ a contributes δ a L 2 ; resolving a linear remainder requires area accuracy o ( L − 1 ) , together with control of points near the two boundaries. The trace enumeration below avoids replacing the norm ball by a polygon.

records.text: Suppose N ( L ) / L 2 → c , put E ( L ) = N ( L ) − c L 2 , and define Δ 2 N ( L ) = N ( 2 L ) − 4 N ( L ) = E ( 2 L ) − 4 E ( L ) . Iterating the latter equality and using E ( L ) = o ( L 2 ) gives E ( L ) = − ∑ j = 0 ∞ 4 − j − 1 Δ 2 N ( 2 j L ) . (30.3) The series is understood as the limit of its telescoping partial sums; it is absolutely convergent under any of the bounds below. Consequently E ( L ) = O ( L ) ⇔ Δ 2 N ( L ) = O ( L ) , and likewise E ( L ) = O ( L log ⁡ L ) ⇔ Δ 2 N ( L ) = O ( L log ⁡ L ) . For example, if | Δ 2 N ( u ) | ≤ C u for every u ≥ L , then | E ( L ) | ≤ C L 4 ∑ j ≥ 0 2 − j = C L 2 . These are asymptotic equivalences, not finite-computation certificates. They eliminate contamination by an inaccurately estimated value of c .
