records.title: 30.3 An exact test independent of the leading coefficient
records.text: If an estimated coefficient c ̃ = c + δ c is subtracted instead, then N ( L ) − c ̃ L 2 L = E ( L ) L − δ c L . Thus a small coefficient error creates a growing normalized drift. The dyadic statistic removes this source of error exactly. It does not remove the possibility of rare large excursions beyond the computed range. For measurements over a block define M ( T ) = sup T ≤ L ≤ 2 T | Δ 2 N ( L ) | L , Q ( T ) = ( 1 T ∫ T 2 T | Δ 2 N ( L ) L | 2 d L ) 1 / 2 . (30.4) The first detects the largest computed excursions, while the second measures their contribution over the whole block. Between events at L = ℓ γ and L = ℓ γ / 2 , Δ 2 N ( L ) is constant. Hence its normalized absolute value decreases between events, and the block supremum is determined by both one-sided event limits and the block endpoints. All events at the same location must be applied together; an arbitrary order of simultaneous positive and negative jumps can create spurious intermediate values. The left limit at the initial endpoint T lies outside the block and is excluded. Its squared integral over such an interval [ a , b ] is exactly D 2 ( 1 / a − 1 / b ) . A coarse integer mesh can miss narrow excursions.

records.text: The exponent-one obstruction does not specify the slowly varying factor in the discrepancy. The local graph itself gives a more precise statement. Let B ⊂ ℝ 2 be strictly convex, compact, and contain the origin in its interior. After an integral unimodular change of coordinates, suppose its unique top point is p = ( α , h ) , with h > 0 and α / h ∉ ℚ . Assume that the upper boundary is a two-sided graph over an open interval about α , and write it as y = h − f ( x − α ) , f ( 0 ) = 0 . For sufficiently small u ≥ 0 , define the one-sided inverse widths ρ + ( u ) = sup ⁡ { s ≥ 0 : f ( s ) ≤ u } , ρ − ( u ) = sup ⁡ { s ≥ 0 : f ( − s ) ≤ u } , W ( u ) = ρ + ( u ) + ρ − ( u ) , where the suprema are restricted to the local graph interval. Strict convexity implies W ( u ) → 0 as u ↓ 0 . The functions ρ ± , and hence W , are concave on a sufficiently small interval: they are inverses of increasing convex functions vanishing at zero. No symmetry between the two sides of the graph is assumed.

records.text: Proposition 30.2 (Inverse flatness controls a primitive-row burst). Let n tend to infinity through primes, put L = n / h , and let δ = δ ( L ) > 0 satisfy δ = o ( L ) . Set T = L + δ . Its width is w n ( δ ) = T W ( h δ T ) . (30.5) The number of primitive lattice points on this row is w n ( δ ) + O ( 1 ) , with an absolute rounding constant, and max ⁡ { | E B ( L ) | , | E B ( L + δ ) | } ≥ 1 2 [ w n ( δ ) − c B ( 2 L δ + δ 2 ) − 2 ] . (30.6) In particular, with δ = L − 1 , max ⁡ { | E B ( L ) | , | E B ( L + L − 1 ) | } ≥ L 2 W ( h / L 2 ) − O B ( 1 ) . (30.7)

records.text: Proof. At scale L = n / h , the row touches L B only at ( L α , n ) . The first coordinate is irrational, so there is no lattice point there. At scale T , the normalized row has height n / T and thus depth h − n T = h δ T below the supporting line. Inverting the two sides of the graph gives the displayed endpoints. Since δ / T → 0 and W ( u ) → 0 , w n ( δ ) n = T h L W ( h δ T ) → 0 . Eventually w n ( δ ) < n . The number of integers in a closed interval of width w differs from w by at most one. Such an interval contains at most one multiple of the prime n . Every other integer k gives a primitive pair ( k , n ) . Therefore the row contains at least w − 2 and at most w + 1 primitive lattice points.

records.text: One can therefore record the local statistic J n = P B , n ( n / h + h / n ) , P B , n ( T ) = # { k ∈ ℤ : gcd ⁡ ( k , n ) = 1 , ( k , n ) ∈ T B } , at prime n . records.text: The height h must also be known accurately. If h ̃ = h + e and | e | ≤ h / 2 , then the exact contact-scale error satisfies | n h ̃ − n h | = L | e | | h + e | ≤ 2 L | e | h . Resolving the window of width L − 1 therefore requires a height error small compared with h L − 2 . Using a larger window relaxes this requirement but changes the depth sampled by (30.5) and increases the background main-term increment. The local statistic is consequently complementary to a global main-term-free discrepancy diagnostic; it does not replace one. In an implemented row count, the floor and ceiling operations in (30.9) also require certified endpoint comparisons with the relevant integers, or an explicit range of possible counts when those comparisons are unresolved. Agreement at two working precisions does not certify a transcendental height or endpoint.

records.text: The count here is N X ( L ) for unoriented essential simple closed geodesics on a once-punctured torus, with the convention N X ( L ) = # { γ : ℓ γ ≤ L } . Each primitive pair ( p , q ) ∈ ℤ 2 is identified with ( − p , − q ) , so this is half the signed primitive-vector count for the corresponding norm ball. A positive trace triple satisfies x 2 + y 2 + z 2 = x y z , x , y , z > 2 , and a Farey edge replaces z by x y − z . The identification of Farey regions with simple curves and this edge relation are described in [ 112 , Sections 1–2] . For the experiment take the reduced triples ( x , y , z ) = ( 3 , 3 , 3 ) , ( x , y , z ) = ( 5 2 , 10 − 11 2 , 4 ) . (30.10) The first is the modular torus; the second is an asymmetric example. Both satisfy 2 < x ≤ y ≤ z ≤ x y / 2 .

records.text: Assign the root curves the slopes ( 1 , 0 ) , ( 0 , 1 ) , and ( 1 , 1 ) , respectively. The three open sectors between these roots enumerate every other unoriented primitive slope once by Farey mediants. In the negative-slope sector use the signed endpoints ( 1 , 0 ) , ( 0 , − 1 ) ; the other two sectors have endpoints ( 1 , 0 ) , ( 1 , 1 ) and ( 0 , 1 ) , ( 1 , 1 ) . Canonical representatives have q > 0 , with ( 1 , 0 ) as the only representative at infinity. Sector endpoints are counted only as roots. After introducing an outward trace c ≥ max ⁡ ( a , b ) > 2 , the two new traces are a c − b and b c − a , both strictly larger than c . Therefore pruning a sector when its new curve exceeds the cutoff does not omit shorter descendants. Equal traces are retained with their curve multiplicities; they are not deduplicated. The hyperbolic length associated with trace x is 2 arcosh ⁡ ( x / 2 ) .

records.text: To avoid overflow the computation uses logarithmic traces. If u a = log ⁡ a , u b = log ⁡ b , and u c = log ⁡ c , then log ⁡ ( a b − c ) = u a + u b + log ⁡ ( 1 − exp ⁡ ( u c − u a − u b ) ) . On the chosen outward edges the subtracted ratio is at most 1 / 2 , so this computation avoids catastrophic cancellation. The supplied draft describes extended-precision arithmetic for this recursion and double precision for sorting the resulting lengths. That reported implementation was not included in the supplied materials. Both maintained replacement calculations below use binary64 logarithmic recursion, with separate multiprecision trace checks. Neither provides an interval certificate of every event location.

records.source: 30 Diagnosing the sharp remainder without fitting its main term
records.title: 30.8 A recent qualification of irrational flatness
records.text: Doan–Li–Nguyen’s preprint [ 113 ] , version 3 dated 9 October 2026, states a Diophantine refinement of the irrational flatness statement. Its Theorem 4.7 on page 23 states that infinite graph-flatness holds precisely when the exponential rational-approximation exponent vanishes; superexponentially approximable irrational directions can have graph-flatness order only one. In slope coordinates the relevant vanishing criterion is limsup ⁡ j ( log ⁡ q j + 1 ) / q j = 0 , where q j are continued-fraction denominators; Lemma 4.8 on pages 25–26 specifies the slope-coordinate normalization. The proposed local convexity mechanism is that a nearby rational corner can remain visible at a much smaller spatial scale than its exponentially small angle.

The preprint also continues to list the McShane–Rivin O X ( L log ⁡ L ) bound as the cumulative counting benchmark; its multiplicity estimate concerns exact length levels, a different question.

Put A B ( u ) = # ( u B ∩ ( ℤ 2 \ { 0 } ) ) , Δ B ( u ) = A B ( u ) − a B u 2 , a B = Area ⁡ ( B ) , and write P B ( L ) = # ( L B ∩ ℤ p r i m 2 ) , E B ( L ) = P B ( L ) − a B ζ ( 2 ) L 2 . All primitive vectors are counted with their signs; an unoriented count for a centrally symmetric body is half this count. The count A B is A 0 of Section 30.1 , and Δ B is its all-point discrepancy D B . The earlier torus count A X in Section 29.1 includes the origin and uses hyperbolic length units; the conversion to the unit-shortest-vector gauge is given at the end of this section.

records.title: 31.1 A transfer estimate with both inputs explicit
records.text: There are two inputs in the primitive problem: the geometric discrepancy Δ B , and cancellation in the Möbius function. A quantitative bound for the second input does not by itself specify the first. The following elementary estimate keeps their roles separate.

records.source: 31 Arithmetic cancellation and the geometric remainder
records.title: 31.1 A transfer estimate with both inputs explicit
records.text: Proposition 31.1 (A large-divisor transfer estimate). Suppose M ( x ) := ∑ n ≤ x μ ( n ) , | M ( x ) | ≤ C x η ( x ) , where η is nonnegative and nonincreasing on [ 1 , ∞ ) . Then, for every integer 1 ≤ D ≤ L , | E B ( L ) | ≪ B , C ∑ d ≤ D | Δ B ( L / d ) | + L 2 D η ( D ) . (31.1) In particular, M ( x ) ≪ x θ , with 0 ≤ θ < 1 , gives | E B ( L ) | ≪ B , θ ∑ d ≤ D | Δ B ( L / d ) | + L 2 D θ − 2 . (31.2)

records.text: Proof. Möbius inversion gives P B ( L ) = ∑ d ≤ L μ ( d ) A B ( L / d ) . Set U = L / D . Reversing the order of summation in its large-divisor part gives the exact identity ∑ d > D μ ( d ) A B ( L / d ) = ∑ m ∈ ℤ 2 \ { 0 } ∥ m ∥ B ≤ U ( M ( L ∥ m ∥ B ) − M ( D ) ) . The summands with ⌊ L / ∥ m ∥ B ⌋ = D are zero. Since A B ( u ) ≪ B u 2 for u ≥ 1 , partial summation gives ∑ m ≠ 0 ∥ m ∥ B ≤ U ∥ m ∥ B − 1 ≪ B U . Monotonicity of η therefore bounds the large-divisor part by η ( D ) ( L ∑ 0 < ∥ m ∥ B ≤ U ∥ m ∥ B − 1 + D A B ( U ) ) ≪ B L 2 D η ( D ) . The area term has the same tail bound, because partial summation yields | ∑ d > D μ ( d ) d 2 | ≪ η ( D ) D . Subtract the area main term in the small-divisor sum and bound its remaining terms absolutely. This proves the first estimate; take η ( x ) = x θ − 1 for the second. ◻

This is an established comparison result, not a claim about the best current exponent or about the flat norm balls considered here. In the opposite direction, the unconditional polygon obstruction Ω ± ( L log ⁡ log ⁡ L ) recalled in Section 30.2 persists regardless of RH. It belongs to rational polygons and is not a lower bound for strictly convex bodies. These examples show why the shape hypothesis must accompany any arithmetic hypothesis.

records.text: For a body satisfying the infinite-flatness and rational-normal hypotheses of Proposition 29.1 , the prime-row construction gives Ω ( L 1 − ε ) along an unbounded sequence for every ε > 0 . This excludes a fixed sublinear power bound for that body even if RH holds. It does not exclude O ( L ) , or even o ( L ) : the quantitative lower bound is L W ( h / L 2 ) up to constants, and W ( h / L 2 ) → 0 under strict convexity. A useful next geometric target is therefore a quantitative modulus. One possible target is Δ B ( u ) = O ( u / log ⁡ u ) , provided it is compatible with that body’s local widths. Under the same supporting-row, two-sided-graph and irrational-contact hypotheses, the row is empty at L = n / h and contributes w n ( L − 1 ) + O ( 1 ) all points at L + L − 1 . The all-point main term changes by only a B ( 2 + L − 2 ) , so max ⁡ { | Δ B ( L ) | , | Δ B ( L + L − 1 ) | } ≥ L 2 W ( h / L 2 ) − O B ( 1 ) . There is no totient density factor in this all-point estimate, and it holds for every sufficiently large integer n , without primality. Consequently the proposed target requires W ( h / L 2 ) = O ( 1 / log ⁡ L ) along these contact scales. Strict convexity and infinite flatness alone do not give that condition; the model f ( s ) = exp ⁡ [ − exp ⁡ ( | s | − β ) ] in Section 30.5 violates it. Establishing a compatible modulus for any specified McShane–Rivin ball remains a separate problem.

For a symmetric torus norm ball, let λ γ be the simple-geodesic length in the same normalization as the gauge of B . records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations

records.text: The ideal volume proposal already has an established measure-theoretic realization in (2.5) , and the tree methods described in Section 4 also compute bordered genus-zero volumes. The following fifteen questions start from the results and explicit hypotheses of the preceding chapters. They isolate further research, not claims that no related results exist. The local formulas, external theorem inputs, conditional estimates, and finite computations supporting each starting point have different roles. Resolving these questions is not a prerequisite for publishing those results with their stated limits.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.1 (Direct hyperideal integration). For four labeled geodesic boundaries of fixed positive lengths, can the domains and local density (4.5) be integrated directly, with all cell and symmetry factors, to recover the already known volume 2 π 2 + 1 2 ∑ i L i 2 in (1.2) ? Which change of variables makes the polynomiality visible in these hyperideal coordinates? The positive-boundary extension described in Section 4 uses a selected pair L 1 < L 2 to give a full-measure decomposition into tree and double-tree cells [ 99 , Theorem 3] . Equal-length volume values follow by continuity. These spine/tree cells are not identified with the hyperideal angle cells.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.2 (A usable measure on general polyhedral cells). The inverse-Poisson formula (4.7) is already a local density on a symplectic leaf. Can it be expressed in independent dihedral-angle variables in a way that makes higher-dimensional cell integrals useful? A calculation must specify the coordinate Jacobian, the fixed hyperideal boundary lengths or compact cone openings, and the geometric chamber and quotient. In the ideal case the disintegrated measure (2.4) supplies a simple model; a determinant in redundant angle coordinates does not by itself supply the replacement.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.3 (Gluing and topology). Can a polyhedral description be combined with Fenchel–Nielsen gluing to give a practical calculation for arbitrary ( g , n ) ? A proposed formula must specify both the cutting multiplicity and the full mapping-class quotient, including stabilizer weights. The twist periods in (1.1) remove the Dehn-twist ambiguity along a chosen cut; they do not make all pants-length coordinates a fundamental domain for moduli space.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.4 (Curvature corrections in period coordinates). Can the correction class Ξ μ in (8.8) be represented by an explicit first curvature correction to the WP form in the actual finite-area conformal coordinates? Equation (12.19) answers the local four-point calculation in a blown-up character chart, whose conversion to conformal coordinates is still required. How does the local density behave in a joint limit toward a balanced collision wall, where the final-chamber expansion is not uniform in the weights?

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.5 (Beyond the regular quantum degeneration). Can Proposition 15.1 , for the pole-cleared equal-label family and bounded real transition parameter, be extended uniformly over compact sets of nondegenerate Euclidean tetrahedral shapes, with a geometric description of the required scalar normalization? Can a geometric state integral in that regime produce the Thurston–Deligne–Mostow measure on the boundary-shape space? The model (11.8) specifies a classical comparison, not an identification with an existing quantum invariant. The exact Liouville identity (12.6) and the torsion limit (12.14) identify two precise boundary constructions; the auxiliary-tetrahedron obstruction and the different regimes in (12.24) explain what remains to connect them to that joint asymptotic. The finite one-screening fusion calculation in Section 13 computes the finite period and residue-sector comparison, with a logarithmic limit at balanced weights. Its direct infinite-spectral derivation uses the continuation and tail-control input (13.3) ; Section 14 fixes the quantum-group normalization, proves the rank-two obstruction, and computes the classical rank-three fold in the regular compact model. Section 15 proves the regular-family formula with its first correction using the exact integration-coordinate dictionary, pole clearing, contour and tail estimates. Its finite exact-integrand evaluations test that normalization on specified inputs. They give no uniform theorem for arbitrary shapes, unbounded transition parameter, or global gluing. The fixed-shape root-of-unity theorems in Section 11 have their own admissible label sequences; the refined Chen–Murakami prefactor has stricter sequence hypotheses than the leading volume limit. Neither supplies this joint degeneration or identifies its measure.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.6 (Uniform quantum Dehn filling). For a knot complement admitting the positive geometric optimization of Section 16 , can an exact quantum surgery representation be controlled uniformly in a complex neighborhood of complete peripheral holonomy, with a nonzero geometric contribution and bounds on all competing terms? Proposition 16.1 already fixes every classical long-slope coefficient, and (16.26) specifies the torsion check. The further issue is the analytic input of Proposition 16.2 , especially in a joint limit where the slope varies with the quantum level.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.7 (Certified realization and quantitative angle bounds). For the planar problem of Section 9 , can the finite-centering certificate and short-step iteration estimate (9.14) be combined with positive-feasibility search, controlled inexact solves, and geometric error certification into a complete complexity theorem with explicit input and precision dependence? The existing iteration estimate starts from a specified centered feasible point; the dense finite examples do not bound the cost of finding that point or certify their floating-point errors. For a three-manifold angle polytope whose maximum is interior, which additional geometric hypotheses bound its smallest angle in terms of the combinatorial input and a quantitative feasible margin? The planar Laplacian sign structure does not extend automatically to the full three-dimensional Hessian.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.8 (A continuum comparison of second variations). Can a family of refined polyhedral functionals, with specified geometric convergence and normalization, have a second-variation limit related to a WP potential? The exact cotangent identity, Schur complement, and Gaussian determinant in Section 9 provide discrete objects for such a comparison, with the stated boundary grounding or quotient by constants. Control of their refinement limits and an explicit identification of the target metric are still required; finite determinant identities supply neither.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.9 (Continuation of a coefficient Laplace transform). For a fixed nonempty multicurve on the closed surface of Section 23 , does D C ( s ) admit a meromorphic continuation beyond the proved half-plane ℜ s > 1 ? The kernel in (23.13) is e − s L . A proof must control coefficient extraction in a suitable topology on the continued character-valued expression: extraction is not bounded for the uniform norm on unitary characters. Pointwise continuation of twisted Selberg functions does not justify that step.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.10 (Control of the globally filtered remainder). Proposition 25.1 gives a bounded global cancellation of every one-crossing primitive and all its iterates. Can the signed residual ℛ X in (25.6) be estimated with constants controlled by the geometry of X ? The exact obstruction (25.7) rules out a perfect selector in the specified class of fixed linear functionals. Length-dependent cancellation or the nonlinear diagonal extraction in (25.10) retains information that such a selector discards. The latter is an exact length-valued construction, whose quantitative stability under approximation remains an additional task.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.11 (Effective selection of connected supports). Can the signed coefficient relations produce the smoothed estimate (24.22) with specified η , m and geometric constants? The elementary lattice remainder, the stable finite support projection (24.19) , and the constructive isolation estimate are available. The global one-crossing filter and the length-valued Euler product now provide concrete aggregate objects. An estimate for the higher-intersection residual or for the nonlinear first-atom extraction, uniform over the growing family of supports and strong enough to yield a counting saving, remains to be proved. Fixed-coefficient isolation does not supply this aggregate estimate.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.12 (From weighted curve counts to mixing). Can the filling-pair coefficient construction of Section 27 produce a norm-controlled estimate for the weighted orbit kernel (27.6) without assuming mixing? Proposition 27.2 gives the exact unfolding with the reciprocal polar Jacobian. Under the assumed estimate for terminal tests H G = ( h + V ) G , with F ∈ L 2 ( μ ) , G ∈ Dom ⁡ ( V ) and 0 < δ ≤ h , Theorem 27.4 preserves the counting exponent δ . A bound for one endpoint test alone has the weaker de-averaging conclusion of Theorem 27.3 . The norm-controlled two-endpoint estimate, its Jacobian weights, and the noncompact tail remain to be established by this coefficient route for the principal-stratum kernel; a scalar area or length count is insufficient. Section 28 settles the separate affine return estimate on the nonsquare ( 2 , 2 ) stratum, and Section 29 gives selected primitive-arc coefficient observables with uniform geometric norms. Can their class be enlarged to control the full two-endpoint kernel, with quantitative stability of the nonlinear coefficient extraction and passage from auxiliary hyperbolic lengths to area on the simultaneous mapping-class quotient? Can the calculation be extended beyond the marked-torus locus with its distinct invariant measure?

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.13 (The sharp norm-ball remainder). Can the qualitative o X ( L log ⁡ L ) remainder of Proposition 30.1 be made effective through a decay modulus satisfying (30.2) , or through cancellation in (30.1) ? The inverse-flatness formula (30.7) quantifies a local lower obstruction, while (30.3) gives a test independent of the leading coefficient. Determining whether the primitive remainder is O X ( L ) , or has an unbounded slowly varying factor, remains open here. Section 31 makes the two inputs explicit: Δ B ( u ) = O ( u / log ⁡ u ) together with any fixed Mertens power saving gives O X ( L ) , whereas an integrable geometric modulus and the prime number theorem already give o X ( L ) . The all-point target is itself conditional on compatibility with the local geometry: under the supporting-row hypotheses of Proposition 30.2 , it requires W ( h / L 2 ) = O ( 1 / log ⁡ L ) at the contact scales L = n / h . The double-exponential model in Section 30.5 violates that necessary condition. No such supporting configuration or compatible modulus is established for the two computed tori. The maintained length- 8192 campaign evaluates the finite diagnostic (31.9) in hyperbolic length units; the unit-shortest-vector gauge requires rescaling by the systole. It reproduces the displayed counts and block values, but the original precision and sensitivity archive remains unrecovered. Its new sampled precision checks and conditional sensitivity envelopes must retain their own provenance. Neither a finite range nor an assumed arithmetic saving determines the missing geometric modulus.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.14 (Beyond closure operations). Which positive constant series have a geometric partition or a useful functional equation behind them? The figure-eight kernel (18.7) and the twist kernel (20.12) provide two concrete models. Their different index sets suggest separating global curve identities from identities for a distinguished twist orbit.

records.source: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.title: 32 Questions suggested by the calculations
records.text: Question 32.15 (A boundary phase-space formulation). Can the endpoint-and-direction matching relations in Section 21 be organized into an integration scheme for general filling curves? Orthogeodesic lengths give the canonical local geometry, while the endpoint phase variables retain the missing gluing information. A useful result would specify the invariant measure, matching multiplicities and convergence of both the itinerary sum and the phase-variable integrals. A cusp version must also retain the truncation convention of Section 22 ; its almost-everywhere cusp-normal-ray discussion assumes no geodesic boundary. Surfaces with geodesic boundary require the additional exiting-ray contributions.

Its local trace, twist, cusp and quantum formulas retain the finite scope of the named groups. The torus campaign adds finite length and event data. These computations are mapped to the questions in book/claims/section32-appendixb.json , with their result paths and limits. They do not implement direct general-cell integration, global quantum gluing, a stable infinite coefficient extractor, or an independent proof of a mixing or lattice-remainder rate. Such extensions require their stated analytic or geometric inputs before a numerical experiment could test a well-defined instance.

records.source: A A trace-coordinate check of the WP factor
records.title: A A trace-coordinate check of the WP factor
records.text: A separate two-dimensional calculation is useful for checking the factor 2 in the local densities. Let A , B , C , D ∈ S L 2 ( ℝ ) satisfy A B C D = I , and set a = tr ⁡ A , b = tr ⁡ B , c = tr ⁡ C , d = tr ⁡ D , x = tr ⁡ ( A B ) , y = tr ⁡ ( A C ) , z = tr ⁡ ( B C ) . With the four peripheral traces fixed, the character surface satisfies the Fricke relation Φ ( x , y , z ) = x 2 + y 2 + z 2 + x y z − ( a b + c d ) x − ( a c + b d ) y − ( a d + b c ) z + a 2 + b 2 + c 2 + d 2 + a b c d − 4 = 0 . (A.1) This is the standard four-holed-sphere trace surface; see [ 59 ] .

records.source: A A trace-coordinate check of the WP factor
records.title: A A trace-coordinate check of the WP factor
records.text: On a chart where x = 2 cosh ⁡ ( ℓ / 2 ) > 2 , put s = sinh ⁡ ( ℓ / 2 ) and X = A B . Twisting across the A B cuff fixes A , B and conjugates C , D by exp ⁡ ( τ 2 H X ) , H X = X − ( x / 2 ) I s . The eigenvalues of H X are 1 , − 1 , so this is a displacement of length τ along the cuff axis. Differentiating y = tr ⁡ ( A C ) gives ∂ y ∂ τ = 1 2 s tr ⁡ ( A [ X , C ] ) = − Φ z 2 s . For the last equality, Cayley–Hamilton gives tr ⁡ ( A 2 B C ) = a d − z , while the two-matrix trace identity gives tr ⁡ ( A C A B ) = x y − b c + z . Their difference is a d + b c − x y − 2 z = − Φ z .

records.source: A A trace-coordinate check of the WP factor
records.title: A A trace-coordinate check of the WP factor
records.text: Since ⁡ d x = s ⁡ d ℓ and ω W P = ⁡ d ℓ ∧ ⁡ d τ , ⁡ d V W P = 2 | ⁡ d x ∧ ⁡ d y | | Φ z | . (A.2) Equivalently, on this twist chart, ⁡ d x ∧ ⁡ d y = − Φ z ⁡ d ℓ ∧ ⁡ d τ / 2 . Reversing the chosen twist direction reverses the signed form but leaves the displayed positive density unchanged. The hyperbolic application requires the smooth geometric component of the relative character surface and Φ z ≠ 0 for ( x , y ) to be coordinates. If Φ z = 0 but ∇ Φ ≠ 0 , another pair can be chosen; if all three partial derivatives vanish, the character surface is singular and this inversion argument does not supply a chart. In particular, arbitrary real solutions of Φ = 0 are not automatically holonomies of four-holed spheres. The formula is local on the marked character surface and does not describe a global mapping-class fundamental domain.

records.source: B Conventions at a glance
records.title: B Conventions at a glance
records.text: Source conventions. The local form scale is fixed by (1.1) and the raw Beltrami pairing in Section 1 . Ineffective stabilizer weights are a separate operation. Penner’s logarithmic triangle form is used with the ordered-endpoint conversion from Mondello in Section 3 ; the direct tetrahedral integral (3.5) and trace density (A.2) give independent normalization checks within the monograph. The Delaunay-form constants of [ 50 , Sections 3.2.3–3.2.4] are therefore not imported unchanged into (3.1) . The metric-map formula (2.5) uses Budd’s disintegrated measure and label-and-orientation-preserving automorphism weights [ 48 , Section 1.1 and Corollary 2] . The ledger book/claims/section32-appendixb.json records inherited source-statement audits, current convention dependencies, and finite computational support. It does not claim a new complete review of the external proofs.
